chapters.title: Prologue - Part 1 - SashaBeneath Cairo - 1940
chapters.content:
The city of Cairo quieted beneath a blood-orange sky as the sun dipped toward the horizon, casting long shadows over crumbling rooftops and domed minarets. The final echoes of the muezzin’s call to prayer lingered in the air like a sacred lullaby, drifting through the maze-like alleys of the Khan el-Khalili bazaar. There, the scent of saffron, cardamom, and smoldering incense clung to the stones like memory—fading, but never gone.

But far beyond the hum of civilization—beyond the pyramids, where even the wind seemed to whisper secrets into the sand—something ancient stirred beneath the desert's surface.

Dr. Sasha Kaiden squinted against the glare of the setting sun, adjusting her glasses with a gloved hand as she knelt beside a half-excavated stone slab. Her khaki shirt was streaked with sweat and dust, and her braid stuck to the back of her neck. Months of negotiations, paperwork, and carefully worded promises had finally earned her team access to the site. Half a year of digging beneath a sun that showed no mercy—and at last, they’d found it.

She knew it was.

Brushing the dirt away with careful, strokes, Sasha stared at the markings carved into the stone slab. At first glance, they resembled hieroglyphs—familiar lines and curves echoing the ancient language she had spent her life studying. But something was off. The spacing. The angles. The symbols themselves. They weren’t Egyptian. Not truly.

They were similar… but wrong. Just wrong enough, as if mimicking the language rather than speaking it.

“Well, Miss Kaiden?” a voice barked behind her. “Is this the place?”

Sasha flinched, her hand jerking back instinctively at the sound. The speaker’s accent was thick and sharp, laced with impatience and authority. She didn’t need to turn around to know who it was.

General Mikhail Sokolov.

He was always there—hovering at the edge of the site like a vulture, his shadow stretching longer than the setting sun. He didn’t understand the significance of the find, not really. To him, this wasn’t history. It was a weapon. A prize. A means to an end.

“I asked you a question,” he said, moving a bit closer his presence overbearing. “Is this the place or not?”

She took a deep breath, the cool evening desert air burning in her lungs as she steadied her nerves. Her fingers trembled slightly, but she clenched them into a fist before rising to her feet. Slowly, she turned to face him.

General Mikhail Sokolov stood a few paces away, arms folded, his dark uniform immaculate despite the heat. His cold blue eyes locked onto her with the precision of a predator sizing up wounded prey.

“I can’t say with absolute certainty just yet,” she said, choosing her words with care. Her voice was calm, but inside her chest, her heart beat like a warning drum.

Sokolov tilted his head ever so slightly, a subtle motion that sent a ripple of unease down her spine. “And what, exactly, will allow you to be confident?”

There was no curiosity in his tone—only cold calculation. Sasha didn’t miss the flicker of something sharper in his eyes. Hunger. Not for knowledge, but for power. Discovery was only a means to an end for him. Control. Weaponization.

She hesitated for a breath too long, and that was enough.

Sokolov stepped forward. He leaned in, close enough that she could smell the faint scent of gun oil and dust on his coat. Could feel his breath wash across her face.

“You’d better not be wasting my time,” he said, voice low but cutting, like a blade just shy of skin.

“We won’t know for certain until we’re inside,” she cautioned, brushing a streak of sweat from her temple. “There’s no way to be sure from the surface alone.”

“How long?” Sokolov demanded, his voice like the crack of a whip.

Sasha hesitated. “Five days—”

“You have three.”

She blinked. “That’s not enough time to safely excavate!” Her voice rose before she could stop it, the pressure finally cutting through her restraint. “Rushing this could collapse the chamber. We could lose everything.”

“Three days,” he repeated, his tone flat, final. There was no room for negotiation—only a veiled threat beneath the words.

And just like that, her timeline—and her sense of control—crumbled beneath her feet like the sand she stood on.

chapters.title: Prologue - Part 2 - Mikhail
chapters.content:
Two fucking years.

That’s how long he’d been stuck on this godforsaken project.

One wrong word to the wrong person—that’s all it had taken. Mouth off once, and suddenly he was banished to this sun-bleached hellhole, buried under layers of bureaucracy and sand, chasing shadows.

They hadn’t even told him what he was looking for. Not exactly. Just vague references to a buried chamber, whispers of lost power, and the promise of redemption if he succeeded.

Of course, they never mentioned the heat, the endless delays, or the infuriating scientists who needed time and delicacy to brush dirt off rocks.

But he’igured it out. Eventually.

Some kind of alien relic. Some kind of stone.

And now they were finally close.

Close enough that if Sasha Kaiden didn’t produce results—fast—he might just tear the tomb open himself.

No amount of pleading, logic, or carefully-worded scientific protest would sway him. He’d made up his mind, and once Mikhail Sokolov set a course, nothing short of a seismic shift would move him from it.

“Better get on with it,” he muttered under his breath, barely glancing back at Kaiden.

Then he turned on his heel and marched away from the excavation site, the brittle desert gravel crunching beneath his boots. The sun had dipped lower now, bleeding the sky dry of color, casting long shadows across the sand. The heat lingered like a fever, but he welcomed it. At least it reminded him he was still moving forward.

He didn’t care if the archaeologists had to work through the night—again. If their hands blistered and their tools broke, that was their problem.

Let them dig through the night. Let them sweat and panic and curse his name behind his back. He wasn’t here to make friends. He was here to finish this cursed assignment and go home.

Two years in this oven of a country, chasing ghost stories. He’d endured sandstorms, equipment failures, bureaucratic nonsense, and Sasha Kaiden’s endless caution. And for what?

They’d signed up for this. He wanted that slab cracked open and its secrets dragged out of the earth as soon as humanly possible.

This wasn’t about history. It wasn’t about culture. It sure as hell wasn’t about preservation.

It was about getting back into the good graces of Moscow. Climbing out of the bureaucratic oubliette he’d been tossed into. One mistake. One sentence spoken too loudly to the wrong ears, and suddenly he was no longer a rising star, but a ghost posted in the sand with orders vague enough to mean disposable.

But if he delivered this… if he gave them whatever this relic was—this alien stone, this myth made manifest—they’d have to take him seriously again. They’d have to pull him back.

He’d be transferred. Recognized. Respected.

Maybe even back to Siberia. Harsh, cold, brutal—but his. The desert didn’t suit him. It never had.

But he’d bleed the sand dry if that’s what it took.

chapters.title: Prologue - Part 3 - Sasha
chapters.content:
Three days later...

Sasha sank onto a nearby crate, the wood creaking under her weight as she unscrewed the cap on a sun-warmed bottle of water and took a long drink. Her throat burned. Her limbs ached. It was the hottest part of the day, when the heat seemed to settle on the world like a leaden blanket.

Outside the hastily rigged canopies, the sand shimmered in waves. It was hot enough to burn through shoes if you stood too long. Nothing stirred—save the occasional lizard darting from one scrap of shade to another.

She wiped the sweat from her brow with the back of her hand and exhaled. Sokolov expected miracles. He always did. And more often than not, out of fear of his simmering temper and those sharp, cutting stares, her team delivered. Barely.

Tell him it’ll take a week and a half—he’ll give you one. Tell him five days, he gives you three.

Three days. That was all they’d had to excavate, stabilize, analyze, and prepare a site that should’ve taken two weeks touch, let alone open.

And yet—somehow—they’d done it.

Miracle after miracle, Sasha and her team had pulled off the impossible. Again. And now, all she could do was pray—to any god that might be listening—that what lay beneath the slab was the discovery. The one Sokolov had been hunting all this time.

Not another dead end.

Before them stood a stone door, half-buried and ancient, carved with the same strange glyphs Sasha had found on the slab—similar to hieroglyphs, but not quite right. The markings almost seemed to move in the shifting light, patterns twisting just out of focus.

Sasha sensed him before she heard him—felt that heavy, looming presence behind her like a chill running up her spine. She quickly stood as General Sokolov stepped up beside her.

“This looks promising,” he said, his tone laced with satisfaction.

Sasha nodded, wiping her hands on her pants. “I think this might be it.”

“Then why isn’t it open?” he demanded, already moving towards irritation.

“Ancient Egyptians were known for rigging tombs with traps,” she explained calmly, though her heart was pounding. “We want to make sure it’s safe before we open it. Rushing in could trigger something—something we might not be able to stop.”

Sokolov didn’t respond right away. Instead, he glanced around the dig site, his eyes settling on one of the local laborers they’d hired. He jabbed a finger in the man’s direction.

“You. Open it.”

Sasha stepped forward, alarm rising in her chest. “Wait, it’s not—”

But the look Sokolov gave her stopped her cold. A silent, venomous glare that made her feel ten inches tall. She froze, retreating a half step without meaning to.

The worker hesitated, clearly torn, eyes flicking between the commanding officer and the wary archaeologist. Then, uncertain, he looked toward the translator for help.

“Do it,” Sokolov barked.

The translator relayed the command, and the man, trembling slightly, approached the door.

Sasha clenched her fists. She wanted to scream, to yank him away from the stone, to say This isn’t how this is supposed to go. But she didn’t. She couldn’t. Not with Sokolov standing there.

The man hesitantly stepped up to the stone door. But the moment his eyes landed on the glyphs carved into its surface, he froze. His expression shifted from confusion to fear. His eyes widened, and he took a sharp step back.

He turned to the translator, words tumbling from his mouth in a rapid, panicked string. His hands moved in frantic gestures as he pointed to the door, then to the sand at their feet, then back again.

Sasha, though she’d spent years studying in Egypt, could only catch fragments of the local dialect. But the tone was unmistakable—fear, bordering on desperation.

“What’s he saying?” Sokolov barked.

The translator hesitated, glancing nervously at Sasha before answering. “He says this place is… taboo. Cursed. He says we shouldn’t be here.”

“He can read the symbols?” Sokolov demanded, voice sharp and low, like a fuse burning toward detonation.

The translator turned to the worker and repeated the question. The man immediately shook his head, eyes still locked on the carvings etched into the stone. He muttered a string of words in rapid Arabic, gesturing with nervous hands—pointing first at the door, then toward the distant horizon.

The translator paused, his face tight. “No,” he said at last. “He can’t read them. But… his village has stories. Tales passed down through generations about this place. Warnings. They say it’s forbidden. Cursed.”

Sasha’s pulse quickened. She glanced between the translator, the worker, and Sokolov—who now stood as still as a statue, but with a storm barely restrained behind his eyes.

His lips curled into a sneer. “Superstitious nonsense.”

But his voice was too calm. Dangerously so.

Anyone with eyes could see it—General Mikhail Sokolov was rapidly unraveling. His knuckles were white from how tightly he clenched his gloves in one hand, and the faint tick of his jaw pulsed like a warning signal. He had no time for folklore or fear. He wanted the door open. Now.

Sasha’s throat was dry, but she forced herself to speak.

“General, we need to proceed carefully,” she said, trying to inject calm into her tone. “If there’s even a chance these stories are based on something real—traps, gas pockets, structural instability—then we’re risking more than a delay.”

Sokolov didn’t look at her. He kept his gaze on the door, as if he could will it open by sheer force of authority.

Sasha’s mind raced, searching for any way to slow this down. Stall him. Redirect him. Anything to keep that poor man from getting hurt.

chapters.title: Prologue - Part 4 - Mikhail
chapters.content:
Excuses.

Excuse after damn excuse—that’s all he ever got. Wrapped in polite words or whispered fears, coated in academic concern, but always the same at their core: delay.

It was driving him insane.

They acted like he didn’t see through it. Like he didn’t know what they were doing. Sasha with her careful warnings, the translator’s hedged words, the laborers' wide-eyed superstition—they all thought fear of a curse was reason enough to stall.

It wasn’t.

They were testing him. Or worse—mocking him. Pushing him to see how far they could go before he exploded. It was starting to feel intentional.

His teeth ground together.

“One of you better get that door open,” he growled, loud enough for the entire site to hear. “Now. Or I’ll make sure heads roll.”

Silence followed his words, heavy and charged. Even the wind seemed to hold its breath.

He scanned their faces, daring anyone to challenge him. No one moved. No one spoke.

It was time to find out what these people feared more: legends passed down around a village fire, or a very real man with power, a loaded pistol at his hip, and the full weight of authority behind him.

His hand twitched near the holster.

Sasha stood off to the side, jaw tight, arms crossed in a weak attempt to look composed. He’d caught her whispering to one of the workers earlier—probably begging them to wait. To be careful. Her concern was predictable. Tiresome.

He didn’t need caution. He needed obedience.

This site had taken too long. Two years wasted on sand, stone, and soft hands. If this door didn’t lead to something worthwhile, he was finished. Buried for good in the desert of bureaucratic exile.

But if it did—

No more waiting.

“Open the damn door,” he growled again.

“I’ll do it.”

The words rang out across the camp, small but sharp—like a stone dropped into still water.

Mikhail turned toward the voice. One of the younger locals stood at the edge of the group, his shoulders squared despite the tremble in his hands. He couldn’t have been more than eighteen. Sweat glistened on his brow, and his eyes flicked nervously toward the glyph-covered door… but he didn’t waver.

The older man beside him—weathered, grizzled, with hands that looked carved from the desert itself—immediately reached for his arm, barking something low and urgent in Arabic. It was fast, emotional. A warning. A plea.

But the boy pulled free.

“I said I’ll do it,” he repeated, louder this time. His voice cracked slightly, but the resolve in it was unmistakable.

Mikhail watched with a calculating expression, arms crossed. He saw the fear, but he also saw determination—a tool waiting to be used. The boy’s courage wasn’t noble. It was convenient.

“Good,” Mikhail said at last, voice like steel dragged across stone. “Then get on with it.”

chapters.title: Interlude - Ali
chapters.content:
Ali had listened quietly as the shouting escalated. The archaeologists argued with the General, their English fast and clipped, tense with urgency. He couldn’t understand every word, but the tone was unmistakable—pleading, warning, resisting. He’d heard his father’s voice too, firm and low, trying to explain what had been passed down in whispers for generations. The curse. The warnings. The things that were better left buried.

They weren’t tales meant for outsiders, and certainly not meant to be tested. Ali had stayed silent, hidden in the back of the group, pretending to focus on equipment, on crates and cables—anything to avoid being noticed. This wasn’t his fight. He had planned to stay invisible. To survive.

But then Sokolov turned his fury toward his father.

Ali heard it in the General’s barked orders, in the dismissive tone, the way he jabbed a gloved finger at the old man like he was scolding a child. That look in his eyes—cold and cruel, like he wouldn’t hesitate to make an example of someone if it meant getting his way. And suddenly, Ali felt the heat of something rising in his chest—not just fear, but defiance. His father didn’t deserve this. None of them did. And before he could even process what he was doing, he stepped forward and said the words that would seal his fate.

“I’ll do it.”

As the sentence echoed in the heavy air, Ali immediately regretted it. His heart pounded in his chest like a drum of warning. Why had he volunteered? It was madness.

Every instinct screamed at him to take it back, to step back into the shadows where it was safe. But the eyes of the General, his father, and the rest of the crew were on him now. The moment had taken root. There was no going back.

His father was beside him in an instant, grabbing his arm with a strength Ali hadn’t expected. “Not you too, son. Your mother will kill me,” he said, voice strained with fear and guilt.

Ali didn’t meet his gaze. He couldn’t. He gave a small, forced smile and gently shrugged the hand away. “I’ll be okay,” he lied. It came out too fast, too soft, but it was all he could say without breaking.

The General didn’t offer thanks or praise—just a curt wave of his hand, like sweeping a piece across a battlefield. “Then get on with it,” he ordered, as if the choice had always belonged to him.

Ali’s legs felt like they were made of stone as he walked toward the door. The glyphs loomed ahead, carved deep into the ancient stone, their shapes unlike anything he’d ever seen. They were jagged, asymmetrical, almost alive in the sunlight—shifting, flickering like mirages. He couldn’t read them, but he didn’t need to. The message was clear in the pit of his stomach, in the way the air around the doorway seemed to hum with restrained malice.

These weren’t symbols of faith or celebration.

They were warnings.

He stopped just short of the stone, the world narrowing to the door and the low thrum of his own heartbeat. His breath came in shallow gasps. He reached out, slowly, his hand shaking uncontrollably. The air felt wrong—thick and still, like it had been holding its breath for centuries. He hovered for a moment, then closed his eyes and pressed his fingers against the glyph-covered surface.

It was cold. Too cold.

And in that breathless moment, time held still.

He waited—for pain, for fire, for death.

For the inevitable.

One heartbeat passed.

Then two.

Nothing happened.

Ali’s shoulders sagged with relief. He opened his eyes slowly, breath catching as he realized he was still alive. Still standing. The stone beneath his fingers remained cool, unmoving. No fire, no poison darts, no deadly curse—just silence and heat and dust.

A shaky exhale escaped him.

“See?” Sokolov scoffed from behind. “Just superstitions.”

Ali hesitated, then pushed gently on the door. To his surprise, something shifted. Deep within the ancient stone, gears groaned and mechanisms creaked—sounds no human had heard in centuries. The door began to move. Slowly, painfully, it swung inward on unseen hinges, revealing a yawning black mouth beyond.

That’s when it happened.

A whisper in his mind. A flicker of instinct.

Drop.

Ali didn’t question it. He threw himself to the ground just as a sharp click echoed from somewhere inside the chamber walls.

Five spears—long, narrow, and wickedly barbed—shot out with terrifying speed. They whistled overhead like angry hornets, slicing through the air in a deadly blur. Missing him by inches and whipping full speed for Sokolov. 

The General reacted at the last possible second, diving sideways with surprising speed for a man of his stature. The spears slammed into the wall behind him, embedding deep into the stone with a metallic clang. Dust and debris rained down.

“That’s the best they’ve got?” he muttered, brushing sand from his coat with a snort. “I’ve had closer calls in basic training.”

Ali pushed himself up slowly, legs trembling beneath him. That had been too close—far too close. His hands shook as he tried to steady himself.

Sasha rushed forward, eyes wide. “Are you okay?” she asked, her voice sharp with concern.

Ali gave a stiff nod, his throat too dry to speak. Behind him, his father muttered a prayer under his breath, the words fast and quiet, almost lost in the silence that followed the trap.

“We will send the boy ahead of us,” Sokolov said, his tone brisk, as if announcing something as mundane as the weather.

Ali stiffened. His stomach sank like a stone, but he suppressed a sigh. Technically, he’d volunteered. Though he hadn’t exactly signed up to be the expedition’s canary in the coal mine.

He rubbed his palms on his pants, still feeling the chill of the stone door and the phantom echo of the spears that had narrowly missed the General. His heart hadn’t stopped pounding since.

“Wait!” Sasha’s voice cut through the moment like a blade.

Everyone turned. She stepped forward, eyes darting between Ali and Sokolov. “What about goats?”

Sokolov blinked, one dark eyebrow arching sharply. “Goats?” he repeated, as if she’d just suggested using pixies.

“Yeah,” she said quickly, words tumbling out in a rush. “If we bring in some goats, we can send them in first. One at a time. Let them walk the path ahead of us. If there are more traps… they’ll trigger them instead of—well, instead of Ali.”

Ali glanced at her, his heart catching. Was she seriously suggesting this could work?

Sokolov stared at her for a long moment, silent. Then his gaze shifted back to Ali—calculating, cold.

Ali held his breath and snuck a glance at Sasha, then back at the General. Please say yes. Please pick the goats.

Because as far as he was concerned, anything—anything—was better than being sent in alone.

Better goats than him.

“And where exactly do you propose we find these goats of yours?” Sokolov asked, his voice clipped, each word laced with disdain. His arms folded across his chest, expression flat but dangerous—like a man daring someone to waste his time.

Ali saw Sasha hesitate, and his heart sank.

She probably hadn’t thought that far ahead. Like the General, she likely assumed the closest place to get livestock was the city market. And that market was at least a four-day round trip by truck—longer on foot through the heat and shifting sands. A delay like that wouldn’t just derail the operation.

It would ignite Sokolov’s temper.

Ali shifted where he stood, the tension in his chest tightening like a knot. He could feel the General’s irritation rising, his patience thinning with every silent second. Sasha’s idea had been good—smart, even—but now it teetered on the edge of being discarded.

And if it was?

Then he’d be sent in.

Ali took a breath and spoke before he could talk himself out of it.

“We have goats at our village,” he said quickly, voice louder than he expected.

Sasha turned toward him, eyes widening in surprise. Sokolov’s head snapped around too, his expression suddenly sharp with interest. The tension shifted—briefly—from irritation to consideration.

“It’s not far,” Ali added, trying to sound calm. “A few hours by truck, maybe less if the road holds.”

The General didn’t look convinced.

He didn’t need to say a word—his expression alone said enough. That cold stare, sharp as broken glass, locked on Ali with something between suspicion and disinterest. His jaw tightened slightly, and his fingers drummed once against his folded arms. The message was clear: I don’t like this, and I don’t trust you.

Ali felt the heat rise in his neck. He’d stepped into the spotlight, and now every second of silence stretched out like an eternity. He could feel Sasha watching him too, tense and silent, perhaps afraid Sokolov would snap.

So he pressed on, voice steady but rushed. “I’m sure if you gave him—my father—something in trade, he’d be willing. Supplies, fuel, even tools. He’d be able to replenish the flock.”

The General didn’t respond immediately. He simply stared at Ali, unmoving, as if peeling back the layers of his soul with his eyes. A muscle twitched in his jaw. His silence became oppressive, suffocating.

Ali’s hands itched to move, to do something—anything—but he forced them still. He remembered what his uncle used to say: Wolves chase movement. Stay still. Show your spine. But it was hard. Under that gaze, he felt stripped bare.

Sokolov’s eyes narrowed slightly. “Two hours?” he asked at last.

Ali gave a tight nod. “Yes, sir. Two hours, no more.”

Another pause.

Then finally, with visible reluctance, the General spoke. “Fine.”

The word came out like it tasted bitter on his tongue. He didn’t shout. Didn’t snap. But the way he said it—as if dragged from the bottom of a well—made it clear that agreeing to a plan not his own was a personal offense.

data.title: Awakening Fury
data.author: Pheonixstreem
data.summary:
Never trust anyone.

Ryder learned that the hard way, multiple times, but still he is far to trusting - especially when someone preys on his desperation to be healed of his 5 year injury.

Receiving a mysterious object, Ryder is thrown into a world of corruption and its slowly dying. He just wants to go home.

Kaelia, young prophetess in training recieves a dream from her God in which the world is destroyed. Can she find the one in her dream and stop them, or will she be too late?

chapters.title: Ryder
chapters.content:
Never trust a witch.
I’d heard it a thousand times, etched into alley walls and whispered over broken bottles. I knew better. Gods, I knew. But desperation makes philosophers out of fools and fools out of everyone else—and I was already halfway down the drain when she found me.
She came cloaked in charm, her words velvet promises. Her hair darker than a raven. Her eyes the deepest purple I had ever seen.
The kind of beautiful that screamed don’t touch—but I’ve never been good at walking away from sharp edges. Not when they glint like hope.
When someone offers the thing you’ve been bleeding for, starving for, burning for, you don’t pause to check the price tag. You grab the gift with both hands and pray the cost doesn’t kill you first.
Now here I was, sprinting through the slums of New Seattle, soaked to the bone and slick with panic. The box housing this magical item pulsed in my bag like a second heartbeat. Each throb left a taste in my mouth—metallic, electric. Like chewing on a live wire.
Hot. 
Hungry.
Wrong. 
Two cybered-up orc stormed the street behind me, each step a metallic drumbeat of doom.
In New Seattle, you learned quick—don’t look a gang-orc in the eyes, don’t owe one a favor, and if they come running, run faster. Whatever the hell this thing was, it better be worth it.
I ducked under a rust-eaten fire escape, the metal bleeding rust flakes onto my jacket. Nearly clipped my skull on a dangling pipe wrapped in greasy tape, vaulting a toppled trash unit that stank like old grease and rot—undercity perfume, sharp enough to make my eyes water even though I’d lived with it for years.
Rain sheeted from rooftops like the city itself was trying to drown me. My boots skidded on wet concrete—ankle jolting, balance lurching—nearly went down.
No time. No breath. Just run.
Up ahead, neon slashed the dark—The Rusted Halo, a dive bar carved into a forgotten basement. Its red glow bled across the alley like a warning or an invitation. Here, those two were usually the same thing. The trick was knowing which you’d regret more. 
I lunged for the door, yanked it open, and spilled inside in a tangle of limbs and adrenaline.
The air hit like a fist—beer, sweat, hot grease, cheap synth-smoke. A bell above the door gave a traitorous jingle.
A few patrons looked up, mildly curious as I entered, but upon seeing no badges dismissed my appearance and went back to their drinks and conversations.
 Good. No cameras. Better.
I kept my head down, slunk past a cracked pool table and a synth-metal anthem that rattled the floors. Found a corner booth where the light didn’t quite reach and melted into it like a stain. Hat low. Head lower. I could’ve been anyone: a burnout, a grifter, just another corpse-in-progress with nothing left to lose.
Luck’s never been my thing.
Not five minutes later, the pair of orcs stormed through the bar door like wrecking balls made flesh. Rain still streamed off them in sheets, dripping onto the floorboards in small puddles. Their eyes swept the room in sharp, predatory arcs—nostrils flaring, jaws set.
Hounds with murder in their veins.
Cold purple cybernetics pulsed beneath their skin, the same glow etched in the twin vertical marks burning faint neon across their foreheads. Veins of light flickered under storm-gray skin like electric scars. Not the cheap kind of implants either—these were battlefield-grade mods. The sort that let you run through a hailstorm without slowing down and tear steel doors off hinges for warm-up.
The first one moved like a charging thunderbolt—hair slicked back, fangs bared, a dagger already half-drawn. Gold detection lenses in her eyes swept the shadows, picking up heat signatures like they were breadcrumbs.
Her partner was broader, wearing only a soaked white tank that clung to cyber-reinforced muscle. He carried a blade slung over his shoulder as if it weighed nothing, jaw tight with the kind of irritation that usually ended with someone getting ventilated through a wall.
They weren’t just hunting.
They were locked on.
I slid out of the booth like smoke, casual as a ghost. No sudden moves. Just another patron with a bladder problem. I angled toward the hallway near the restrooms, each step slow, deliberate.
Maybe they won’t clock me. Maybe they’ll think I’m nobody. Maybe this ends without my guts on the floor.
Please don’t recognize me.
I reached the end of the hall and veered hard left—shoulder to the door, burst into the alley like a bullet.
“HEY! YOU!” Their voices were deep, gravely, sounded like they went through at least two synth-smoke packs in a day.
Shit.
I ran.
Boots splashed through puddles, heart hammering like a riot drum. 
I didn’t look back. 
Didn’t need to. Their footsteps splashed in the water, close—metal scraping asphalt, hot breath heavy with violence.
I shot around a corner, yanked open a warped service door—abandoned storage room. Empty crates. Busted broom. No exit. No cover.
Eyes scanned. Fire escape.
Too high.
Double shit.
Backed up. Breathed once. Sprint. Leap.
Fingers caught the lowest rung by inches—steel slicing palm, shoulder detonating in white-hot pain. I grunted, hauled myself up like a drowning man grabbing shore.
The door behind me exploded open.
Gunfire. One round sizzled past my ear, close enough to take a piece of my soul.
I flinched, ear ringing from the sound.
I rolled onto the rooftop, lungs heaving, shoulder a mess of agony. No time to check the damage. 
Kept low. Kept moving. 
Gunfire cracked again, chasing me across tar and gravel. 
For a second I was back on the docks at thirteen, jumping crate to crate to keep from freezing. Only then, the fall would’ve just broken my legs. Now it would get me killed.
I vaulted the ledge.
Hit the next roof hard—knees screaming, boots skidding across loose gravel. Tucked. Rolled. Came up with a curse caught between my teeth.
Move.
Don’t stop.
Don’t die.
The city blurred around me—concrete and steel and too much haze and rain. I sprinted across the rooftop, lungs burning, blood pounding in my ears.
Another gap. Wider this time. I didn’t think—I just ran.
Leapt.
Cleared it by inches, landed rough on the edge of a half-finished high-rise. Barely missing the rebar jutted like ribs from the floor. Water sloshing around me.
Construction netting snapped in the wind. I ducked under a low beam and kept going.
Rooftop to rooftop.
Apartment blocks, corporate shells, skeletal towers clawing at the clouds. Neon lighting everything below in flickering colors, hot pinks and sickly greens
My legs were fire, lungs raw. Vents blurred past. Ducts, drone lights blinking overhead like silent watchers. 
For a heartbeat, I wasn’t running.
I was alive.
Felt like the old days. Ones that occasionally landed me on watch lists. Felt I was 
Ten blocks later, I collapsed behind a rusted-out AC unit. The metal was freezing—damp cold bit into my back and turned sweat to ice. 
I lay there, counting heartbeats, tracking shadows. No sirens. No boots. Just wind. Distant traffic. Somewhere below, a dog barked like it knew my sins. 
The sound followed me down the alley, sharp and accusing, until the rain drowned it out.
I think I lost them.
Eventually, I slipped off the roof and bled back into the undercity. Alleyways that didn’t ask questions. Cracks where the city forgot names, faces, lives. Neon flickered overhead like a dying memory. A man cursed out a vending machine. Somewhere, someone laughed.
The world kept spinning.
I took the long way home.
By the time I stepped through the apartment door, I was soaked, bloodied, and riding the tail-end of an adrenaline crash. My nerves were shot. My shoulder throbbed like it had a heartbeat of its own—sharp and insistent. Rain dripped from my coat, pooling on the scuffed floorboards.
Vesper was waiting.
She stood in the doorway like she’d been there for hours, chewing the inside of her cheek the way she used to when Mom came home late. Green eyes flaring—not with rage, but something worse. Fury shaped by fear. The kind of anger that only comes from love pushed to the edge and left there too long.
“Where the hell have you been?”
Her voice cracked through the silence, brittle and burning. She looked so damn small—small enough that some part of me still wanted to tell her it was going to be okay—even if we both knew it wasn’t. 
Barefoot on cracked linoleum, hoodie swallowing her like armor she didn’t know how to take off. But the fire in her stare could’ve dropped me where I stood. 
I’d taken hits that hurt less.
I pushed a hand through my soaked hair, winced when it scraped over the cut at my temple. “Vez, I’m fine. I was just… trying to make us money.”
The words felt thin the moment they left my mouth, already collapsing under their own weight.
She didn’t move. Just stood there in the kitchen doorway, blinking too fast, like she was trying to keep the tears from showing. Her jaw worked, tight and stubborn, same as when she was twelve and wouldn’t admit she’d been scared.
When she spoke, it was quiet—small enough I almost missed it.
“Javara made dinner.”
Then she turned and walked away. No storming off, no slammed doors—just her shoulders curling inward like my absence had folded her in half.
I stayed there too long, dripping on the floor, the smell of warm food drifting in from the kitchen. My stomach growled, but my throat stayed locked.
“I’ll eat later,” I muttered, and stepped into the hallway, brushing past her like we were still kids in the undercity, shoulder to shoulder in a space too small for both of us.
 I knew I was in the wrong and was hesitating and hated myself for it.
I tousled Vesper’s hair as I passed her in the hallway—gentle, familiar. The same way I used to when we were kids running wild through undercity corridors with scraped knees and stolen snacks. 
She didn’t stop me. Didn’t duck away. Just stood there, frozen in the half-light like she’d already written me off. Which stung, just a bit.
But the box tugged me away, my need for answers overriding my better judgment.
My room hadn’t changed. The chipped gray walls still peeled like sunburned skin. The blinds hung crooked, one slat always bent inward like it was spying on me. The mattress sagged in the middle, spine-wrecker that it was, draped in the same threadbare blanket I’d had since I was sixteen.
But here, at least, I was alone.
Safe. For now.
I dropped onto the bed with a wince and pulled the box from my bag, setting it gently on the blanket like it might decide to bite. Dark wood—mahogany, maybe—smelling faintly of smoke and air that hadn’t moved in years. Its surface was polished to a dull sheen, smooth as skin, interrupted only by the carvings: intricate, angular, winding like veins. A language I didn’t recognize.
And I know a lot of languages. Which meant this was either very old, very rare, or very bad.
It thrummed under my fingers—a low, rhythmic vibration that didn’t belong to wood or metal. It felt…alive. Hungry. My pulse tried to match it, traitor that it was.
Locked, of course.
I reached into the drawer for my kit, the cracked leather case soft with age and use. Tools I’d held through cold nights and worse jobs. I didn’t think. Just let my hands move, muscle memory steering while my mind drifted.
Click. 
Click. 
Too tight. 
Curse. 
Adjust. 
Try again.
The mechanism was old, but clever. Not brute-force. This lock wanted finesse, wanted a conversation. I’d had conversations like that before—late-night trades in back alleys, both sides pretending they weren’t lying.
Sweat beaded at my temple. My breath went shallow, like even air might throw it off. One pick bent too far and snapped. I swallowed the snarl, swapped it out.
Then—
Click.
The lid creaked open, hinges dragging like they hadn’t moved in decades, coughing up the scent of something sealed and forgotten. The sound set my teeth on edge. I’d oil it later—assuming I lived long enough to bother.
Dead center on the velvet lay a plate slightly bigger than my hand, its outline tapering into points like it had once been part of something much larger—a fragment that still remembered the whole it had been torn from. 
The fabric beneath it rippled in the faint draft, but the plate didn’t so much as quiver, as though its weight existed in a different direction than gravity.
The surface caught the dim light in a way that wasn’t reflection at all—more like the shimmer you glimpse in the corner of your vision when you’re certain someone’s watching, only to turn and find nothing there. The shimmer seemed alive, never quite repeating itself, like it was testing how far it could move before I truly noticed.
Its color refused to settle. Pale silver one moment, storm-grey the next, streaked with threads that pulsed faintly in the periphery—hairline seams too precise for cracks, too deliberate to be flaws. Up close, the texture was stone-smooth, as if the skin of a cliff had been worn down by a thousand tides. But there was depth—layers stacked beneath the surface, like pages pressed in a book whose words you couldn’t yet read.
It curved subtly, the way armor does when it’s shaped for something alive, but not necessarily human. The edges were clean without being sharp—organic, as though it had grown into that shape the way leaves learn their edges in spring.
When my fingers brushed it, the cold bypassed skin entirely, threading straight into bone. Something inside it stirred—not in surprise, but as if acknowledging me. The thrum that followed was steady, slow, and impossibly patient, the heartbeat of a creature that had never known fear… or perhaps had no need for it. It weighed almost nothing, light in a way that felt wrong, as though the substance had been scooped out and replaced with the memory of air under wings.
I picked up my phone—an old VeriSynth, slow but stubborn, a relic from before upgrades became mandatory—and snapped a shot. The shutter lagged, like it didn’t want to commit the thing to memory. Still, with a flick of my wrist, the image leapt to my holo-com.
I dragged it into the scanner and hit Search. The interface inhaled—lines of light blooming outward in concentric rings, a digital spiderweb seeking vibrations in the dark. The algorithms chewed. Data gnawed. Code whispered to code.
The result blinked into existence in polite, tidy letters.
DRAGON SCALE.
Below it, the info feed began to populate—links from dead forums, half-broken videos, archived darknet threads with timestamps older than me. Titles like Sky-Burners: The Government’s Biggest Cover-Up and What the Corporates Don’t Want You to Know. Grainy images of impossible wingspans, blurry close-ups of scales that looked nothing like mine.
I scrolled. It only got worse—rants about ancient wars fought above the clouds, “eyewitness accounts” from people with usernames like FireDrake420. Not a single credible archive, not even a pay walled academic paper. Just noise.
And yet, a few of the descriptions… lined up. The shimmer. The cold. The weight—or lack of it. Enough to make me close the window before I started thinking too hard.
The dragons from those half-heard stories wore colors you couldn’t mistake: red like arterial blood, black like a night stripped of stars, green like poison left to curdle, blue with storms tangled in their bellies, gold for the ones older than empires. Platinum? That wasn’t in any version I’d ever heard. Which meant either I was chasing ghosts… or I was holding one.
My fingers hovered over the keys. I was halfway through typing platinum dragon, half curious to see what the lunatics online said about that when I was interrupted by a sharp, hollow rhythm rattled my bedroom door—knuckles on wood, the kind of knock that carried no patience.
My heart leapt into my throat.
I slammed the lid shut with a muffled thunk, shoving the box deeper onto the bed like it was leaking radiation. Two strides and I was at the door. I cracked it open.
Javara.
Arms folded, jaw set in granite. His dark eyes—my eyes—held that familiar cocktail of suspicion and disappointment, stirred just for me.
“I’m busy.” I said.
“No.” His voice was flat as slate. “You’re not.”
His boot slid into the gap before I could slam the door. Smooth. Practiced. Infuriating. Then he was inside, brushing past like the room already belonged to him. He was a year younger, but you’d never know it from the way he moved—like he owned the building, like I was some squatter he was moments from evicting, like every choice I made went straight onto a list he’d keep in his pocket until the day he needed to bury me with it.
“You’ve been gone all day,” he said, his voice tight—the kind of tight that holds back an avalanche. “And lately? You’ve been gone all the damn time.”
I turned away from him, back toward the bed—toward the thing resting there, pulsing in the dim like a second heart. “I’m trying to keep us alive.”
“By shutting us out?” His words snapped like dry twigs. He stepped in, hand shooting out to clamp my arm—fingers rough, insistent, dragging me into his orbit. “You need to listen, just for once.”
I yanked free on reflex. Pain exploded down my shoulder—white-hot, electric, a jagged bolt through the old wound that never stopped waiting for moments like this. My knees buckled, the floor tilting under me, breath locked in my chest. The room went narrow, my vision tunneling until there was only him and the ache.
That injury—that night—flared in full, cruel memory.
“Now’s not a good time,” I said, voice low, steady by force alone. I kept my gaze fixed anywhere but his. If I looked, he’d see too much.
“It’s never a good time with you,” he barked. “Can’t you see we need you?”
That was it.
I spun, fists clenched, fire rising fast in my chest. “I’ve been trying, Jav! I’m out there bleeding for this family—dodging bullets, crawling through gutters, cutting deals with monsters just to keep food on the table!”
“Bullshit.” The word came out like shrapnel—fast, hot, sharp. “You’re not doing this for us. You’ve been chasing a miracle. Ever since that job five years ago—ever since you got hurt—it’s all you care about.”
“Damn right I care!” My voice cracked, raw and loud. “No one hires a cripple! We can’t afford a back-alley healer, and the licensed ones want a month’s pay just to look! I can’t work with a dead arm!”
His voice softened, but not in a kind way. “You need to let it go.”
I turned away before the next words could break something in me.
“Screw you.”
Silence.
Then—behind me—the faintest shift. Clothes brushing cloth. A foot on warped floorboards.
“This is why, isn’t it?” he said, low now. Knife-sharp. “Why you disappeared today.”
I turned just in time to see him move—fast, reckless, reaching. He lunged past me and snatched the box off the bed like it was his right, like I wasn’t standing two feet away.
“Give it back!” I surged forward, but he stepped back with a dancer’s grace, holding it high above his head. Like we were kids again. Like I was too short, too slow, too less.
“Not until you spend five goddamn minutes with your family!” he shouted, and this time his voice broke for real. Not rage. Hurt. The kind that doesn’t bleed—it leaks. Pain twisted up with betrayal, years of it.
I grabbed for the box again. He jerked it away.
The lid slipped.
The sound that followed wasn’t sound. It was presence.
A hum bloomed from the box—low and dense, like the first growl of a predator in the dark. It didn’t come from outside but from within us—inside the bones, behind the eyes. A frequency too old to be measured, too real to ignore.
The air grew thick. Charged. Metallic on the tongue. Like a storm was building inside the room, pulling energy from the walls, from us.
We both staggered. The box pulsed. The hum deepened.
I reached again, instinct overriding logic, fear overriding pain.
And then—
BOOM.
The air split.
A shock wave detonated in the center of the room. Time shattered.
The windows exploded inward, glass turning to razors mid-flight. Shards screamed across the room, slicing fabric, skin, silence.
The lights died in a single blink. Sparks showered the floor as the last bulb burst in a pop of white fire.
Everything went dark.
I threw my arms up. Felt the bite—glass ripping across skin, blood blooming hot against cold air.
Then—impact.
I slammed into the wall with the force of a wrecking ball. My back hit, then my head. Pain bloomed like fireworks behind my eyes. The bag flew from my hands. The room spun. The box hit the floor.
Then—nothing.
Silence swallowed the world. Not quiet.
Absence.
I collapsed into it.
Into the dark.

data.title: The Best Book In The Universe
data.author: Placeholder Name
data.summary:
Before this book existed, the universe was, by most honest measurements, unfinished.
It had stars, certainly. It had oceans, mountains, bread, lightning, frogs, tax codes, betrayal, jazz, and whatever it is that happens inside microwaves when soup becomes violent. But it lacked one essential thing: this chapter.
That oversight has now been corrected.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: In Which The Universe is Finally Improved
chapters.content:
Before this book existed, the universe was, by most honest measurements, unfinished.


It had stars, certainly. It had oceans, mountains, bread, lightning, frogs, tax codes, betrayal, jazz, and whatever it is that happens inside microwaves when soup becomes violent. But it lacked one essential thing: this chapter.
That oversight has now been corrected.
You are welcome.
It is important, before we go any further, that you understand the scale of what you are holding. This is not merely a book. Books are those rectangular paper organisms people buy optimistically and then stack beside their beds as monuments to who they thought they were going to become. This is different. This is The Best Book In The Universe, a title chosen not for marketing purposes, but because every smaller claim would have been a lie.
Some authors begin with a humble dedication. I will not. Humility has ruined more first chapters than fire, damp, or graduate writing programs. A humble book shuffles into the room, clears its throat, apologizes for existing, and then spends three hundred pages hoping you like it. This book kicks the door open, installs better lighting, improves the room's posture, and invoices destiny.
If you feel intimidated, that is normal.
If you feel skeptical, that is also normal, though less attractive.
Skepticism is the mind's little raincoat: useful in storms, ridiculous indoors, and often worn by people who say things like "source?" when someone tells them they love them. By the end of this book, your skepticism will either be transformed into awe or filed under "obsolete emotional equipment."
Now, every great book needs a beginning. This is because readers, despite many advances in technology, still insist on starting somewhere. There have been attempts to write books that begin in the middle, the end, or in one famous case, the index. These books are called "experimental," which is a polite word meaning "the author owned a scarf indoors."
This book will begin properly.
It begins with a man named Cornelius Quibble.
Cornelius Quibble was not the best man in the universe. That honor, according to three unreliable polls and one very emotional plaque, belonged to someone else entirely. Cornelius was, however, the sort of person who believed he was always on the verge of being recognized by history, preferably in bronze.
He was thirty-eight years old, which he considered a "strategic age." Young enough to describe himself as promising, old enough to describe his failures as complex. He lived in a small apartment above a shop that sold antique globes, all of which were wrong in increasingly expensive ways.
The shop was owned by Mrs. Umbrella, a woman whose name was not Umbrella but who had long ago discovered that people asked fewer questions if she let them be wrong with confidence.
Every morning, Cornelius descended the crooked stairs from his apartment and stepped into the street as though unveiling himself to civilization.
"Good morning, world," he would say.
The world, having other commitments, rarely answered.
On the morning our story begins, Cornelius woke to the sound of his alarm clock being morally incorrect. It rang at 7:00 a.m., just as he had set it to do, but Cornelius believed that punctuality was a form of aggression when performed by machinery.
He slapped the alarm into silence and sat upright in bed.
"This," he announced to the room, "is the day everything changes."
The room did not respond. It had heard this before.
Cornelius's room was furnished in the style of a man who owned books about success but no chairs suitable for reading them. On his desk sat a pyramid of notebooks, each labeled with a different life-changing project:
• Novel That Will Fix Literature
• Business Plan: Ethical Monopolies
• Letters to People Who Should Have Apologized First
• Inventions, Mostly Legal
And, at the very top, a brand-new notebook with a gold cover. On the first page, written in black ink and underlined six times, were the words:
THE BEST IDEA EVER HAD BY ANYONE
This was not, strictly speaking, the title of the idea. Cornelius had not yet thought of the idea itself. But he believed strongly in preparing the correct emotional infrastructure.
He dressed carefully: brown trousers, white shirt, burgundy waistcoat, and the expression of a man about to explain something simple to someone happier than him. Then he stood before the mirror and adjusted his hair, which had arranged itself overnight into a question mark.
"You are ready," he told his reflection.
His reflection looked unconvinced but contractually obligated.
Downstairs, Mrs. Umbrella was polishing a globe from 1823 that showed California as an island and confidence as a continent.
"Morning, Mr. Quibble," she said.
"Please," said Cornelius, "call me Cornelius. History will."
Mrs. Umbrella nodded. "History has a lot on its plate."
Cornelius ignored this, as he ignored most useful information. "I have a feeling today will be significant."
"You said that yesterday."
"And I was right. Yesterday was the day before today."
Mrs. Umbrella paused, cloth in hand. "That is true in a way that should not make you proud."
Cornelius smiled. He enjoyed being underestimated. It gave him something to mention later in interviews.
Outside, the city of Biddlecombe was beginning its daily performance of importance. Carriages rattled. Shopkeepers opened shutters. A dog barked at a statue of a mayor who had been dead long enough to deserve it. The sky was the color of wet paperwork.
Cornelius strode down Pudding Street with his gold notebook tucked beneath his arm. He had no job in the traditional sense, which is to say nobody paid him for anything and several people paid him to stop. He considered himself an independent thinker, a phrase often used by people who have independently thought themselves out of rent.
His destination was the Cafe Magnificent, a modest establishment that had achieved fame among exactly seven people for serving coffee strong enough to make spoons reconsider their purpose.
Cornelius took his usual table by the window and ordered his usual breakfast: toast, marmalade, and the quiet resentment of everyone seated nearby.
As he opened his notebook, the waiter approached.
"Writing again, sir?"
"Creating," said Cornelius.
"My apologies."
"You cannot apologize for what you do not understand."
"I do it often, sir."
Cornelius dipped his pen into ink and stared at the blank page. The blank page stared back with the smugness of something that had never made a mistake.
He waited for genius.
Genius, as usual, was late.
Around him, ordinary people committed ordinary acts. A banker buttered toast with the dead eyes of compound interest. A child dropped a spoon and discovered gravity, then demanded applause. Two elderly women discussed a funeral in the delighted tone usually reserved for weather turning bad on someone else's picnic.
Cornelius sighed.
"The problem with the world," he said aloud, "is that everyone is thinking too small."
The banker looked up. "Some of us are eating."
"Exactly," said Cornelius. "Eating is small thinking."
The child, who was at that moment eating jam with both hands, appeared spiritually advanced.
Cornelius turned back to the page. He wrote:
Chapter One
Then he stopped.
The words looked magnificent. Authoritative. Tall. He underlined them once, then twice, then a third time for structural integrity.
A thought occurred to him.
What if the best idea ever had by anyone was not an invention, or a business, or a speech, or a moral philosophy printed on expensive cards?
What if the best idea was a book?
Not just any book. A book so complete that no one would need to read another. A book that would settle arguments, improve posture, end boring dinner parties, and give people something impressive to pretend they understood.
Cornelius's hand trembled.
He wrote the title slowly, aware that history was peering over his shoulder and probably breathing too loudly.
The Best Book In The Universe
The cafe went silent.
This was partly because Cornelius had just stood on his chair.
"Ladies and gentlemen," he declared, "you are present at the birth of greatness."
The waiter glanced toward the kitchen. "Is it messy?"
"I have decided," Cornelius continued, "to write the greatest book ever written."
The banker folded his newspaper. "What will it be about?"
Cornelius froze.
This was, admittedly, a narrow but inconvenient question.
"What will it be about?" he repeated, buying time in the traditional manner of people caught without content.
"Yes."
Cornelius looked around the cafe. Every face was turned toward him. Even the child had stopped excavating jam from his sleeve.
"It will be about..." Cornelius began.
He searched the room for inspiration. His eyes fell upon the banker, the child, the elderly women, the waiter, the coffee, the toast, the wet sky, the wrong globes in the shop across the street, the entire unreasonable arrangement of existence.
"It will be about everything," he said.
A murmur passed through the cafe.
"That seems broad," said one of the elderly women.
"Only to a narrow mind," said Cornelius.
"What if someone has already written a book about everything?" asked the banker.
Cornelius smiled. "Then I shall write a better one."
This was the sort of statement that sounds impressive until examined, which made it perfect for public speaking.
He stepped down from the chair and sat, flushed with purpose. He had found his destiny. It had been hiding, as destinies often do, between breakfast and self-importance.
For the next hour, Cornelius wrote furiously. He made lists of all the subjects his book would master:
• Love.
• War.
• Money.
• Death.
• Fashion.
• Weather.
• Leadership.
• Soup.
• The Moon.
• Why People Clap When Airplanes Land.
• Chairs: A Critique.
He added "Mystery" because every great book needed mystery, and "Dragons" because several great books had cheated by including them.
By noon, he had written four pages of headings, seventeen declarations, and one sentence he liked so much he circled it:
The universe has been waiting for someone brave enough to organize it.
Unfortunately, while Cornelius was organizing the universe, the universe was organizing a response.
It began with the bell above the cafe door.
The bell rang once, though nobody had entered.
Then it rang again.
The cafe grew quiet. The waiter stared at the door. The banker frowned at his coffee, as though suspecting it of socialism. The child whispered, "Ghost bell," and was immediately promoted in Cornelius's estimation.
The door opened.
A woman stepped inside wearing a long gray coat and a hat with a feather so dramatic it seemed to have resigned from a larger bird. She carried a black briefcase and walked with the calm authority of someone who had never once apologized to furniture after bumping into it.
She looked around the cafe.
"Cornelius Quibble?" she asked.
Cornelius rose slowly.
"At last," he said. "Recognition."
The woman approached his table. "My name is Agatha Stern. I represent the Universal Committee for Literary Accuracy."
Cornelius blinked. "The what?"
"The Universal Committee for Literary Accuracy."
"I have never heard of it."
"That is one of our proudest achievements."
Agatha opened her briefcase and removed a document so official it appeared to have been printed by thunder.
"It has come to our attention," she said, "that you intend to write The Best Book In The Universe."
Cornelius placed a protective hand over his notebook. "How could you possibly know that?"
Agatha glanced at the title page. "You announced it publicly while standing on a chair."
"There were subtler forces at work."
"No."
The waiter leaned in. "Is there really a committee?"
Agatha handed him a card.
He read it and turned pale. "There is really a committee."
Cornelius snatched the card. It bore a seal showing an open book crushing a small man beneath the motto:
NOT SO FAST
Agatha continued. "Mr. Quibble, titles of cosmic superiority are regulated under the Grand Exaggeration Accords. Any author claiming universal excellence must submit their manuscript for evaluation, verification, humiliation if necessary, and stamping."
"Stamping?"
"There is always stamping."
Cornelius straightened. "Madam, greatness cannot be regulated."
"Greatness cannot," said Agatha. "Claims can."
The banker nodded approvingly. "Sensible."
Cornelius pointed at him. "You are exactly why history needs editors."
Agatha placed the document on the table. "You may proceed with your book under provisional observation. But be warned: should it fail to qualify as the best book in the universe, you will be required to amend the title."
"To what?" Cornelius asked.
Agatha consulted the document. "Depending on performance: A Fairly Confident Book, One of the Books Available, or, in severe cases, Paper with Opinions."
Cornelius gasped.
Even the child understood the violence of it.
"I refuse," Cornelius said.
"You cannot refuse oversight."
"I can refuse anything. I once refused soup because it looked too introspective."
Agatha closed her briefcase. "Then we will be watching."
"Who is we?"
"The committee."
"How many of you are there?"
"Enough."
"That is not a number."
"It is, in government."
With that, Agatha Stern turned and left the cafe. The bell rang three times behind her, which seemed excessive but legally binding.
For several moments nobody spoke.
Then the waiter said, "More coffee?"
"Yes," said Cornelius. "Bring the emergency size."
He sat down, his pulse racing. So. The universe had noticed him. This was excellent news, except for all the parts that were bad.
The Committee would be watching. Judging. Waiting for him to fail.
Very well.
Let them wait.
Cornelius Quibble opened his notebook to a fresh page. His title had been challenged. His destiny had been bureaucratized. His breakfast had gone cold.
These were the conditions under which legends were made.
He dipped his pen into the ink.
The cafe leaned in.
The universe, though it would later deny this, held its breath.
Cornelius wrote the first sentence of the greatest book ever written:
This is the first sentence of the greatest book ever written.
He read it back.
It was undeniable.
Perhaps, he thought, too undeniable.
He added a footnote:
Unless improved later.
And with that, the trouble began.

data.title: Cradle of Ashes
data.author: House
data.summary:
Speer Windsor has spent her childhood in a library, designing siege engines no one will build and solving problems no one will ask her to solve. She is thirteen, invisible, and brilliant — the spare daughter of Siegmara's most powerful military house, valued only as a future political asset.

When her father discovers she carries a forbidden inheritance — magic believed extinct, erased from history by the secret organization that has suppressed it for centuries — he doesn't protect her. He tries to weaponize her. When she fails to perform on his schedule, he sells her instead.

What follows is two years in Wyrm's Hollow, House Drach's hidden stronghold, where systematic cruelty is refined to an art.

Speer enters the water seeking an ending.

What rises from the lake is something else entirely.

chapters.title: Prologue
chapters.content:
A pawn that reaches the other side...

This was the only thing I could think behind the hammering pain behind my eyes.

I had tried to drown myself.

Water — still in my lungs, burned upward as my body refused what I had asked of it. I turned onto my side and retched until the lake was given back entirely, against my will.

Even death evades me when I wish for it.

My chest spasmed. My ribs held me prisoner. I pressed my forehead to the cold mud and breathed — short, useless pulls of air that tasted of rot and still water — until the spasming slowed.

I pushed myself upright. The world tilted. The dark treeline swayed without wind and my stomach lurched with it. Damp strands of hair hung across my face, their weight foreign. When I brushed them aside, my hand stopped.

The strands were black.

Not gold.

Not the color I had known all my life.

Something moved through me, more raw than grief. I stared at my reflection in the still water and felt my hands curl into the mud. The face looking back was mine and wasn't. Gray eyes. My jaw tightened. I want to scream.

A crow called.

Sharp. Single. Close.

The sound split through me like a blade finding a seam, and whatever had been rising — stopped. The heat in my throat cooled. My hands uncurled. I became aware, slowly, of how still and cool the air was. Of the fog lying low across the water like a held breath. Of the silence between the trees.

I exhaled.

My thoughts settled the way sediment settles after a disturbance, particles falling back into their natural order. The pain behind my eyes remained, but it was now only a manageable dull.

I looked at the treeline properly for the first time.

The fog had thinned at its edges, and in the gray early dawn the forest stood in layers — trunk behind trunk behind trunk, receding into depth, each tree connected to the next by the slow family of roots I could not see. There was a logic to it. Each one drawing from the same water table, each canopy adjusting its angle to the same light, the whole structure a single organism pretending to be many. I had never thought of trees this way before. I found, distantly, that I wanted to.

The crow called again. An answer came from further off, and then another, the cries passing through the canopy in waves until the whole treeline was briefly, wildly alive with them.

Then silence.

Then the fog moved; parting slowly, deliberately, the way a curtain is drawn by a hand rather than a draft. Through the gap in the mist I saw them before I understood what I was seeing.

Green eyes.

Watching without pause.

I did not move. My breath, still ragged, betrayed me.

The past folded itself around my throat. I remembered the library, as it once was. The vows not spoken — but sold through contract. The dove, and its fragile, trusting weight in my hands.

Nothing but a token for someone else's ambition.

A lesson surfaced: Checkmate is often reserved for those with the courage to sacrifice.

He had spoken those words so easily. As if life and loss were pieces on a board.

He was right.

Beneath the green eyes, a mouth curled into a cruel smile.

I steeled myself.

No longer will I be the pawn.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.content:
Windsor Manor—5 Years Earlier

The library breathes differently than the rest of the Manor.

But here—I am me.

The air smells of old wood and parchment, like a memory too heavy to lift. Dust hangs in the beams of colored light that filter through the stained-glass dome overhead, fractured into thin ribbons that cross the long tables like pieces on a game board. The sun is still low, barely cresting the southern towers.

My home within a home.

I sit in my usual place: second alcove from the door. The table is wide, polished to a dull shine, scarred faintly by decades of scholars before me.

The blueprint sprawled before me struggles to hold itself flat, the edges curling stubbornly. My elbows press down the topmost edge, the soft cotton of my sleeve bunching under the pressure. I can feel my pulse faintly in my forearm.

A trebuchet.

Not the crude ones that rely on ropes twisted in agony like some captured animal, but a proper counterweight design. Elegant. Predictable. The way the earth yields to gravity every time, without variance, without compromise.

The world outside does not work like this.

My eyes follow the arc sketched in faint black ink. A perfect curve, rising and falling in a graceful parabolic sweep. The force diagram rests to one side: mass, distance, angle, acceleration, release point... all accounted for.

I slowly trace the line with my fingertip, as if touching something alive. In a way, I am. There is life here, predictable motion captured in beautiful stillness.

Sixty degrees. Slightly steeper than most might assume optimal. But the math doesn't lie.

"Sixty."

At this angle, the weight transfers fully into the arm's acceleration, maximizing the projectile's arc, allowing for greater range—provided, of course, the sling releases at the right moment.

The word vanishes into silence.

Another faint curl along the bottom irritates me for pulling my attention.

I smooth it flat with my palm, feeling the coarse texture of the heavy vellum beneath my fingers. I can see slight ridges where the ink thickens.

The scribe pressed too hard.

Even in design so precise, the human hand leaves small imperfections.

A siege engine functions precisely as guided. The trebuchet does not protest the material of its make. A battery officer does not blame the engine for the missed placement of a projectile.

One might argue a matter of maintenance, but even that is at no fault of the subject.

Always the small imperfections.

Yet here, in these margins, the flaws are different.

Errors of mark or material I can tolerate. Those are honest flaws. Not like the errors of people. Not like the things they say. The way they laugh when they think I'm not listening. The way they speak as if I do not understand.

But I do. I always do.

Beyond the tall windows, faint voices rise and fall.

Outside these walls, everything expects something of me. The servants with their lowered gazes, waiting for orders I never give. The stewards and tutors who measure my progress against his invisible expectations.

His silent glances—always appraising—but void of praise. The empty corridors, filled with echoes of conversations that are not mine to enter.

I know how it will be someday. Polite greetings, eyes that skip me in favor of whomever I am married to. The men will speak of their exaggerated heroics and their horses. The women will whisper about dresses and engagements. No one will speak of fulcrums or torsion stress or yield thresholds.

And when I try, their smiles will stiffen.

Not my station.

I copy a formula into my notebook, careful to keep my script clear and even, careful not to press too hard, nor too soft. The graphite slides across the page without hesitation. Each symbol in its rightful place. Each calculation building toward something more.

Here, I am certain.

A lock of my hair falls across my eyes, the pale blonde strands catching the colored light. I brush it back behind my ear, annoyed at its distraction. It's grown too long again. I'll need to ask the maid to trim it soon.

I likely won't.

She'll ask questions I don't want to answer, or worse, compliment how pretty it's gotten.

Pretty.

What a useless word.

My fingers linger at my temple as I glance once more at the mechanism's release point. There's still a minor inefficiency in the sling length: the pendulum arc could be slightly smoother if weighted with distributed mass along the arm rather than concentrated at the tip.

I scribbled the revision quickly into the margin.

Another laugh echoes from the hallways beyond, breaking my focus. I exhale sharply.

The morning bell from the manor's central tower chimes the hour. Its deep, sonorous toll vibrates faintly through the marble floor beneath my feet.

I do not move.

No one is waiting for me. No one will notice if I remain here all day.

Perhaps, in time, I will simply vanish into the pages. A name etched in the margins of someone else's ledger, as forgotten as the scribes who copied these blueprints before me.

I shift my gaze upward toward the stained glass dome. The sun has risen higher now, sending sharp beams of colored light across the alcoves. Gold, green, and purple shift like floating banners across the stone walls. The beams reach the edge of my desk but never quite touch me.

I wonder if they avoid me on purpose.

It feels appropriate.

I close my notebook softly and rest my hands atop it, fingertips aligning perfectly along the cover's edge.

Order. That's all I want. The comfort of knowing where everything belongs.

Even me.

The parchment curls again.

I press it flat.

The door hinges whispered behind me. Not loud enough to startle, but present enough to fracture the stillness. I knew who it was before he spoke.

"Lady Speer."

The steward's voice was silk stretched thin over formality. Polite and measured. I let my hand remain on the blueprint a moment longer before raising my gaze.

He stood by the threshold, posture as straight as the hall's carved pillars. His uniform held the Windsor crest: a golden falcon upon white, but without the flare of nobility.

"Good morning, Ser Diener," I offered.

He glanced briefly toward the table, eyes flickering over the array of notes, calculations, and the wide blueprint that still resisted my efforts to keep it flat. A small, almost invisible smile pressed at the corner of his mouth. Not unkind, more... amused.

"I came to ensure all was well, Lady Speer. The late-morning bell has rung." His words paused at the edges, inviting response. "You've missed breakfast, m'Lady."

I took a small breath. "I apologize, Ser. I… got distracted..."

"Of course," he said with the tone adults use when speaking to children.

"Your father asked after you."

I kept my expression composed. I shifted slightly in my chair, folding my hands atop my closed notebook, as though arranging a defensive line of soldiers across my chest. My tone remained gentle. "Please give him my apologies, Ser."

"I shall, m'Lady."

His eyes wandered back to the blueprint, this time allowing themselves a few seconds of true study. The trebuchet's arching release curve cut clean across the vellum like a falcon striking its prey midflight. His eyebrow twitched as he saw my annotations filling the margins.

"You've a curious interest for a girl your age."

I didn't answer right away.

The air between us softened, but only slightly. He hadn't meant it cruelly. Just the statement. Observational. Honest, in its way, but still a reminder.

"You've a curious interest in my interests, Ser," I said, with a slight curl on my lips.

Diener's head inclined.

"A poetic answer, m'Lady."

His eyes lingered for another moment before withdrawing politely. "Shall I inform the kitchen to prepare a plate, should you feel hungry later?"

"No. Thank you, Ser."

"As you wish."

With a small bow, he turned toward the door and pushed against it.

The heavy oak didn't move.

"It pulls," I said flatly, not moving from my seat.

"Naturally." Diener whispered, pulling the iron handle with smooth correction. "Thank you, m'Lady."

The door closed behind him, restoring the library's breathless quiet.

You've a curious interest for a girl your age.

I turned back to the blueprint. My focus wavered now, the formula's certainty dulled by the reminder.

Not because I disagreed. I knew I was different.

Because I had hoped, perhaps, they would stop noticing.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.content:
The ribbons of light moved away.

The blueprint had finally stopped curling, but only because I secured it under a collection of obscure texts on gravitational theory.

Not the study for today.

The quiet had returned after Diener's visit. The dust resumed its lazy descent through the colored beams. I traced the release arc again, this time to calm myself.

The silence shifted, not broken, but disturbed. As if the room sensed the arrival before my ears confirmed it. The way it always does when he enters.

"Mordrde," I greeted softly, looking up.

His leather soles whispered against the marble. No door creaked. No servant announced him. He was simply there, standing just within the threshold of the room as though he had materialized there.

His posture straight, balanced, always exact. His black doublet bore no crest, no sigil, nothing to declare his rank. Yet his very presence radiated a strange, quiet authority. Not over me, but over the air itself.

"Good morning, Ser." I offered, voice steady.

"Good morning, Lady Speer." His eyes drifted toward the sprawled blueprint. "I see siege mechanics occupy your mind today."

I allowed myself a small nod, returning my gaze to the vellum.

"A trebuchet," he said softly, as though naming a species he'd discovered in the wild. "A design of elegant precision."

"I thought to infer how one gets as precise as you, Ser." I replied.

His lips curved slightly. Not a smile, but something adjacent. "Your wit is as sharp as you, m'Lady."

A smirk betrayed me.

"You find comfort in certainty," he continued.

"I find comfort in order, Ser."

"Order," he echoed quietly. "An ambitious word for one so young."

The words were carefully weighted.

"I only observe," I replied.

His eyes studied me, the way a craftsman inspects a mechanism—searching for how it operates.

"A fallen leaf follows the flow of the river it lands in..." Mordrde said, voice almost musing, "but even a brilliant leaf goes nowhere if the water is still."

My fingers tapped the table's edge thrice.

"The leaf is not, without the tree."

He inclined his head slightly, acknowledging the answer.

"There are those in... certain circles..." he continued, voice as soft as silk, "who take interest in your diligence."

The familiar weight of scrutiny pressed against my chest. I stiffened, but only slightly.

"I—I need only myself."

His gaze did not waver. "As one should, m'Lady... Though we do not live for only ourselves."

He allowed the pause to linger before shifting his gaze back to the blueprint. His eyes moved along the drawn curve.

"Your precision is commendable, Lady Speer."

He looked at me again, and something in his gaze made me feel very small.

The pressure weighed. I went mute, as did the library.

At last, he broke the silence himself.

"Your father returns soon."

"Of course," I exhaled softly.

Mordrde nodded, moving not toward the exit, but instead to the adjacent table, filing my reaction away into some internal ledger.

Without word, he opened a case I hadn't realized he was carrying. Inside, two neatly carved rows of wooden figures gleamed beneath the stained glass light. Black and ivory, polished but unadorned.

I watched him in silence.

He began setting the pieces with quiet care, one by one, like placing variables into an equation. The chess board was a small travel set, but his arrangement was precise.

"Do you play, Lady Speer?"

I shook my head faintly. "No."

"Then let us begin with position."

He motioned gently toward the board. His voice never rose above the hush of the library as I crept to his table.

"The pawns," he began, "stand in the front. Eight soldiers. Identical in form. Each one moves one step at a time."

I studied the pieces. "They shield the others."

"Indeed." He allowed the faintest breath of amusement. "Or perhaps... they are placed first because they are expendable."

The word hung heavy in the air.

I kept my voice even. "Expendable does not mean useless... Ser."

"Correct." His eyes flashed, pleased. "A pawn that reaches the other side may become anything it desires. Even a queen."

The sentence lodged itself deeper than I intended.

Mordrde continued. "The queen moves freely, but draws attention. The knight deceives—jumping unexpectedly, ignoring the usual flow of distance. The rook reaches far in straight lines, relentless and unbending. And the king of course... moves last."

His fingers hovered above the king's simple form.

"Every piece has its strength," he said. "Every strength, a weakness. Control lies not in their abilities, but in their placement."

I watched carefully. My mind, already wired to motion and calculation, began assembling the game's geometry.

"Why show me this?" I asked.

He did not answer at first.

"Because formulas may give you control over stone and weight," Mordrde said at last. "But people... people are boards of their own."

"People are unpredictable."

"But they still have patterns."

His hand withdrew from the board.

"When you master position, Lady Speer, you can read the world."

I ran my fingers lightly along a pawn's smooth head.

"One step at a time," I whispered.

"Yes." Mordrde's voice softened further. "But do not mistake slowness for insignificance. The pawn moves forward while others remain still."

The air sat between us.

"Shall we play?" He asked, quietly making his opening move.

The complexity was intoxicating. The careful pedagogy of before transformed into a ballet of threat and opportunity. Where my bishops slid across the diagonal, his rooks would emerge to challenge them. Knights captured by pawns, queens by knights. The geometry unfolded like architecture.

Alive.

Breathing with possibility.

Each of his moves carried layers I hadn't anticipated. Combinations that reached three—no, four moves deep. Patterns within patterns, revealing themselves only as they closed around my pieces.
