His rook appeared from nowhere once — I had been watching his queen entirely. The game ended before I understood how.

Each game ended in loss.

I felt no frustration. Only fascination.

As quickly as we had begun, shadows started to stretch.

With the same methodical precision he brought to everything, Mordrde began packing away the chess set, each piece finding its designated place in the lacquered box.

"Your father draws near, m'Lady," Mordrde said quietly, securing the chess box with careful hands.

My breath remained steady, but the mention of Father tensed my shoulders.

Mordrde observed my reaction without comment, then added with neutral diplomacy: "He will be pleased with your studies."

I gave a small nod, my eyes lowering toward the empty table. "Of course."

There was nothing else to say.

He allowed one final breath to pass, then stepped back toward the door, the chess box tucked securely under his arm.

"In chess, even the king may fall to a properly placed pawn... Lady Speer."

The door closed.

Position is power.

But who decides where the pieces stand initially?

I glanced toward my usual alcove, seeking the comfort of familiar books and study. But something had shifted—literally. The carefully stacked gravity tomes had moved slightly, curling the blueprint once more.

"Persistent."

data.title: Herald of Shadow
data.author: House
data.summary:
Speer Windsor survived Wyrms Hollow, and wakes up at the lake after her suicide attempt, forever changed. She now sees the world clearly. She journeys to the national institution in the company of new friends, but those in power are not who they seem. 

WIP

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.content:
The water was supposed to be the end.

I break the surface gasping, my lungs screaming for air. The obsidian lake is freezing—spring meltwater fed from mountains streams that have never seen sunlight. My limbs are lead, my clothes waterlogged anchors dragging me down. I shouldn't be alive.

But I am.

My fingers scrape against smooth stone as I drag myself onto the shore, each movement agony. Water pours from my mouth, my nose, my lungs rejecting what they'd so recently accepted. I collapse onto the black rocks, coughing until my throat burns, my body wracked with spasms.

The morning mist hangs low over the water, diffusing the pale spring sun into something soft and grey. Peaceful, almost. As if the lake hadn't just witnessed suicide. As if something hadn't spoken to me in the depths.

As if I hadn't accepted.

When my breathing steadies—when the coughing subsides to occasional shudders—I push myself up on trembling arms. My reflection stares back from the mirror-still water.

Storm-grey eyes meet mine where cobalt blue should be.

Void-black hair clings to my face where golden blonde ought to frame it.

I touch my cheek with pruned fingers, tracing features that are mine, but wrong. The shape is the same. The bone structure is identical. But the coloring—the Windsor coloring, the Ismeria heritage—has been burned away like morning frost under harsh sun.

Physical manifestations of metaphysical transformation. The girl who walked into this lake is dead. What emerged is something else entirely. Feels entirely different.

My hand drops to my lap. I stare at the reflection—at the stranger wearing my face—and feel... nothing. Not horror. Not grief. Not even curiosity. Just vast, yawning emptiness where emotions should live. And something else...

Understanding.

"A pawn," I whisper to my reflection.

The words came unbidden, emerging from somewhere deeper than conscious thought. A pawn that has been sacrificed. A piece removed from the board. But what am I now?

My reflection doesn't answer. The grey eyes stare back, flat.

A voice cuts through my dissociation like a blade through silk: "You know, I thought you were dead... I was about to poke you with a stick."

My head snaps up, water dripping from my hair. My body tenses—fight or flight instincts screaming after two years of torture teaching me that other people mean pain.

A young woman stands perhaps a dozen feet away, half-hidden in the morning mist. She's lean and wiry, built like someone who learned to run before they learned to fight. Red hair catches what little sunlight filters through the fog, and her jade colored eyes—bright with mischief despite the situation—assess me carefully.

Her posture is casual, weight on one hip, but her hand rests near her belt where a knife handle is just visible. Not threatening... just... prepared.

She mutters, almost to herself: "I'm glad it didn't come to that..."

"Are you... real?" The question escapes my lips before I can stop it. My voice is hoarse, scraped raw from coughing up half the lake.

She blinks, and something like amusement flickers across her face. "I mean, I hope so. Otherwise you are hallucinating a very stylish corpse-poker."

She pauses, studying me with a gaze that's somehow both sharp and gentle. Waiting. Giving me space to respond or retreat as I need. When I say nothing, she continues, her tone carefully light: "So are you... running—sorry, swimming away from something?" She glances toward the lake's horizon, giving me the mercy of not being directly observed.

My throat closes around the words that won't come. My hands grip the wet fabric of my shirt—expensive material, now ruined. Drach property, technically. Evidence of ownership I tried to drown.

"No... I'm..." The attempt dies. Emotion begins flooding the emptiness—grief and rage and shame, all crashing together like waves against a breaking dam.

A crow caws somewhere in the trees.

The sound cuts through the rising panic like cold water, and something shifts inside my chest, flipping me back to a useful numbness.

The words come easily this time, smooth and certain: "I'm Speer."

The red-haired girl's head tilts slightly, her eyes narrowing with interest rather than suspicion. She's quiet for a moment, clearly weighing something in her mind.

"Right. I'm Kiarra..." she pauses, a shadow passing over her features so quickly I almost miss it. "But no one calls me that anymore. I just go by Kiwi."

Kiwi approaches slowly, watching for any flinch or recoil. Each step is deliberate, telegraphed, giving me every opportunity to retreat or protest. When I don't react, she kneels beside me on the black stones, swinging a backpack off her shoulder.

"I won't pry," she says simply, rummaging through her pack. She produces a slightly bruised apple and offers it. "But you look like you could use this more than I can."

I accept the fruit mechanically. My hands are still shaking—from cold or exhaustion or something else entirely—but I bite into it anyway. The sweetness explodes across my tongue.

*When did I last eat?

I devour half the apple before remembering to breathe between bites.

"Wow." Kiwi's voice carries amusement and something that might be concern. "That's how it starts, you know..."

I pause mid-bite, looking at her warily. "Starts?"

"Fruit addiction," she whispers conspiratorially, leaning in like she is sharing state secrets.

I raise an eyebrow—an expression that feels foreign on my face but comes naturally anyway.

"I'm not called Kiwi for no reason..." She winks, shrugging with exaggerated innocence.

The absurdity of it—sitting by the lake where I just drowned, discussing fruit addiction with a stranger—strikes something in my chest. Not quite laughter. But close enough that it feels like remembering how.

We sit in companionable silence as I finish the apple and Kiwi produces a threadbare blanket from her seemingly bottomless pack. I wrap it around my shoulders, letting the spring sun slowly leech the cold from my bones.

"Do you know the Pillared Academy?" she asks eventually, her tone casual but her eyes sharp.

My mind supplies information automatically—Siegmara's premier institution, founded after the First Noble War, designed to train the next generation of nobility. "I know of it... why?"

"That's where I'm headed. Well, more like tagging along." She picks at a loose thread on her sleeve. "I have a friend nearby. Goody-ranger type. Believes in truth and justice and all that noble nonsense—except he's not actually a noble, which makes it adorable and tragic all the same." She glances at me. "You are... welcome to join us?"

I ponder that. I have no friends. No family. Nowhere to go that wouldn't recognize my face—except my face isn't recognizable anymore, is it? An academy is an institution. Institutions mean structure. Structure means libraries.

It's been so long since I've read a book.

The though surfaces with surprising intensity. At Windsor Manor, before everything, the library was my sanctuary. Knowledge as escape. Understanding as armor.

"I'll come," I say, perhaps too eagerly. My voice is steadier now, the hoarseness fading.

"Yea?" Kiwi's grin is bright and genuine. "Excellent. Fair warning though—my friend Koaltan is aggressively optimistic. Like, offensively wholesome. You'll either love him or want to strangle him. Maybe both."

We stand together, my legs shaky but functional. The blanket stays wrapped around my shoulders like a cloak as we begin walking away from the obsidian lake. I don't look back. The water is still, reflecting grey sky, keeping its secrets.

The forest is quiet in the way only early morning can be—birdsong just beginning, last night's predators returning to their dens, the world caught between darkness and day. Kiwi moves through it like she belongs, her steps sure even on uneven ground.

I follow, my mind splitting attention between the present and deeper analysis. Kiwi's comfort in the wilderness. The casual competence of someone used to living outside normal society. The way she approached a potentially dangerous stranger with caution, but not fear.

"So," Kiwi says, hopping over a fallen log, "Fair's fair. I told you where I'm going. What's your story? And before you say 'I don't want to talk about it'—which is fine, by the way—at least tell me if anyone's going to come looking for you.

"House Drach might," I say after careful consideration. "But they're looking for someone else."

"Drach?" Kiwi's voice goes flat. The playfulness evaporates.

"Yes."

"Fuck them." The venom in her voice is startling. "They enforce made up numbers with very real steel."

I look at her sharply. Her face has gone hard, rage burning behind the mischievous facade.

"So if Drach's looking for you... or someone else..." she continues, as we approach a small cabin set back from the path. "That's just one more reason to get you somewhere else."

Before I could reply, Kiwi stops, surveying the scene with professional interest.

"Wait here," she says, darting forward with surprising stealth. The cabin looks vacant but lived-in—washing hanging on a line outside, a vegetable garden showing early spring growth, curtains drawn against morning light.

I watch as she approaches the washing line, glances at the cabin windows, then smoothly plucks a shirt and trousers form the line. She's back beside me within thirty seconds, grinning triumphantly.

"These should fit well enough." She says, offering the clothes.

I stare at the stolen garments. "You just... took them."

"Yup."

"What if they need them?"

"Then they'll wash more clothes. That's how laundry works." She shrugs. "Look, if it makes you feel better, these are way nicer than anything I own. Whoever lives here can afford the loss. You on the other hand, are currently wearing what I'm guessing is very soggy evidence of wherever you came from."

The logic is sound, if morally questionable. But morality is a luxury for people who have the choice, isn't it? I learned that lesson thoroughly.

I take the clothes and change behind a tree, Kiwi watched without embarrassment or apology. I felt suddenly, acutely aware of myself—and just as suddenly, aware that she wasn't.

The shirt is slightly too large, the trousers slightly too short, but they're dry and warm and smell like soap instead of lake water.

When I emerge, Kiwi gives me an appraising look. "Better. You almost look like a person instead of a vengeful lake spirit. Very mysterious, very... 'I have a dark past but won't talk about it.' The nobles will eat it up."

We resume walking, and something has shifted between us.

I find myself watching how Kiwi moves through the world.

"So what's the Academy actually like?" I ask as we walk.

"Beyond the official propaganda, you mean?" Kiwi snorts. "According to Koaltan, it's a beacon of meritocracy where anyone can rise based on talent and hard work. According to reality, it's probably another gilded cage where nobles pretend to care about unity while maintaining all their advantages."

"That sounds appropriate."

"Right? But Koaltan's convinced he can change things from the inside. Become a noble himself, advocate for reforms, be the voice of reason in a corrupt system." Her tone is affectionate despite the cynicism. "I give him credit for trying, even if he's doomed."

"And you're going because...?"

"I owe him. He saved my life—pulled me out of a Vhaldrun Heart-Forge after I fell off of my floating isle," she teased theatrically. "I figured I'd tag along." Her grin turns more mischievous. "Plus, academy full of rich noble kids? That's basically a buffet for someone with my particular skills."

"You're going to rob them."

"Redistribute—yes. I want their money." She says, cutting off her obviously rehearsed explanation.

I feel that almost-laugh again. "You're either very brave or very stupid."

"Little bit of both, probably. And what about you? I'm sure there must have been some other reason you agreed so easily...?"

"Books," I say simply. "The Academy has books. And I have nowhere else to be."

Kiwi seems to accept it, nodding like it makes perfect sense.

We walk in companionable silence after that, the morning warming around us. Birds sing in earnest now, and somewhere ahead, I can hear the sounds of human settlement—voices carrying on the wind, the creak of wagon wheels, the everyday noise of people living their lives.

Eventually, the forest thins, giving way to cultivated fields and the outskirts of small settlement. Even from a distance, I can see a tavern at the edge of town, and even from here, I can hear the commotion.

Shouting. Laughter. The crash of something—furniture, maybe—hitting the ground.

Growing more comfortable with Kiwi despite myself, I allow a hint of resignation into my voice: "Don't tell me..."

"Yup." Her pace quickens to something between a walk and a skip, her energy suddenly infectious. "That would be Koaltan. Probably trying to break up a fight. Or accidentally starting one. Honestly... it's fifty-fifty with him."

As we approach the tavern, the sound of chaos grows louder. Through the open door, I catch glimpses of movement—bodies in motion, someone laughing, someone else swearing creatively.

Kiwi pauses at the threshold, turning to me with a grin that promises trouble and entertainment in equal measure.

"Ready?"

My heart begins pounding at the activity.

"No."

Kiwi winks, and burst through the door with theatrical flair.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.content:
The noise hits me before I am even through the door.

Voices—dozens of them—layered over each other in a cacophony that makes my chest tighten. Laughter. Arguments. The clatter of dishes and the scrape of chairs.

I force myself to follow Kiwi. The blanket is still wrapped around my shoulders, a thin barrier between me and the world.

Inside, the tavern is packed with mid-morning crowd—merchants breaking their journey, locals sharing gossip over ale, travelers looking for work or trouble, or both. The air is thick with the smell of cooking meat, stale beer, and too many unwashed bodies in close proximity.

I freeze just past the doorway.

I can't handle this.

Too many people. Too much noise. Too many eyes that could look at me, recognize me, report me back to—

My breath catches. The edges of my vision start to grey.

"There he is!" Kiwi's voice cuts through the rising panic. She's already halfway across the room, waving at someone near the back. "Koaltan! Stop flirting with the barmaid and get over here!"

A figure disentangles himself from the bar—tall, broad-shouldered, with the kind of easy physicality that comes from a life spent outdoors. He has honey-dark windswept hair, sun-kissed skin, and a smile that could probably charm birds from trees. He's also, I notice with a detached portion of my brain, at least a decade older than Kiwi and I.

"Flirting?" He spreads his hands in mock offense, his voice carrying that particular warmth of someone who genuinely enjoys being alive. "Now, I was merely expressing the appropriate gratitude for excellent service, Red."

"Sure," Kiwi rolls her eyes. "And I'm the Queen of Solmiris."

He laughs—a genuine, unguarded sound—and starts making his way toward us. Then his gaze lands on me, still frozen by the door, and something in his expression shifts. The easy humor doesn't disappear, but it... softens. Becomes more careful.

"Well, hello darlin'," he says softly. "You didn't mention you ran off to find your friend, Red."

"I didn't know I was either, until about an hour ago." Kiwi gestures at me with the casual confidence of someone introducing a stray cat she's decided to keep. "Koaltan, this is Speer. Speer, this is Koaltan—'Siegmara's most wholesome.'"

"Hardly the most—" He cuts himself off, his attention sharpening on my face. His eyes widen slightly. "Those are—Darlin, you have some striking eyes."

And just like that, I'm the center of attention.

Conversations around us falter. Heads turn. I can feel their stares like physical weight—assessing, curious, suspicious. Black hair and grey eyes.

Exceptionally rare in Siegmara, where most people have brown or blonde hair, brown or blue or green eyes. Where the nobility prize their hereditary colorings like badges of legitimacy.

Where a girl with golden hair and cobalt eyes is missing, and House Drach is surely searching.

My hands clench the fabric of my borrowed shirt. The walls are too close. The ceiling too low. There are too many people between me and the door, and if I need to run, I won't make it. I won't—

"Hey." Koaltan's voice, quiet and steady. He's moved closer—not touching, but near enough that I can focus on him instead of the crowd. "Look at me. Just me. Can you do that?"

I force my eyes to his face. He has kind eyes, I notice distantly. Brown and warm and completely unthreatening.

"Good. That's good." He keeps his voice low, pitched just for me, and breathes slowly—in, hold, out—until I follow without being asked.

The grey edges recede. The panic loosens its grip on my throat.

"There we go." Koaltan's smile is approving but not patronizing. "Better, Darlin'?"

I manage a nod. I mouth "Thank you," though the words don't come out.

He winks, and glances at Kiwi, something unspoken passing between them, then back to me. "First time in a crowd in a while?"

"Something like that."

"Well, the good news is most of these folks are too drunk or too busy gossiping to care about much beyond their own business." He gestures toward the table in the corner, partially hidden behind a support beam. "Why don't we grab that spot? More private, I think. Kiwi, you want your usual?"

"You know me so well." Kiwi's already moving toward the corner table, and I follow gratefully, keeping close to the wall.

The corner is better. I can see the whole room from here—all the exits, all the potential threats. My back is to solid stone instead of open space. The panic recedes further, settling into a manageable tension.

Koaltan returns with three mugs of something that smells like spiced cider, overly sweet milk, and a plate of bread and cheese. He slides into the seat across from me while Kiwi perches on the edge of the table itself, ignoring the perfectly good chair beside her.

"I apologize if my traveling companion here has caused you any trouble," Koaltan says, his tone carefully casual.

"When have I ever caused anyone trouble?" Kiwi scoffs, downing half of the sweetened milk. "Not sweet enough, Koaltan." She finishes with a burp.

Koaltan responds with a glare. "You stole a horse last week."

"Borrowed. I borrowed a horse. And I returned it."

"After you rode it into a pond."

"The horse was hot! I was doing it a favor!"

Koaltan catches my gaze and grins. "See what I have to deal with?"

I realize I am smiling. What I notice is this: when he looked at Kiwi just now, his exasperation was completely genuine—and so was hers. Neither of them was performing for me. The argument wasn't for my benefit. I was simply allowed to witness it.

I don't have a category for that.

He leans back and laces his fingers behind his head in a posture of deliberate relaxation.

"So here's the situation. The Pillared Academy is accepting applications. That is where we are headed." His tone carries just a hint of idealism struggling against realism. "Nobles and commoners studying together, proving that ability matters more than bloodline. Can you imagine?"

"It's propaganda," Kiwi says flatly, tearing off a chunk of bread. "But useful propaganda. They have to at least pretend to accept commoners, which means Koaltan here can pretend to be a noble-in-training."

"I'm not pretending," Koaltan protests. "I'm genuinely trying to represent my community within the system."

"You're trying to change a corrupt institution from the inside, which is adorable... but futile." Kiwi pats his shoulder patronizingly. "But I support you anyway."

"And you?" Koaltan asks me. "Why have you decided to tag along?"

"Books," I say simply.

"She's the sophisticated type, Koaltan. You wouldn't understand." Kiwi quips. "Wait, Koaltan... do you even know how to read?"

"I reckon I can learn!" Koaltan responds earnestly. "And what better place to start than the Academy? The library there is supposed to be the best in Siegmara."

Around us, the tavern's noise continues—a constant backdrop of conversation and commerce. I'm starting to tune it out, focusing on my companions instead of the crowd, when fragments of nearby discussion catch my attention.

"—terrible tragedy, the King—"

"—just a child on the throne now, can you imagine—"

"—Tether's getting bold, that's what—"

My attention sharpens on that last fragment. The speaker is an older merchant, leaning close to his companion with the careful tone of someone sharing dangerous information.

"Three estates burned in the last month. Always the same. Nobles dead, staff unharmed. They're calling it the 'Stone Rebellion' in some quarters."

"Bloody terrorists is what they are," his companion mutters. "Going to get us all killed when the houses retaliate."

"Maybe. But you notice they only hit the nobles? Not a single commoner harmed. Makes you think."

"Makes you dangerous is what. Keep your voice down."

King Surdus Solmara is dead? When did that happen? I've been... disconnected from current events.

But a child king means instability. Instability means opportunity for the ambitious. Or danger for those trying to hide.

And this Tether... burning estates but sparing commoners. Selective violence. Strategic violence.

"Did you hear about the King?" I ask quietly.

Koaltan's expression sobers. "Passed two weeks ago. Some kind of sudden illness, they're saying, though there are rumors of poison. His son—barely twelve years old—was coronated just a couple of days ago. I don't envy him."

"Civil war within a year," Kiwi predicts, rolling her eyes. "Watch. The noble houses will start 'protecting royal interests' which really means grabbing as much power as they can."

"You're probably right," Koaltan admits. "Which is exactly why institutions like the Academy matter. We need—"

He cuts off abruptly, his gaze shifting toward the tavern entrance. His posture changes—still relaxed to casual observation, but I can see the tension suddenly coiling in his shoulders.

I follow his gaze and feel my blood turn to ice.

Four men in dark green tabards have entered the tavern. The serpent sigil of House Drach emblazoned across their chests. Drach inquisitors.

"—escaped—"

"—young woman, sixteen or seventeen—"

"—blonde hair, blue eyes—"

"—dangerous—"

I'm not breathing. My hands have gone numb around the mug.

They are looking for me.

Of course I knew they would.

I killed the serpent masters.

I escaped.

I'm branded property with knowledge of their operations. They can't let me go.

Under the table, Kiwi's foot presses against mine. A warning. A reassurance. Stay calm.

One of the investigators scans the room, his gaze passing over faces with professional efficiency. When he reaches our corner, his eyes linger on me.

Black hair. Grey eyes. Borrowed clothes. Nothing like the description they're circulating.

But there's something in his expression—suspicion, maybe, or just thoroughness. He starts moving toward our table.

"Afternoon," Koaltan greets him with easy friendliness before the man can speak. "Can we help you with something, my Lord?"

The inquisitor ignores him, focusing entirely on me. "You. Girl. What's your name?"

My throat has closed. I can't speak. Can't breathe. Can't—

"This is my cousin Corvus," Kiwi says smoothly, lounging back in her chair with aggressive casualness. "Visiting from Qadesh. Got in last night."

"Corvus," the investigator repeats flatly. "That's not a Qadeshen name."

"It's not a Siegmaran name either, which is kind of the point." Kiwi yawns, unconcerned. "Her family's weird about naming conventions. Very philosophical. You'd have to ask them about it."

"Quiet, rogue. I'm asking her." His attention hasn't wavered from my face. "Have you papers? Travel documents? Answer."

I should say something. Anything. But words won't come out. My mind is spiraling back to Wyrm's Hollow—to interrogations that ended in pain, to questions that preceded torture, to the smell of my own burning flesh.

A crow caws outside the tavern window.

The sound cuts through the panic like a blade through silk, and something inside me shifts. The emptiness floods back in, washing away the terror and leaving only cold conviction.

I meet the inquisitor's eyes steadily. "I don't carry my papers on me. Too easy to lose or have stolen." My voice is flat, emotionless. "They're back at the inn with the rest of my things."

It's a complete lie, delivered with perfect confidence. Because the girl they're looking for—Speer Windsor—wouldn't lie smoothly. Wouldn't meet their eyes.

He studies me for a long moment. I can see him comparing me to his mental image of their target. Wrong coloring. Wrong demeanor. Wrong everything.

"Which inn?" he hisses.

"The Broken Wheel," Kiwi supplies before I can answer. "Two streets over. We're staying there tonight before heading inland tomorrow. You're welcome to check with the innkeeper—she'll confirm we arrived last night."

Another lie, seamlessly integrated with my own. I feel a flash of appreciation for Kiwi's quick thinking.

The investigator's jaw tightens with frustration, but he has nothing to hold us on. We don't match the description. We have a plausible story. We're not acting guilty—or at least, I'm not. Kiwi's default demeanor is suspicious.

He pulls a small poster from his belt and slaps it on our table. A sketch—crude but recognizable—of a young woman. Me. The text below offers a substantial reward for information leading to her capture.

But beneath the poster, something else catches my eye. Another piece of paper, partially visible in his document pouch. Distinctive black text, weatherproofed. He notices my glance and his expression hardens.

"Keep an eye out for this one," he says, tapping my wanted poster. "Dangerous criminal. Escaped from a House Drach holding. If you see her, report to the nearest authorities immediately."

He starts to turn away, then pauses. Reaches into his pouch and pulls out the other paper. Unfolds it deliberately.

"And if you see anyone distributing this..." He drops it on the table beside my wanted poster. "Report them as well. Sedition carries the same penalty as murder."

The pamphlet is simple. Single sheet, dense text, professional printing. At the top, large and bold:

CONVICTION DISMISSED AS CHAOS

I force myself to look at both papers with equal disinterest. At my own face rendered in charcoal. At the revolutionary text promising to tear down systems.

"We'll keep watch," Koaltan says seriously. "You have our word."

The investigator grunts, apparently satisfied, and moves on to question other patrons. The other three Drach men spread through the tavern, showing the same posters, asking the same questions, collecting seditious materials from corners where they've been tucked.

I don't move. Don't breathe. Just watch them work the room with professional efficiency before eventually giving up and leaving.

Only when the door closes behind them do I allow myself to exhale.

"Well," Kiwi says brightly, "That was exciting."

"That was too close," Koaltan mutters. His eyes find mine, sharp understanding. Then he looks down at the papers still on our table. "They left these."

Kiwi reaches for the Tether pamphlet first. Reads it quickly, eyebrows rising. "Huh. Revolutionary propaganda. Very nice quality too. Someone's funding this properly."

"Don't touch that," Koaltan says quietly. "If they come back and see us with it—"

"They already left it here," Kiwi points out. "Might as well see what has the Drach so nervous."

She reads aloud, voice low enough not to carry beyond our table.

"'You have been told this system serves you. That the noble houses protect you. That the king's law guarantees your safety. These are lies.'" She grins. "I like it already."

"Kiwi—"

"'The system serves those who built it. The houses protect their own interests. The law exists to maintain their power.'" She's enjoying this entirely too much. "'You cannot negotiate with architecture. A building designed to crush you will not be reformed by asking the stones to be lighter. It must be demolished and rebuilt with different foundations.'"

Koaltan looks genuinely distressed. "That's sedition. That's calling for revolution."

"That's accurate," Kiwi counters. "Everything it says is true. The system doesn't serve us. The nobles do protect their own interests. And you can't fix something that's designed to crush you."

I'm reading over her shoulder now. Cataloging the language. The structure. The careful distinction between violence against nobles and protection of commoners.

"'We are the Tether. We do not negotiate. We do not reform. We rebuild,'" Kiwi continues. "'Our methods are precise. Our targets are chosen. We harm no worker, no farmer, no commoner trying to survive. We remove only those who maintain the crushing weight. One stone at a time.'"

"They're killing people," Koaltan says quietly.

"They're killing nobles," Kiwi corrects. "There's a difference."

"Not to the law."

"The law is written by nobles. Of course it protects nobles."

I reach out and take the pamphlet from Kiwi. Read the rest myself.

'You are not our enemy. You never were. Your labor builds this realm. Your taxes fund it. Your compliance sustains it.'

'We ask only that you stop complying.'

'When they come to collect taxes—delay. When they demand labor—resist. When they issue orders—question. Small acts. Safe acts. But coordinated, they erode the foundation.'

'The nobles rule because we pretend they should. Stop pretending.'

'The system is fragile. Their power is performance. Call the bluff.'

At the bottom, a symbol. Simple black lines forming an abstract pattern that might be a broken chain, or might be something else entirely.

I fold the pamphlet carefully. Tuck it into my pocket.

"Speer—" Koaltan starts.

"Evidence," I say simply. "If we're questioned again, we can show we reported it."

It's a reasonable lie. He accepts it with visible relief.

But the truth is different. This pamphlet is remarkably sophisticated. The rhetoric is educated. The strategy is sound. Whoever leads the Tether understands both institutional power and mass psychology.

And that phrase. You cannot negotiate with architecture.

Philosophical. Abstract. Memorable. Exactly the kind of doctrine that builds movements.

"We should go," I say, standing. "The investigators might come back. And we still have three days to the Academy."

Kiwi and Koaltan follow my lead. We settle our bill and slip out through the tavern's side entrance.

As we leave, I glance back. See the wanted poster still on our table. My face in charcoal, offering rewards for my capture.

Beside it, the empty space where the Tether pamphlet was.

Outside, the road stretches east. We walk in silence for perhaps a mile before Koaltan speaks.

"Speer. Is there something you need to tell us?"

"Same reason you picked me up, Koaltan. Leave her alone. She'll talk when she's ready." Kiwi interjects.

Koaltan's face softens. "Well, I can't argue with that, Red." He says with a chuckle.

I say nothing. But I note that Kiwi stepped in front of that question before I had to decide what to do with it. Without being asked. Without even looking at me first.

We walk in silence for several more minutes. The tension slowly bleeds away, replaced by the rhythm of travel. Boots on packed earth. Wind in the trees. The ordinary sounds of a world continuing despite everything.

Finally, I break the quiet.

"Corvus?"

"What?" Kiwi shrugs. "You remind me of a magpie."

My smile returns.

Behind us, the tavern and its wanted posters fade into distance. Ahead, the Academy waits.

And in my pocket, folded carefully, the Tether's revolutionary doctrine.

Conviction dismissed as chaos.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.content:
Morning light filters through the inn's single grimy window, turning dust motes into lazy constellations. I wake to the sound of Kiwi's rhythmic breathing in the bed beside me and Koaltan's soft snoring from his bedroll on the floor. For one blissful moment, I forget where I am. Who I am. What I've become.

Then memory returns like cold water.

I sit up slowly, careful not to wake Kiwi. My body aches—not from torture anymore, but from sleeping on an actual mattress for the first time in years. Muscles that learned to rest on stone floors don't quite remember comfort.

Koaltan stirs, rolling onto his back with a groan. His eyes open, find me in the dim light, and he offers a sleepy smile. "Morning, Darlin'. Sleep alright?"

I nod. The truth—that I woke three times convinced I was back in Wyrm's Hollow—seems unnecessary.

He stretches, joints popping, and starts rolling up his bedding with practiced efficiency. "We should get moving soon. Academy doesn't wait, and the road's a good day's walk."

"Or two days if Koaltan keeps stopping to help every injured bird," Kiwi mumbles from under her pillow. "Or lost dog. Or sad rock."

"I helped one turtle cross a road—"

"It was going the wrong way!"

"Who are we to judge the turtle's intentions?" Koaltan's tone is mock-serious. "Maybe he had business on that side."

I feel that almost-laugh again. It's becoming easier, this approximation of normalcy. Like wearing someone else's face that's slowly molding to fit mine.

Kiwi throws her pillow at him and rolls out of bed in one fluid motion, already fully dressed. Did she sleep in her clothes? Probably. Everything about her suggests someone ready to run at a moment's notice.

Koaltan spreads a worn map across the small table, smoothing creases with calloused fingers. "Academy's here." He taps a spot marked with an official-looking seal. "We follow the main road northeast, stay at the waystation tonight, arrive tomorrow evening."

"Assuming no delays," Kiwi adds, now rummaging through her pack. She produces an apple—likely stolen—and takes a bite. Through her chewing: "Delays like, oh I don't know, Drach patrols. Random acts of heroism. Koaltan adopting orphans."

"That was one time—"

"You tried to adopt a grown man."

"He was clearly lost!"

I watch their banter while examining my reflection in the small, cracked mirror hanging on the wall. Black hair. Grey eyes. A stranger's face that I'm slowly learning to recognize as mine.

"Speaking of Drach," Kiwi says, her voice dropping to something more serious. She produces a second apple and tosses it to me. I catch it automatically. "Those investigators yesterday. They'll keep looking."

"They're looking for someone else," I say quietly, biting into the apple. Sweet. When did I last taste sweetness that wasn't laced with pain?

"Sure," Kiwi agrees. "But they're still looking. So we stay smart. Stay quiet. Get to the Academy where there are enough people that three more won't be noticed."

Koaltan folds his map with careful precision. "The Academy's neutral ground. Even Drach can't just walk in and start interrogating students without proper justification."

"Can't, or won't?" Kiwi asks.

"Both, hopefully." He shoulders his pack. "Either way, it's safer than staying here."

We settle our bill—Koaltan pays, Kiwi protests that she could have gotten us a discount through "negotiation," Koaltan pointedly ignores her—and step out into the morning street.

The town is already alive with activity. Merchants setting up stalls. Children running between buildings. A blacksmith's hammer ringing out in steady rhythm. Normal. Peaceful. The kind of mundane safety I'd forgotten existed.

Then I hear the voices.

Not the casual chatter of commerce. Something else. Commanding. Cold. Familiar.

"—proceed with the identification—"

"—matches the physical description—"

My blood turns to ice.

Kiwi hears it too. Her hand finds my wrist, fingers tight. "Don't react."

But I'm already moving forward, drawn by horrible fascination toward the town square. Koaltan and Kiwi follow, the former's concern radiating like heat, the latter's wariness sharp as a blade.

A crowd has formed in the square's center. Not the curious onlookers of yesterday's tavern—this is different. Tighter. Quieter. The silence of people watching something terrible and pretending they aren't.

Four Drach inquisitors stand in a loose semicircle. Dark green tabards. Serpent sigils. Professional disinterest masking as duty.

And between them, a girl.

She's blonde.

Blue-eyed.

Sixteen, maybe seventeen.

Crying.

Insisting through tears: "I don't even know what you're talking about—please, I live here, my father owns the mill, you can ask anyone—"

I can't breathe.

She looks like me.

Not me as I am now—black-haired and grey-eyed and changed. Me as I was. Golden hair catching morning light. Eyes the color of deep water. The same age. The same build. The same desperate expression I must have worn in Wyrm's Hollow when I still thought begging might help.

This is my ghost standing in the town square.

The lead inquisitor—the same one from yesterday's tavern, I realize with distant horror—holds up the poster. His voice carries across the square with practiced authority: "You match the description provided by House Drach. Blonde hair. Blue eyes. Approximate age. Last known to be traveling through this region."

"But I'm not—I've never even left this town—please—"

"If you are innocent," the inquisitor says with terrible calm, "the House will determine that."

The girl tries to pull away. Her movement is instinctive, terrified. Not calculated escape—just the animal response of prey trying to flee.

The nearest inquisitor moves with casual efficiency. He doesn't grab her arm. Doesn't tackle her. Doesn't need to.

His boot catches her knee at precisely the wrong angle.

The crack echoes across the square like breaking wood.

Her scream is immediate. Visceral. The sound of agony rendered into noise. She crumples, leg bent at an angle that makes my stomach turn, and the scream continues, high and terrible and endless.

The crowd recoils. Gasps. Turns away.

No one moves forward.

No one intervenes.

I watch it happen from somewhere outside my body. Detached. Analytical. The same cold observation I applied to my own torture, noting the efficiency of the break, the precision of force applied, the calculated brutality designed to subdue without killing.

This is happening because of me.

Because I escaped.

Because House Drach needs a body to prove they're still in control.

Because I'm standing here, safe and changed and alive, while this girl—this innocent girl who only shares my coloring—pays the price.

I should do something.

I should step forward. Confess. Trade myself for her.

I should—

A crow caws from a nearby rooftop.

The sound cuts through the girl's screaming, through the crowd's horrified silence, through my rising panic. Something inside me shifts like a door closing. The guilt remains, but it's suddenly manageable. Compartmentalized.

Beside me, Koaltan has gone rigid. His jaw is clenched so tight I can see the muscle jumping beneath his skin. His hand moves toward his belt—not for a weapon exactly, but toward something. Decision. Action. The heroic intervention he's spent his whole life believing in.

He takes half a step forward.

Kiwi's hand shoots out, grabs his sleeve. "Don't."

"We can't just—" His voice is strangled.

"We can't do anything," Kiwi hisses. "There are four of them. They're armed. You'd lose. We'd all get caught. And that girl would still be broken."

The mathematics of it are clear. Koaltan knows it. I can see the knowledge warring with everything he believes about justice and righteousness and standing up for the weak.

The girl's screams have dissolved into sobbing. The inquisitors are binding her arms now, preparing to transport her. One of them produces a leather gag.

"We should have done something," Koaltan whispers.

Kiwi's grip on his sleeve tightens. On my wrist too—I hadn't noticed she was still holding me. "And then what? Died with her?"

She doesn't wait for an answer. She pulls us both backward, away from the square, away from the crowd, away from the girl who's still crying through her gag while they load her onto a cart like cargo.

We walk.

The girl's muffled screams fade behind us, replaced by the normal sounds of town life resuming. A merchant calls out his wares. Children laugh. A dog barks. The world continues because the world always continues, even when terrible things happen in town squares in full view of witnesses who choose to look away.

No one speaks for a long time.

I count our steps automatically. Forty-seven before Koaltan breaks the silence.

"We should have done something." His voice is hollow now. Not arguing. Just... stating a fact that hurts him.

Kiwi's response is gentle despite its pragmatism: "And then what? Died with her?"

"Maybe that would have been better than—" He gestures vaguely behind us. At what we left. What we allowed. "—than this."

"You dying doesn't save her," Kiwi says. "It just means there's two bodies instead of one."

"Three," I hear myself say. Both of them look at me. "If Koaltan had intervened, they would have identified me. That's three bodies."

The mathematics of it feel important. Precise. Three deaths versus one injury. The calculation is straightforward.

But the guilt isn't.

Because I know what waits at the end of that cart ride.

We reach the edge of town before anyone speaks again. The main road stretches ahead, cutting through farmland and forest toward Academy and whatever waits there.

Koaltan stops walking. Turns to face us. His eyes are red but dry. He opens his mouth, closes it. Tries again.

"I need to be in a position where that can't happen," he finally says. "I don't know how yet. But I need to be."

It's not a philosophy. It's not a plan. It's just the shape of something that hasn't formed yet — the outline of a vow he doesn't have words for.

"We should keep moving," Kiwi says quietly. She's still holding my wrist, I realize. Grounding me. Keeping me here instead of spiraling into the guilt that wants to pull me under.

We start walking again.

I look back once. Just once.

The town is barely visible now, morning mist softening its edges. From this distance, it looks peaceful. Safe. The kind of place where nothing bad happens. Where innocent girls don't get their legs broken in public squares while crowds watch in silence.

The inquisitors are still there. The cart is still loaded. The girl is still broken and crying and being transported to horrors she can't imagine yet.

And the crowd has already dispersed, returning to their lives, pretending they didn't see anything worth remembering.

This is what power looks like.

Not righteousness. Not morality. Not even strength.

Just control.

Drach has that power. Windsor has that power. All the Great Houses have that power, each in their own way, enforcing their own systems, maintaining their own control.

And people like Koaltan believe they can change it from the inside. People like Kiwi know to stay small and survive it. People like that girl never even knew to fear it until it was too late.

But me?

I turn back to the road ahead, where Academy waits with its libraries and its lessons and its careful illusion of meritocracy.

I don't know what I believe yet.

I just know I'm still walking.

Still alive.

Still counting steps.

Still not the girl in the cart.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
chapters.content:
The road northeast is well-maintained — smooth packed earth bordered by drainage ditches that speak to systematic investment. Dopsen territory, Koaltan explains as we walk. House Dopsen controls the river networks, the lock systems, the waterways that connect Siegmara's interior to its coasts.

"Water rights," Kiwi says, adjusting her pack. "Which is a fancy way of saying they tax everything that floats."

"They also maintain the infrastructure," Koaltan counters. "Locks don't build themselves. Neither do the ferries, the docks, the flood management systems—"

"Very noble of them to maintain the systems they profit from."

I listen to their banter while watching the landscape change. We're leaving the rolling hills of Windsor territory — all strategic positioning and defensible high ground — for flatter terrain carved by rivers. In the distance, the glint of water and the geometric precision of canal systems.

The girl from the town square hasn't left my mind. I keep seeing her face — my face, as it used to be — twisted in pain. Keep hearing the crack of breaking bone. Keep counting the steps she's taking toward Wyrm's Hollow or somewhere equally terrible.

Forty-seven steps before Koaltan broke the silence.

I wonder how many steps she took before the cart arrived. How many before they gagged her. How many before she stopped screaming.

"Speer?" Kiwi's voice cuts through the spiral. "You're doing that thing again."

"What thing?"

"That thing where you go somewhere else in your head and forget to blink." She studies my face with concern that feels foreign. "You need to eat something?"

I shake my head. I ate this morning — bread and cheese at the inn. My stomach hasn't quite remembered how to process regular meals yet, and the thought of food makes it twist.

"Water, then." She passes me a canteen. "Drink."

I drink because arguing seems more exhausting than compliance.

The sun climbs toward midday as the road slopes gently downward into a river valley. Stroud takes shape ahead — not large by Siegmara's standards, but substantial. Buildings cluster along both banks of a wide river, connected by an impressive stone bridge. Everywhere, water — canals cutting through streets, lock gates controlling flow, boats moving in orderly procession.

We join the flow of travelers funneling toward the main gate. It's in the press of bodies at the checkpoint that I first hear it.

"—still in the infirmary, all three of them—"

"—eyes like that, I looked right at one before they got him inside and I couldn't sleep after—"

"—lucky the thing moved on. Last town it passed through, the thralls burned a granary—"

Kiwi's head tilts. "That sounds like a story."

The speakers are two merchants sharing a doorway, one gesturing broadly while the other nods with the grim satisfaction of someone whose worst fears have recently been confirmed. The guards wave us through before I can catch more than fragments.

A feign-grin. Here. Recently.

"What's a feign-grin?" Kiwi asks, directing the question at neither of us in particular.

Koaltan answers before I can. "Imp," he says, folding his map back into his pack. "Infernal thing. Small — about the size of a large cat, maybe smaller. The dangerous part is the grin. It hypnotizes. Once you're caught in it you do whatever it wants — or nothing at all, depending on its mood." He pauses, expression darkening with memory. "Couple years back on a ranger posting I found a farmstead, whole family just sitting in a field. Staring at clouds. Twenty people. Took two days for the effect to wear off naturally. Nobody was hurt that time."

"Experiences vary based on the creature's disposition," I say. "When they're simply curious the thralls might dance, or embrace strangers, or stand completely still as you're describing. But when they're agitated or territorial the outcomes are—" I pause, recalibrating. "The taxonomy classifies them as third-layer imps, which is the part that doesn't make sense. A third-layer creature surfacing this far from a known rift without—"

We round the corner into the main thoroughfare.

A voice rises above the crowd — broad, carrying, entirely comfortable with being heard.

"—increase the wage allocation for lock maintenance by fifteen percent. The work is dangerous, and dangerous work deserves appropriate compensation."

A young nobleman in fine clothes stands near the canal locks, surrounded by dockworkers listening with the careful attentiveness of people who have learned to look grateful. He is perhaps mid-twenties, with the easy charisma of someone who has never had reason to question his place.

Kiwi stops walking. A particular quality of attention enters her expression — not the idle curiosity of the feign-grin conversation, but the focused interest of someone assessing value.

Koaltan stops for different reasons entirely.

The feign-grin question folds itself away, unanswered, into the part of my mind where unresolved things wait.

Third-layer. This far from a rift. Without apparent provocation.

It will matter or it won't. Either way, I want to know why.

The dockworkers nod, grateful. One bows slightly.

"Lord Cedric understands us," someone in the crowd murmurs.

"Always fair, he is."

"His father was the same way."

Lord Cedric smiles warmly, says something else I can't hear, then moves on to speak with a merchant. The crowd watches him go with something approaching affection.

Koaltan turns to us with barely contained enthusiasm. "See? That's what I'm talking about. Nobles who actually care. Who use their position to help people. That's what the system should be."

I watch Lord Cedric work the crowd. The way he touches shoulders. Makes eye contact. Remembers names. Practiced. Smooth. Every gesture calibrated to generate exactly this response — gratitude, loyalty, affection.

"It's performance," I say quietly.

"What?" Koaltan looks at me, surprised.

"He's performing." I gesture toward the noble, now laughing at something the merchant said. "Look how he positions himself. Always slightly elevated. Always the one bestowing favor. The wage increase — he announces it publicly, makes sure everyone sees his generosity. Makes sure they know it comes from him, not from policy or necessity."

"Maybe he's just a good person doing good things—"

"Maybe," I agree. "But good people don't need audiences. This is about control. Make them grateful. Make them loyal. Make them think their prosperity comes from his benevolence rather than their own labor."

Kiwi grins at me. "I knew I liked you."

Koaltan looks troubled. "You're saying every act of kindness is manipulation?"

"I'm saying public acts of kindness from people in power are usually both kind and manipulative." I watch Lord Cedric accept another round of thanks. "It can be genuine and strategic simultaneously. Those aren't mutually exclusive."

"That's a cynical way to view the world."

"That's an accurate way to view power."

We stand in uncomfortable silence — Koaltan's idealism crashing against my analysis like water against stone. Neither of us is wrong, exactly. But we're speaking different languages.

"I'm hungry," Kiwi announces, breaking the tension with characteristic bluntness. "And Speer needs actual clothes that fit. Come on."

She grabs my wrist and pulls me toward the market district. Koaltan follows, still mulling.

"Where did you get money for shopping?" I ask as we navigate through stalls.

Kiwi just looks over her shoulder, one eyebrow raised.

Right. Stupid question.

The market sprawls across three interconnected squares. Kiwi moves through it with practiced efficiency, assessing quality, calculating value, occasionally palming small items when vendors aren't looking. She stops at a clothing stall run by an older woman with kind eyes and suspicious hands that track merchandise carefully.

"We need travel clothes," Kiwi says. "Sturdy. Nothing fancy. Something that won't fall apart after a week on the road."

The woman nods, assessing my build with professional accuracy. "The girl there — she's what, size small? Narrow frame?"

"Yes."

She produces several options — practical shirts, reinforced trousers, a jacket with actual pockets. Browns and greys that won't show dirt.

I change behind a curtain. The clothes fit better than the stolen ones from yesterday. Not perfect, but close enough.

When I emerge, Kiwi is mid-haggle, examining boots at the adjacent stall simultaneously.

"These are worth at least four silver—"

"These are worth three silver and you know it—"

"The stitching alone—"

"The stitching is adequate, which makes them worth three silver and two copper, and I'm being generous—"

They settle on three silver, one copper, and Kiwi's solemn promise not to steal anything else from this stall today. The vendor laughs like this is expected.

We continue through the market. Kiwi acquires bread, cheese, dried meat. She pays for some of it. At a fruit stand she buys apples — paying full price this time, I notice — and tosses me one.

"For your addiction."

I catch it automatically, and feel that almost-smile again.

We pass a toy-maker's stall where children cluster around a mechanical bird, gears visible through transparent panels, movements smooth and lifelike. One child, maybe seven, reaches out to touch it. His mother gently pulls his hand back.

"We can't afford it, love."

The child nods and keeps watching, content to observe.

I think about Windsor Manor. About how I would have been given such a toy without question, without thought to cost. How it would have bored me within hours.

"You doing okay?" Kiwi asks quietly, appearing beside me while Koaltan examines fishing equipment he clearly can't afford.

"I don't know," I answer honestly. "It's strange. Seeing people just... living. Without fear. Without calculation."

"Dopsen territory's not perfect," Kiwi says. "But it's better than most. House Dopsen figured out that prosperous commoners are more useful than desperate ones. Enlightened self-interest."

"Like Lord Cedric."

"Exactly like Lord Cedric." She grins. "Except you saw through it faster than Koaltan will. He wants so badly to believe in noble nobility."

"And you?"

"I believe in taking care of my own. Everything else is just weather." She bumps my shoulder gently. "Come on. One more stop."

We collect Koaltan — who has reluctantly put down the fishing rod he was admiring — and Kiwi leads us through narrower streets toward the river district. The buildings here are older, more worn, but still maintained. Temple bells ring in the distance.

Kiwi stops in front of a modest temple marked with Lady Tyrna's symbol — a silver crescent moon over flowing water. She shifts her weight, suddenly uncertain.

"I, um." She clears her throat. "Would you mind if we stopped here? Just for a minute?"

Koaltan's face softens immediately. "Of course. Take all the time you need."

"You don't have to tell us why," I add.

She nods, grateful, and pushes open the temple door.

Inside, the space is quiet. Cool. Light filters through high windows, creating patterns on stone floors. The air smells of incense and water — a fountain bubbles somewhere in the darkness.

I feel nothing.

I used to pray. Used to whisper devotions in Windsor's library, asking Lady Tyrna for wisdom, for understanding, for purpose. Used to believe those prayers were heard.

Now I know Tyrna either doesn't exist or doesn't care. Either way, prayer is just talking to yourself with extra steps.

Koaltan removes his shoes at the threshold, bows his head respectfully. He moves through the temple with genuine reverence — not performative like Lord Cedric's public kindness, but real. Private. The kind of faith that doesn't need witnesses.

Kiwi approaches the altar slowly. Her usual confidence has evaporated, replaced by something anxious. Almost childlike.

The idol of Tyrna stands carved from pale stone — a woman with kind features, hands extended in blessing or offering. Water flows around her feet, the fountain's source.

Kiwi stops a few feet away. Her lips move, forming words I can't hear. Her hand reaches out, almost touches the idol's extended palm, then falls.

She looks down and to her right, as if consulting someone who isn't there. Or maybe avoiding the idol's stone gaze.

Finally, in a voice barely above a whisper: "I got what I needed."

She turns and walks out quickly, brushing past us without explanation.

Outside, Kiwi has already moved several yards down the street, her posture defensive.

"Kiwi?" Koaltan calls gently.

"I'm fine." She doesn't turn around. "Just... needed to check something. We should keep moving."

We don't push.

By the time we reach the riverside docks, afternoon has stretched toward evening. The sun hangs low over the water, turning the river gold.

Koaltan purchases three tickets from a bored attendant. The ferry is already half-loaded — merchants securing cargo, families settling into passenger areas, a few students clustered near the bow whom I recognize by age and the nervous excitement they're trying to hide.

We board as the sun touches the horizon. Kiwi immediately scouts the best sleeping spots. Koaltan ensures our packs are secured.

I move to the rail.

The city recedes as the ferry pulls away from dock. Stroud with its clean streets and canal locks and Lord Cedric performing benevolence for an audience. The toy-maker's mechanical bird. The temple that gave Kiwi nothing she'd name aloud.

Behind me, Kiwi and Koaltan are settling in for the journey. Making plans. Discussing Academy logistics.

The ferry's bell rings.

I lean against the rail and count the ripples in the water.

Forty-seven before I lose track.

Forty-seven before I stop counting and just watch.

The river flows.

We flow with it.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
chapters.content:
The ferry docked with a gentle thud against weathered stone. I was first off, boots meeting cobblestone before the ferryman had even secured the moorings. Kiwi followed, stretching theatrically, while Koaltan offered the ferryman a polite nod of thanks.

"Finally," Kiwi muttered. "I thought we'd die of boredom before we died of drowning."

"The crossing was perfectly safe," Koaltan said.

"Safe and boring aren't mutually exclusive."

I didn't contribute. I was already scanning the valley ahead.

The Pillared Academy sprawled before us — not a single campus but an entire valley converted into an institution. Distant buildings dotted the landscape: dormitories climbing hillsides, lecture halls carved into cliff faces, practice grounds spanning cleared meadows. Stone pillars — ancient, pre-Champion era — rose at intervals throughout the valley, giving the Academy its name.

Other travelers disembarked behind us. Nobles, mostly. Their fine clothes and bored expressions marked them as clearly as any crest.

"Look at them," Kiwi said, jerking her chin toward a cluster of young aristocrats. "Forced here for 'experience.' Translation: their parents couldn't stand them anymore."

"That's uncharitable," Koaltan said.

"It's accurate." Kiwi grinned. "I can spot a spoiled brat at fifty paces. It's a survival skill."

I let them talk. My attention fixed on the valley's layout — entry points, choke points, exits. Old habits. Probably pointless. I catalogued them anyway.

We joined the flow of travelers moving up the main road. The path was wide, well-maintained, bordered by those ancient pillars at regular intervals. Each pillar bore carvings — geometric patterns that predated the current era's understanding of Glyphwork.

I slowed as I passed one, studying the symbols.

"Do you think they know what those mean?" Kiwi asked, falling into step beside me.

"Probably not."

We walked for another twenty minutes. The valley's scale became apparent — buildings that looked close from the ferry were actually miles distant. The Academy wasn't just an institution. It was a small city dedicated to education.

A checkpoint appeared ahead. Simple enough: a gate across the road, sentinels in Academy uniforms, a station for processing arrivals.

The line moved steadily. Nobles complained about waiting. Kiwi mimicked their accents under her breath. Koaltan pretended not to notice.

Then — shouting.

A man broke from the crowd, sprinting toward the checkpoint. Dirty, disheveled, wild-eyed.

"She is here!" he screamed. "I must find her!"

The sentinels moved with professional calm. One stepped forward, hand raised.

"Stop. State your business."

The man didn't stop.

"She is HERE! I know it! I saw her get on the ferry! I must—"

"Final warning."

The man lunged past the sentinel.

The halberd came down across his leg, dropping him to the cobblestones mid-scream. The sentinel's follow-through was immediate — a single clean arc that ended the screaming. The head rolled. The body stilled.

No one screamed. No one panicked.

The line simply... adjusted. Travelers stepped around the body. The sentinels dragged it to the roadside without ceremony. One made a note in a ledger.

Kiwi whistled softly. "Efficient."

"Cold," Koaltan murmured.

I said nothing. My focus was not on the event itself, but the bystanders. Just like when the girl was taken. Or even when the boy threw food.

The line moved forward.

The Enrollment Hall was impressive — three stories of marble and stained glass, wide doors open to admit the stream of new students. Inside, the space opened into a grand atrium with enrollment stations arranged in rows.

Administrators sat behind desks, processing arrivals with varying degrees of patience.

"Alright," Kiwi said quietly. "We go in order. Koaltan, you're up first. Boring and honest."

"I prefer 'straightforward and truthful,'" Koaltan said.

"Same thing. Speer, you go while I'm making a scene. Slip through unnoticed."

I nodded. "What scene?"

"You'll know it when you see it." Kiwi's grin was predatory.

Koaltan approached first. His enrollment was unremarkable: name, origin, purpose for attendance. The administrator barely looked up. Stamp, seal, acceptance token. Done in under three minutes.

Kiwi waited for Koaltan to clear the station, then strode forward.

I hung back, watching.

Kiwi reached the next available administrator — a middle-aged woman with the patient exhaustion of someone who'd processed hundreds of nobles this week alone.

"Name?" the woman asked without looking up.

"Lady Trebeledleuckledoo," Kiwi announced, voice pitched to carry. "Of House Trebeledleuckledoo. Vassal to the Vassal House Wickershindlebobblebottom of the Greater Fractured Isles Estate Holdings."

The administrator's pen stopped. She looked up.

"I'm sorry, what?"

"Lady. Trebeledleuckledoo." Kiwi enunciated each syllable with exaggerated care. "Tre-bel-ed-le-uck-le-doo. Honestly, I thought the Academy would have records—"

"I'll need documentation."

Kiwi produced a travel sigil — definitely stolen from some minor noble while we were waiting.

The administrator examined it. Frowned.

"This seal—"

"Is perfectly legitimate," Kiwi interrupted. "My family has served House Wickershindlebobblebottom for seven generations. We are, technically, through a series of marriages and inheritance disputes, heirs to one of the Great Houses. I can explain the lineage if you'd like."

"That won't be—"

"It all started when my great-great-grandfather married the second daughter of—"

"Miss, I need to—"

"—which created an inheritance claim through the maternal line that—"

Another administrator approached, attempting to intervene.

Kiwi launched into increasingly elaborate detail. The crowd began to gather, half-amused, half-appalled at the spectacle.

I moved.

I slipped to the far end of the hall where a younger, overwhelmed administrator sat, struggling with paperwork while trying to ignore the commotion Kiwi was creating.

I placed my enrollment papers on his desk.

He barely glanced at them.

"Name?"

"Speer Corvus."

"Origin?"

"Qadesh."

Qadesh was distant enough, chaotic enough post-genocide, that records were unreliable.

"Purpose?"

"Study."

He stamped the papers. Handed me an acceptance token — a small bronze medallion stamped with the Academy's seal.

"Dormitory assignments will be posted tomorrow. Next!"

That was it. I was enrolled.

Across the hall, Kiwi was still explaining her genealogy.

"—and when my father was tragically eaten by a horse—"

The administrator's face went blank. "I'm sorry, eaten?"

"Yes. Horrible accident. His last words were 'Go get help, you stupid girl.' I understood him philosophically, of course. Not literally. He meant I should pursue education, better myself, honor our house through—"

"A horse ate your father."

"It was a very large horse."

I caught Koaltan's eye. He was fighting a smile.

The administrator sighed. "Fine. You're approved. Take your token and go."

Kiwi accepted the medallion with exaggerated grace. "You've been most helpful. I'll be sure to mention your professionalism in my letters home to the Vassal House of—"

"Please. Just... go."

Kiwi swept away, head high, every inch the entitled noblewoman.

We regrouped near the exit.

"Lady Trebeledleuckledoo?" Koaltan whispered.

"It has a ring to it." Kiwi examined her token. "Can't believe that worked."

"You're shameless," I said.

"Thank you."

We moved toward the ceremony hall, following the flow of newly enrolled students.

The ceremony hall was deeper in the valley — another fifteen-minute walk through Academy grounds. Students clustered in groups, already forming alliances based on house affiliation or shared origin.

I noticed the stares immediately.

Whispers followed. Not loud. Just... present.

"—black hair—"

"—grey eyes, did you see—"

"—Siegmaran, maybe? But the coloring—"

"—certainly not Solmara blonde—"

I kept walking. Eyes forward. Posture neutral.

But my shoulders tensed.

"Ignore them," Kiwi muttered.

"I am."

"You're doing a terrible job of it."

Koaltan walked closer, subtly positioning himself between me and the nearest cluster of nobles. Protective. Unnecessary, but appreciated.

The whispers intensified.

"—Windsor, you think?—"

"—can't be, they're all blonde—"

"—maybe a bastard—"

My jaw tightened.

Black hair. Grey eyes. The visible proof of what I'd become.

I'd known this would happen.

We reached the ceremony hall — another grand building, this one with doors tall enough to admit giants. Students filed inside, sorting themselves by some invisible social hierarchy.

I paused at the entrance.

Inside, rows of seats faced a raised platform. Hundreds of students, all watching, all judging, all wondering about the girl with the wrong coloring.

"You good?" Kiwi asked quietly.

"Fine."

"Liar."

I stepped through the doors.

The attention was immediate. Heads turned. Conversations stuttered. Eyes tracked my movement.

I found a seat near the back. Isolated. Away from the clusters of nobles who'd already established territory.

Kiwi sat beside me. Koaltan on my other side.

A shield. Whether I wanted one or not.

"Breathe," Kiwi whispered.

I realized I'd been holding my breath.

I exhaled slowly.

The ceremony would start soon. Then there would be dormitory assignments, class schedules, orientation activities. Structure. Routine. Things I could control.

Just had to survive the stares until then.

Someone three rows ahead glanced back. Made eye contact. Whispered to their companion.

I looked away.

The hall's doors closed with a resonant boom.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
chapters.content:
The Academy's grand hall is designed to overwhelm.

Vaulted ceilings soar three stories high, supported by columns carved with scenes of historical battles and diplomatic triumphs. Eight massive banners hang from the rafters, each representing one of the Great Houses of Siegmara. They're arranged in deliberate hierarchy that everyone pretends not to notice but everyone absolutely does.

House Windsor occupies the position of honor — golden falcon on white, catching the morning light streaming through stained glass windows. My family's banner.

House Drach hangs opposite, serpent coiled around a crown on deep green. The sight makes my stomach clench, but I keep my expression neutral.

House Solmara — the royal house — displays the Pillared Sun, though everyone knows the child king holds power in name only now.

The other five houses follow: Vhaldrun with their forge and hammer, Nocturne with the eclipse, Verdant with their oak and plow, Marinha with crossed tridents, Dopsen with the twin lakes.

Each banner is a statement of influence. A reminder of whose children fill these halls. Whose interests this institution serves.

The incoming students — perhaps two hundred of us — crowd the hall's center. We've been segregated by enrollment status: nobles to the front on cushioned benches, commoners standing in the back, provisionals scattered in the middle depending on how convincing their documentation was.

I sit among the nobles.

It wasn't difficult. Kiwi's theatrical performance at the gates created enough confusion that when I presented myself as "Speer Corvus, foreign noble from the nation of Qadesh."

Kiwi ended up classified as a provisional despite her best efforts. She sits three rows behind me, somehow managing to slouch on a hard wooden bench with the same irreverence she brings to everything. When our eyes meet, she winks.

Koaltan stands in the back with the other commoners. Even from here I can see his barely contained excitement. He's actually taking notes during orientation. The earnestness is almost painful to witness.

"Pathetic, isn't it?"

The voice comes from my left. A young man — around my age, with the kind of calculated dishevelment that only money can buy. His dark hair is artfully tousled, his Academy uniform already tailored to fit perfectly despite orientation only starting an hour ago. A small golden falcon is embroidered on his collar, but beneath it, a ram's horn in silver thread — the mark of a vassal house.

I don't respond. Just turn my attention back to the front where the orientation is about to begin.

"The commoners, I mean," he continues, undeterred by my silence. "Look at them. Practically trembling with gratitude for being allowed in the same building as their betters." He leans closer, voice dropping to a stage whisper. "Between you and me, I give most of them three months before they wash out. The Academy's 'meritocracy' is really just an elaborate way to prove bloodlines matter, just as our forefathers established."

I finally look at him properly. He's watching the commoner section with unconcealed contempt, a smirk playing at his lips. His posture screams entitlement — the kind of person who's never faced real consequence.

"Pierce Battlehorn," he introduces himself without being asked. "First son and heir. You're new, obviously — I'd remember that face." His gaze travels over me with the casual assessment of someone used to evaluating assets. "Corvus, was it? I don't know that house."

"You wouldn't," I say flatly.

He raises an eyebrow, apparently amused by my curtness. "Mysterious. I like it. Tell me, Lady Corvus—"

"Just Corvus."

"—Corvus, then. What brings an unaffiliated noble to our prestigious institution? Family too poor to maintain their seat? Bastard line trying to reclaim legitimacy?"

Each question is designed to provoke.

Pierce Battlehorn is a child playing at power games he doesn't fully understand.

"I'm here to learn," I say simply.

He laughs. "How disappointingly earnest. You'll fit right in with the commoner section." His attention shifts back to the front as movement indicates the ceremony is beginning. "Try not to embarrass yourself too badly. The first culling comes quickly."

He straightens slightly, and I notice how his eyes track toward the Windsor banner with something like hunger. A vassal house heir, desperate to prove himself worthy of his liege lord's attention. My father's attention.

I file him away. First son of House Battlehorn, vassal to Windsor. Arrogant enough to insult students before classes even begin. Cruel enough to enjoy it.

The ceremony begins with procession.

Faculty members enter in formal robes, each color-coded by department. They arrange themselves on the raised platform at the hall's front, a physical representation of the Academy's hierarchy. At their center stands the Headmaster — an elderly man with silver hair and the kind of face that suggests he's seen everything twice and wasn't particularly impressed either time.

But it's the figure beside him who draws my attention.

Late forties, impeccably dressed, with the lean build of someone who's always been too busy to bother with excessive dining. His robes carry the deep green trim of House Drach.

One professor near the end of the row is, inexplicably, levitating.

The Headmaster raises his hands for silence. The hall settles immediately.

"Students of the Pillared Academy," he begins, his voice carrying with practiced authority. "Today you join an institution with a singular purpose: to forge the future leaders of Siegmara. Within these walls, you will be tested. You will be challenged. You will discover whether you possess the strength of character necessary to serve the pillars of this Kingdom."

Standard inspirational rhetoric. I let it wash over me, watching the crowd instead. The nobles in front sit with varying degrees of attention. Some genuinely engaged, others performatively bored. The commoners in back hang on every word, desperate to prove they belong.

The provisionals — Kiwi among them — occupy the uncomfortable middle ground, uncertain which group they're supposed to emulate.

"The Academy operates on principles established in the aftermath of the First Noble War," the Headmaster continues. "Merit above birth. Ability above lineage. Service above yourself." He pauses for effect. Pierce stifles a snort. "We do not care who your parents were. We care only who you will become."

Pierce is right. It's a beautiful lie, delivered with perfect sincerity.

I glance at the eight house banners hanging overhead. At Pierce Battlehorn smirking beside me. At the clear contradictions.

"Of course," the Headmaster adds, "such an education comes at great cost. The Academy invests tremendous resources in each student. In exchange, we expect loyalty. Dedication. An understanding that the opportunity you've been given carries with it a debt — not of coin, but of service."

I lean forward slightly, attention sharpening.

"Professor Supplice will explain the particulars of your obligations," the Headmaster says, stepping aside.

Supplice. Vassal of House Drach.

Supplice moves to the podium with fluid efficiency. His smile is pleasant, professional, completely absent of warmth.

"Thank you, Headmaster." He surveys the crowd with the same expression I imagine he uses when reviewing ledgers. "Let us be frank, students. Education is expensive. The Academy maintains the finest library in Siegmara, employs the realm's most accomplished scholars, provides room and board for hundreds. Someone must pay for this."

He lets that settle before continuing.

"Noble students typically have family sponsorship. Your houses consider Academy education an investment in future influence. Commoner students receive provisional scholarships—" he nods toward the back, "—contingent on maintaining acceptable performance. Prove your merit, and your debt is forgiven. Fail to meet standards, and you will owe the Academy reimbursement for resources expended on your education."

I watch Koaltan's face shift as he processes this. The excitement dimming slightly as reality asserts itself.

"For all students, noble and common alike," Supplice continues, "the Academy expects loyalty in exchange for opportunity. You will serve where assigned upon graduation. You will represent the institution's interest in your future positions. You will remember that everything you achieve here is built on the foundation we provide."

"This is not tyranny," Supplice says, as if reading my thoughts. "This is social contract. Order. The alternative is chaos — every person for themselves, no common purpose, no greater good. The Academy asks only that you recognize your place within the broader structure and fulfill your obligations accordingly."

Pierce leans toward me again. "Supplice understands how the world actually works. My father says Windsor relies on his counsel more than the Headmaster's." A naive notion, but there's pride in his voice — pride in being connected, however distantly, to power.

I don't respond, but I file that away. Supplice has influence under House Drach. Pierce is probably trying to leverage anything he can to get someone to notice him.

"Now then," Supplice says, his tone brightening artificially. "Let us discuss the specifics of your academic program..."

He outlines the structure — required courses, electives, assessment standards, dormitory assignments.

I absorb it all, building mental maps of the institution's power structure. The Headmaster provides ceremonial legitimacy but limited actual authority. Supplice controls resources and therefore controls everything that matters. The faculty presumably have their own agendas and allegiances.

"Before we conclude," the Headmaster says, reclaiming the podium, "you will now take the Student Oath. Please rise."

The hall fills with the sound of movement. Nobles stand with practiced grace. Commoners scramble to their feet. I rise with the others, keeping my expression neutral.

"Repeat after me," the Headmaster intones. "I pledge my loyalty to the Pillared Academy."

"I pledge my loyalty to the Pillared Academy," two hundred voices echo.

"I will uphold its principles of merit, service, and order."

"I will uphold its principles of merit, service, and order."

"I recognize my debt to this institution and vow to honor it through dedication to the realm."

I speak the words clearly. Note that I do so without hesitation. File that away too.

"So sworn. So bound."

"So sworn. So bound."

The hall erupts in polite applause. I look back and my eyes lock with Kiwi's. She raises crossed fingers from behind her back.

I remain standing as the crowd begins to disperse, watching Supplice speak quietly with several faculty members. Watching Pierce immediately cluster with other noble students, already forming the social hierarchies that will define the next few years. Watching Koaltan try to navigate toward the noble section before being redirected by a staff member toward the commoner dormitories.
