The crowd funnels toward the exits, students separating by dormitory assignment. I let myself be carried along with the noble section, studying my supposed peers as we walk.

Most are exactly what I expected — products of wealth and privilege who've never questioned whether they deserve either. They move through the world with unconscious confidence, their biggest concern which electives to take or which social circles to infiltrate.

A few stand out. But one in particular — he doesn't look like he's from Siegmara. A foreigner?

"Corvus!"

Pierce has materialized beside me again, apparently having decided I'm worth cultivating. "You're in the West Wing, yes? Noble dormitories?"

"I assume so."

"Excellent. I'm hosting a small gathering tonight — nothing formal, just getting to know our fellow students of quality." His smile is sharp. "You should come. Meet the people who actually matter here."

It's simultaneously an invitation and a test. Refuse, and I mark myself as an outsider. Accept, and I subject myself to scrutiny from the noble social sphere.

"Maybe," I say noncommittally.

He laughs. "I'll take that as a yes. West Wing, third floor, common room. After dinner." He leans closer, voice dropping. "Fair warning — we tend to be honest about our opinions of the... lesser students. If you're going to clutch pearls about commoner feelings, this might not be your crowd."

"I'll survive," I say flatly.

"I'm sure you will." He straightens, already scanning the crowd for other prospects. "Until tonight, then, Lady Corvus."

He disappears into the flow of students.

In the crowd ahead, I catch a glimpse of Koaltan being directed to the East Wing. He looks overwhelmed but determined, clutching his course assignment papers like they're religious texts.

Somewhere behind me, Kiwi is presumably navigating her own introduction to Academy life, figuring out which rules are actual boundaries and which are merely suggestions.

The Windsor banner catches my eye one last time as I exit the hall.

Golden falcon on white. Symbol of protection and nobility. The face my family shows to the world.

The same banner Pierce Battlehorn serves under, desperate to prove his vassal house's worth.

I turn away and follow my assigned group toward the dormitories.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.content:
The dormitory is nicer than anything I've had access to in years.

A central living area with worn but comfortable furniture — two couches arranged around a low table, bookshelves mostly empty, windows overlooking the Academy courtyard. Three doors lead to private bedrooms, each small but sufficient. And in the corner, a kitchenette with a small stove, basin, and cupboards.

I explore methodically, checking each room. The bedrooms are identical — narrow bed, writing desk, wardrobe, single window. I claim the one farthest from the main door.

The kitchenette draws my attention next. Most cupboards are empty, but in the back of one I find a small ceramic teapot, abandoned by some previous tenant. It's chipped at the spout, painted with faded blue flowers. Someone cared about it once.

I leave it where it is and close the cupboard.

The question of roommates surfaces. Two empty bedrooms means two other people will share this space. Nobles, presumably, given the dormitory assignment. The thought of navigating constant social performance even in what's supposed to be private space makes my chest tighten.

The door bursts open.

"Thought you could hide from me, Speer? After all I've done for you?" Kiwi stands in the doorway, grinning in theatrical offense.

I can't help it — I roll my eyes. "How did you manage this?"

"Quite easy, really. Nobles are so careless with their paperwork." She strolls in like she owns the place, immediately claiming the couch by flopping onto it. "Anyway, your supposed-to-be roommate is now doomed to the East Wing commoner housing. Hopefully Koaltan makes her feel at home."

Despite everything, I smile. "You swapped the assignments."

"I prefer to think of it as creative reinterpretations of bureaucratic intent." She's already surveying the room with exaggerated nobility. "Though I must say, this is rather... pedestrian for noble accommodations. Where's the gilded furniture? The imported rugs? The general sense of unearned opulence?"

"It's a school dorm, not a palace."

"Details, details." She's moving now, inspecting everything with running commentary. "Windows could be larger. Furniture is positively common. And this color scheme—" she gestures vaguely at the walls, "—the king will be hearing about this."

She opens the kitchenette cupboards, discovers the teapot, and her eyes light up. "Ooo, mine now."

"Must you comment on everything?"

"Just stuff that's wrong. I'm a noble, remember?" The sarcasm is thick enough to cut.

We settle into ambient conversation. She tells me about the provisional student chaos — apparently half of them are trying to prove they're secretly nobility while the other half are trying to blend in with the commoners. The Academy's "meritocracy" is already fracturing into tribal allegiances.

"We should hit the cafeteria," Kiwi says eventually. "I'm starving, and I want to see if the food is as bland as the decor."

"I had other plans," I say. "I got invited to a little gathering."

Her eyebrows rise. "Ooo, fun. Nobles I'm guessing?"

"Yes, nobles."

"I see." She studies me for a moment, something calculating behind the humor. "Let me know if they're hiding anything particularly juicy. I, however, am going to find Koaltan. I don't think he's heard my voice for at least a couple of hours. He's hopeless without me."

She grabs her bag and heads for the door, pausing at the threshold. "Be careful with the noble crowd, Speer. They bite."

"I'll manage."

"I know you will." She winks and disappears down the hallway.

The West Wing third floor common room is exactly where Pierce said it would be.

I stand outside the door, fist raised to knock, and pause.

Why am I even here?

I don't want to spend time with nobles performing superiority contests. I don't care about their imaginary hierarchies or their attempts to network. I came to the Academy for books and anonymity, not politics.

But Pierce's invitation wasn't just social courtesy. It was a sorting mechanism. Show up, and I'm part of the acceptable crowd. Don't show up, and I mark myself as an outsider who'll be marginalized or targeted.

I'm about to turn around anyway when the door opens.

Pierce stands there, grinning like he'd been watching through the peephole. "Ah, Corvus! I'm glad you made it. Come, come. There are people you must meet."

No escape now.

I enter, taking in the environment with practiced neutrality.

Seven other nobles occupy the common room, arranged on furniture in deliberate casual poses. Most wear the subtle markers of vassal houses — secondary sigils embroidered on collars or cuffs. One wears Verdant green, marking them as Great House bloodline. All conversation stops as I enter.

All eyes on me.

On my black hair and grey eyes. On my foreign appearance that doesn't match any Siegmaran noble lineage they recognize.

I take a seat on the edge of a couch, keeping my posture neutral. Neither aggressive nor submissive. Just present.

They resume their conversation after a moment, though I notice peripheral attention still tracking me. Pierce holds court from his position near the window, gesturing with the kind of affected casualness that suggests he's practiced this.

"And my father was telling me all about how Lord Commander Windsor is going to elevate House Battlehorn into a Great House!" His voice carries conviction that borders on desperation. The others seem hooked on his words, leaning forward with interest. "It's only a matter of time. Our service, our loyalty — it will be recognized."

Then his attention shifts to me.

"So. Tell me, Crow. How are the lands of Qadesh? The war is truly awful. A shame those Khitaran brutes think it appropriate to attack their superiors."

Crow?

"Crow?" It slips.

"Corvus? Crow? I see no difference." He smiles like it's clever, looking around to gauge the reaction of the others.

I let it pass. Correcting him would only encourage it. Instead, I address the question.

"It truly is terrible," I say carefully. I know there's conflict in the west — I remember fragments from my first days in Wyrm's Hollow — but I don't know the details. Pierce probably doesn't either, but he's testing whether I do. "Though I cannot blame them. If they were sitting on the resources my family controls, I too would be compelled to conflict."

Pierce laughs, apparently satisfied. "Well spoken. Well spoken indeed. I think you and I will get along well, Crow."

I suppress a cringe.

One of the vassal nobles — a river lord from his blue-and-silver colors — speaks up. "Have you seen that red-haired girl? The one with the annoying smirk?"

They're talking about Kiwi.

"I would do anything to see her bend the knee," he continues, grinning nastily. "I can hardly believe she's a noble. Probably bought her way in with stolen coin."

The others laugh. I keep my expression neutral, my hands relaxed in my lap.

"She'll wash out within the month," someone else adds. "These provisional students always do. The Academy has standards."

They continue in this vein — discussing which commoners will fail fastest, which provisionals are clearly fraudulent, which professors are too soft on lower-born students. It's exactly what Pierce promised. Honest opinions about "lesser students."

Honest cruelty, more accurately.

They address me periodically — always "Crow," never correcting when I don't respond to it — asking shallow questions about Qadesh that I deflect with equally shallow answers. Testing whether I'm one of them. Whether I'll participate in the casual contempt.

I don't. But I don't object either. Just remain neutral. Observing.

After perhaps an hour of this, I've had enough.

"I should go," I say, standing smoothly. "I want to locate the library before it gets too late."

"The library?" The river lord looks genuinely confused, like I've just announced plans to clean the stables. "Why waste your first evening there?"

"I heard the library here is the greatest in all the kingdom."

Pierce waves dismissively. "Of course, of course. I already knew you were the bookish type. Very respectable, Crow. We'll see you at classes tomorrow, yes?"

"I suspect we will." I say with a subtle curtsy.

I leave before they can delay me further.

The hallway is blissfully quiet after the common room's noise.

I walk without direction at first, just needing distance. My skin feels wrong.

But sitting among them as "Corvus" instead of "Speer Windsor" hit differently. Being somebody completely different than the daughter of the man Pierce worships felt... liberating. They don't know the red-haired provisional they mock is my roommate. They don't know anything real at all.

I find myself heading downward, following signs in twilight toward a northern building.

The library. That's what I came here for.

Books.

The thought is almost soothing. Knowledge doesn't care about bloodlines or performance.

I've waited long enough.

It's time to find out if this place lives up to its reputation.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
chapters.content:
I push open the great doors of the library.

My eyes widen as I take in the scale. Three stories of books rising toward a vaulted ceiling painted with constellations. Spiral staircases connecting balconies lined with more shelves. Reading alcoves tucked into corners. Tables scattered throughout with oil lamps providing pools of warm light against the darkness beyond the windows.

"Home," I mutter under my breath, smiling.

The word surprises me. I haven't called anywhere home since Windsor Manor. Certainly not Wyrm's Hollow. Not the obsidian lake. Not even the dormitory.

But this? This might qualify.

I walk down the aisles between grand bookcases, gazing up at the balconies of even more bookshelves extending into shadow. My fingers brush along the spines as I pass — leather, cloth, some so old the titles have worn away. The familiar texture grounds me. Real. Solid. Here.

I'm positively overwhelmed by the sheer volume of options. Where do I even begin? History? Philosophy? Applied sciences? I could spend years here and barely scratch the surface.

At the end of a particular aisle, I find a common area — comfortable chairs arranged around a larger table. It's occupied by a single figure: a boy around my age, maybe seventeen, bent over some kind of mechanical device. Foreign features. Dark hair, bronze skin, the distinctive angular bone structure of —

Varnori.

I stop, processing this.

The same student I noticed during the entrance ceremony. Now that I see him closer, I'm certain. Varnori features are unmistakable once you know what to look for.

Strange.

Varnori are isolationists. Their island nation barely acknowledges Siegmara, let alone sends students to foreign academies. What is one doing here?

More importantly, what is he working on?

He doesn't notice me approaching. He's completely immersed in the gadget, tweaking something with tools so small I can barely see them from here. His focus is absolute — the kind of concentration that blocks out the entire world.

I recognize it. I used to lose myself in the same way, reading.

"What is this?" I ask, curious.

He startles, nearly dropping a tiny screwdriver. "Ah! Hello!" His accent confirms it — Varnori, though his Siegmaran is fluent. "This is a retractable auto-canopy... for rodents!"

"For rodents?" I can't help the light chuckle that escapes. It feels alien in my throat, like a voice I haven't used in years. "What would a rodent need a canopy for?"

"I have no idea!" He says it with such genuine enthusiasm, grinning ear to ear as he hands me the device.

The craftsmanship is immediately apparent. Retracted, it's barely larger than my palm — a small cube of polished metal with seams so precise they're almost invisible. There's a button on one side, tiny enough that I have to search for it with my fingertip.

I press it.

A small umbrella pops out with a soft click, perfectly formed miniature spokes spreading fabric taut.

I look at him inquisitively, head tilted slightly to the side.

His smile somehow gets wider.

Then it happens.

The umbrella begins to rotate. Slowly at first, then picking up speed, the mechanism inside whirring so quietly I can barely hear it.

My eyes widen.

"You have a delayed rotational gearbox inside!" The words come out before I can stop them. "How — I was never able to get the spoke-count right for gear differentials when I was experimenting with timed siege engine models! The ratios never balanced. How did you compensate for the torque?"

His face lights up like I've just handed him a gift.

"You know about gear differentials? Most people just ask why I'm wasting time on toys." He's already pulling out sketches, spreading them across the table. "The spoke-count was the hardest part! I had to create a custom tooth pattern — see here? — that distributes the load across multiple contact points instead of relying on traditional meshing..."

For the next two hours, we get lost in conversation.

Micro-mechanics and physics. The challenges of miniaturization. Why certain metals hold tolerances better than others. How water resistance affects rotational friction in enclosed mechanisms. He shows me three other devices he's working on — a self-winding spring mechanism, a pressure-sensitive locking system, something he calls a "perpetual timer" that absolutely isn't perpetual but is still impressively efficient.

I find myself genuinely engaged. Just... talking. About things I used to love before everything else happened.

His name is Lazhar Vennick. He mentions in passing how others look down on his obsessions, call them "useless" or "without practical application." But what strikes me is how little it affects him. The perception of others barely registers. He's too fascinated by the work itself to care whether anyone else values it.

I envy that. The ability to pursue interest without the weight of judgment crushing it.

He asks about my siege engine models, and I realize I've said too much. Siege engines aren't typical noble lady pursuits. But Lazhar doesn't seem to notice or care about the social implications. He just wants to know the technical details — what I was trying to achieve, what failed, why I stopped.

I give him curated history, leaving out details. Just talk about the mechanics.

It's easier than it should be.

Eventually, twilight deepens into full night beyond the windows. Lazhar glances up, startled by how much time has passed.

"I should get back before curfew, commoners are on a tight schedule," he says, gathering his tools with practiced efficiency. "This was... thank you. Most people don't want to hear about any of this."

"I enjoyed it," I say honestly. Something in my chest has shifted slightly off-center — not unpleasant, just unfamiliar. I make a note of it the way I'd make a note of anything I can't immediately explain.

He grins. "We should do this again. Compare notes. I'd love to see your engine calculations — maybe we can figure out what went wrong with the differentials."

"Maybe," I say, noncommittal but not dismissive.

He leaves with a wave, still smiling, and I'm alone in the library.

I stand abruptly, needing movement.

The library is properly quiet now — late night, students in dormitories, staff asleep. Just me and the books and the gentle creaking of old wood settling into darkness.

I walk to one of the reading tables and pull out a piece of paper from a nearby desk. There's a pencil in the drawer. I settle into the chair.

I'm not consciously thinking about what I'm doing when I start to draw.

Squares. Small ones subdividing larger ones. Geometric precision, each line measured against the previous, creating pattern within pattern. It's meditative — the kind of precise repetition that requires just enough concentration to quiet the chaos in my head.

My pencil moves. Subdivide. Subdivide again. And again.

The patterns are perfect, mathematical, controllable.

Then a noise from the hallway — footsteps, distant but real.

My pencil stops mid-line.

My breathing stops with it.

I wait, every muscle locked, listening for whether the footsteps are moving toward the library or away from it. My hand rests on the paper, the pencil hovering uselessly above my geometric meditation.

Ten seconds of silence.

Twenty.

The footsteps have passed.

I release a breath I didn't know I was holding. My hand is trembling slightly. I notice this fact clinically, the way one observes a physical symptom without emotional attachment.

The footsteps were nothing. Someone returning from the latrines. A staff member doing night rounds. No threat. No consequence.

But I still stopped breathing.

I look at the paper. The geometric patterns are elegant, orderly. They comfort me because they're controllable in a way the world isn't. Every line follows logically from the previous one. There's no surprise. No danger. Just pure, mathematical inevitability.

I set the pencil down deliberately and focus on breathing. In slowly. Hold. Out slowly.

This is paranoia, I tell myself. This is survival instinct from a different environment. This is trauma response.

All true. All useless as explanations.

Because the point isn't why I'm doing it. The point is that I am doing it.

After my heart settles, I glance around the library. Truly alone now. No footsteps. No movement. Just the silence of thousands of books and the slow creep of darkness beyond the lamplight.

I need to test something.

I'm not sure when I decided this, but the impulse is clear: I need to know if the world reacts to me.

At the edge of a nearby table, someone has left a chess set mid-game. Abandoned match, pieces positioned mid-play. I walk over to it and study the board.

White king in a defensible position. Black queen threateningly close. A game in progress, waiting for continuation.

I reach out and move a black pawn forward one square.

Then I wait.

No one appears. No voice calls out. The library doesn't change. The world doesn't shift to punish my action.

I move another piece — white knight, repositioning it slightly.

Still nothing.

The silence is absolute.

I wait for ten full minutes, barely breathing, listening for any reaction. A professor appearing to scold me. A student arriving to resume their game and finding it altered. Some consequence, however small, that acknowledges my action.

Nothing comes.

It's a small test — absurdly small. Meaningless in the larger scope of things. Moving chess pieces proves nothing except that moving chess pieces produces no immediate reaction, which is obvious and stupid and exactly what should happen.

But I need to know.

I need to confirm that I can act in the world without automatically summoning punishment.

When I'm satisfied that no consequence is coming, I carefully — very carefully — move each piece back to its original position. White king restored. Black queen returned. Every piece reset exactly as it was, leaving no evidence of my tampering.

If no one was watching, they won't even know I was here.

If someone was watching, they'll see that I was careful enough to restore what I'd altered.

Both possibilities are acceptable. Both prove something I need to believe.

I step away from the chess set turn to the aisles.

Finally. No more distractions.

It's time to read.

I walk down an aisle and select a tome detailing recent events over the last five years. King Surdus's death. The boy-king's coronation. The political maneuvering behind the scenes. The western conflict of my alias.

I settle into one of the reading chairs and lose myself in information.

The history tome leads to a physics text — theoretical applications of force multiplication that keep making me think of Lazhar's gearbox in larger contexts. I find myself reading the same passage three times, not because it's unclear but because each reading suggests a different application.

I set it down only when something else catches my eye.

A locked door.

It's tucked into an alcove on the second floor, easy to miss unless you're actively exploring. Heavy wood, no handle, just a brass plate where a lock should be. And on the plate, a glyph seal — faintly luminous in the lamplight.

I approach it slowly, studying the seal's construction.

Durvis. The basic warding glyph. Simple but effective. Designed to recognize authorized access and reject everything else.

Why would you lock books away like this?

"It is locked for a reason, Lady Corvus."

The voice comes from slightly above me. I turn to find a man floating a foot off the ground, watching me with interest. Middle-aged, with sharp features and the kind of eyes that miss nothing. His uniform marks him as a major figure of the Academy.

The levitating professor from the ceremony.

I realize how incriminating this looks — me standing in front of an obviously forbidden section in the middle of the night, studying the lock.

"What is in there, Ser?" I ask, keeping my voice neutral.

"Dusty old books. Hardly of interest to most..." He assesses me carefully. "Most students don't even notice this door."

"And to the few?"

He doesn't answer immediately. His eyes narrow, almost imperceptibly, like he's recalculating something.

"Answers," he finally responds.

My gaze shifts back to the door.

"Durvis," I say, identifying the glyph aloud.

One eyebrow raises slightly. "Ah, familiar with the arts? Most neglect even the most basic of glyph theory."

"I have some familiarity." I keep it casual, not elaborating.

"I see." He studies me for another moment. "The night grows old, Lady Corvus. First day of classes tomorrow. You'll want to be rested."

He's right. I should sleep.

I nod acknowledgement and turn away from the locked door, aware of his gaze following me as I descend the stairs and head toward the exit.

Behind me, I hear the soft sound of his levitation adjusting — moving toward the locked door, perhaps, or simply watching to ensure I actually leave.

I don't look back.

The dormitory is quiet when I return.

Kiwi's door is wide open, and I can see her sprawled across her bed, fully clothed, snoring softly. She didn't even bother closing the door before passing out.

I close it for her, then retreat to my own room.

The bed is comfortable. The room is safe. Tomorrow will bring classes and complications and the continued performance of being Speer Corvus, foreign noble, here to learn.

But tonight, for a few hours, I got to talk about mechanisms and physics. I got to stand in a library surrounded by knowledge. I got to feel something approaching normal.

I close my eyes.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
chapters.content:
The lecture hall is tiered like an amphitheater, rows of wooden benches ascending toward the back. Noble students claim the lower seats without discussion — closer to the professor, better sightlines, cushioned benches. Commoners fill the upper rows, standing room only for latecomers.

I arrive early and take a seat in the third row. Not front row — that invites too much scrutiny. Not back — that suggests disengagement. Third row is perfect. Close enough to hear everything, anonymous enough to blend.

Kiwi slides in beside me moments later, yawning dramatically. "It's too early for thinking. Why do they schedule classes at civilized hours? Don't they know nobles need their beauty sleep?"

"It's nearly nine," I point out.

"Exactly. Uncivilized."

Other students filter in. I recognize faces from the noble gathering — the river lord, the Verdant girl, Pierce Battlehorn who gives me a casual wave and mouths "Crow" with a grin.

Koaltan appears in the upper rows, settling among the other commoners with his ever-present notebook already open. Even from here, I can see his excitement. First real class at the Academy. He's practically vibrating with anticipation.

The professor enters from a side door. He doesn't walk — he maintains a steady foot of elevation above the floor, robes drifting slightly with his movement. His uniform marks him as senior faculty. His eyes, sweeping the room before he reaches the lectern, miss nothing.

He hovers behind it.

"Metaphysics," he begins without preamble. "The study of fundamental reality. What Elyntricity is. Where it comes from. Why some can wield it and others cannot." His voice carries effortlessly through the hall, perfectly projected. "This is not a practical course. I will not teach you to cast spells. I will teach you to understand the underlying principles that make spellcasting possible. For those with the aptitude, this knowledge will enhance your understanding. For those without, it will at least allow you to comprehend what you're witnessing when you perceive reality."

He waves a hand and glyphs appear in the air — luminous symbols that hang suspended like they're carved from the light itself.

"Glyph magic," Oskar continues. "Humanity's workaround for a lost art. Once, in ages past, humans wielded an innate ability to alter their environment at will... with nothing more than their mind. That age ended with the Plane Meld. What remains is glyph theory: the codification of magical principles into repeatable patterns that anyone with sufficient study and sufficient components can employ."

I lean forward slightly, pencil moving across my notebook. I know this already — Father ensured I had comprehensive magical education despite my inability. But hearing Oskar's framework is useful. Understanding how the Academy teaches helps me understand what assumptions students will carry forward. What assumptions the general population have.

"Innate magic still manifests occasionally," Oskar says. "Rare individuals born with natural talent. But such manifestations are typically weak, uncontrolled, and often dangerous. Glyph magic provides structure. Control. Reliability."

He pauses, his gaze sweeping the room.

"Which brings us to our first critical principle: the relationship between trauma and magical awakening."

The room's energy shifts. Students sit up straighter. This is clearly the controversial part.

"Documented cases across centuries show correlation between profound suffering and magical manifestation," Oskar continues. "The trauma-based theory posits that extreme physical or psychological stress can force open channels in the body that would otherwise remain dormant. The body, faced with unbearable circumstances, reaches for any tool available — including magical potential it previously couldn't access."

Kiwi shifts beside me. I can feel her tension.

"This is not universal law," Oskar clarifies. "Not everyone who suffers manifests magic. But statistical analysis suggests trauma increases likelihood of awakening by significant margins."

He pauses.

His gaze moves across the room and settles on me for exactly one beat before continuing.

"The worst atrocities in history have sometimes produced the most powerful magic users."

His attention returns to his notes.

I keep my expression neutral, pen still moving. I file the glance separately from the lecture — a question to sit with rather than answer yet.

"Which raises," Oskar says quietly, "difficult ethical questions. If we know trauma unlocks power, does that justify inflicting it? Can we morally experiment on subjects to test the limits of this theory?"

The room is silent now. Even Pierce looks like he is contemplating the dilemma.

"The Academy's official position," Oskar states firmly, "is an unequivocal no. Regardless of potential magical benefits, deliberate torture is prohibited. We study phenomena academically, but we do not replicate it experimentally."

I think about Wyrm's Hollow. About the Serpentmasters who absolutely did replicate it experimentally. Who spent two years testing how much suffering a human body could endure before something broke or awakened.

About how, despite all that "trauma," my magic remained dormant. Until the dove.

Oskar's theory is incomplete. Trauma isn't sufficient. I know this.

There's something else — some other variable he hasn't identified. But I'm not going to correct him.

"To illustrate the dangers of unchecked magical experimentation," Oskar continues, shifting topics, "who here knows of the Holy City, Horalang?"

A few students raise their hands.

He waves his hand again and a new image appears — a city rendered in light, frozen mid-motion. Buildings caught between standing and collapsing. People trapped in the act of running.

"Over two centuries ago, Horalang was a Holy City — critical in the defense of humanity during the Cataclysm. A thriving center of trade and scholarship thereafter." He pauses, his expression darkening. "Then came the Third Rift."

I sit up straighter. The rest of the class is completely immersed in the lesson.

"The Third Rift opened directly within Horalang's city center," Oskar continues. "Unlike the previous two incursions, which were contained using established banishment protocols, this breach manifested a threat of unprecedented magnitude. A greater demon—" he pauses deliberately, "—one whose name we do not speak, for names carry power even in academic discourse."

The image shifts, showing the frozen city with visible cracks spreading through reality itself — tears in space where something vast and dark bleeds through.

Pain. Just — there, all at once, directly behind my eyes, like something pressing outward from inside my skull. I go completely still. My pencil stops. I set my jaw and breathe through my nose, slow and even, and stare at my notebook as though I'm reading, because moving or reacting is not an option.

It lasts perhaps four seconds.

Then it's gone, as abruptly as it arrived. No residue. No explanation.

I look up.

Oskar is watching me.

Not with alarm. Just — watching. His lecture hasn't paused. The class hasn't noticed.

He looks back at his notes without a word.

"The entity that emerged was beyond anything previously encountered. Banishment glyphs that had proven effective against lesser manifestations simply... failed. The arrays shattered. The wards collapsed. Traditional containment measures were inadequate. The infernals... were getting smarter."

Murmurs ripple through the classroom. This is history, but it carries the weight of a nightmare.

"Horalang's defensive forces fought for three days," Oskar says quietly. "Mages, soldiers, anyone capable of wielding a weapon or a glyph. The death toll climbed into the thousands. The demon could not be killed, could not be banished, and showed no signs of weakening. Meanwhile, the Rift itself continued to widen."

He lets that settle before continuing.

"Faced with the certainty that the demon would consume not just Horalang but spread across the entire region — risking a collision of Planes once more — the city's... leadership... made an impossible choice."

Why did he hesitate?

The image shows glyphs appearing around the entire city — a massive array that dwarfs anything else Oskar has shown us.

"They enacted the Horalang Temporal Lock. A glyph sequence of such complexity and scale that it had never been attempted before. Its purpose: to freeze the entire city — Infernals, citizens... everything. In a single instant of time."

He takes a breath.

"Permanent stasis."

The silence in the room is absolute.

"Twenty-three thousand people — the very city where Lady Tyrna and Sol the Eternal became Gods — all trapped forever, in that moment."

His face is solemn. But there is something more there. Something I can't quite discern.

"The mages who activated the Lock — they designed it knowing they would be caught in their own spell. No escape. No exceptions."

"That's horrific," someone says from the upper rows. Koaltan. His voice carries clear moral outrage. "They killed everyone. Twenty-three thousand people. How is that a solution?"

Oskar turns his attention upward, delighted at the question and engagement. "The alternative was worse, of course. The demon had already killed thousands and showed no sign of stopping. The rift was expanding. Predictive models suggested that within days, the breach would destabilize the entire planar membrane across hundreds of miles. Hundreds of thousands. Potentially millions, if the cascade couldn't be stopped."

"There's always another choice," Koaltan insists. "Always. They could have evacuated. Retreated. Regrouped and found another way."

"Mr. Kirdunsk, is it? Your conviction is virtuous. We should all strive for a modicum of this quality." He sighs. "They tried evacuation. The infernals were faster."

"Then they should have—"

Koaltan's face flushes, but he doesn't back down. "I don't have... an alternative... But accepting that killing twenty-three thousand people is ever the right answer means we've already lost whatever we were trying to protect. If we become monsters to fight monsters, what's the difference?"

"The difference," Oskar says carefully, "is that the Horalang leadership included themselves in this honorable sacrifice. They didn't save themselves and doom others. They made an impossible choice and paid the same price they asked of their people. That is the difference between monstrous pragmatism and moral cowardice."

He returns his attention to the classroom at large.

"The Horalang Temporal Lock remains active to this day. The city exists, frozen, a testament to the limits of our power and the terrible calculus of necessary sacrifice. A monument to our sins. It is also a warning: there are threats we cannot simply defeat. Sometimes containment is the only option. Sometimes sacrifice is the only mathematics that works."

My pencil races across the page. In the margins I write "Checkmate."

Twenty-three thousand versus hundreds of thousands. A known death toll versus projected escalation. The leadership choosing to die with their city rather than escape.

The calculus is brutal, but I understand it. Contain the fire before it consumes the forest.

"The Horalang incident introduces our central concept of this course," Oskar continues. "The Infernal Cascade. The theory that demonic incursion doesn't occur in isolation but rather triggers progressive planar failure. One breach widens. One demon attracts others. The initial manifestation is merely the beginning of geometric escalation. Speculation... of course."

He's drawing diagrams now — branching patterns showing how a single Rift could theoretically spread across entire continents if left unchecked.

"This is why containment protocols exist. Why Academy study of demonic entities is strictly regulated. Why certain knowledge is locked away... where students cannot accidentally trigger catastrophe." His eyes find mine for just a moment. "One mistake can cascade into continental devastation."

"Modern glyph theory," Oskar says, "allows us to study these phenomena safely. We can model demonic behavior, calculate cascade probabilities, design containment measures — all without requiring actual Rifts or demons. The knowledge exists in controlled form, accessible to those with proper authorization and oversight."

"Who decides what's properly authorized?" I ask before I can stop myself.

Oskar's gaze finds me immediately. He hesitates again.

"The... Academy administration, in consultation with House Solmara and the eight Great Houses. Knowledge is dangerous, Lady Corvus. Access must be earned through demonstrated wisdom and restraint."

"And who judges wisdom?" I press. "The Horalang leadership were presumably wise — educated, experienced. They still couldn't prevent the Rift or defeat the demon. If wisdom couldn't save them, how does it qualify someone for dangerous knowledge?"

The room has gone very quiet. Several students are staring at me.

Pierce is mouthing "Stop," subtly shaking his head.

Kiwi is mouthing "Yes," subtly nodding, mischief exploding from her eyes.

"Wisdom," Oskar says slowly, "is not omniscience. The Horalang leadership did the best they could with incomplete information and impossible circumstances. But they had access to advanced knowledge precisely because they had demonstrated judgment in less extreme situations. Would you prefer we give catastrophic power to those who've never proven they can handle lesser responsibility?"

I nod slightly and return my attention to my notes. He acknowledges with a wink and an almost imperceptible grin.

Beside me, Kiwi leans over and stage-whispers, "So what you're saying is... twenty-three thousand people got turned into the world's saddest statue garden because someone opened the wrong door?"

A few nervous laughs ripple through the room. The tension breaks slightly.

"A window, technically... Lady... Kiwi." Oskar acknowledges in equal absurdity.

Kiwi's head snaps to him. Her expression reads: not bad.

"Class dismissed."

The lecture hall turns into a flood of bodies. I approach the floating professor.

"Professor," I say quickly, "regarding the Infernal Cascade — you mentioned geometric escalation. What determines the rate of expansion? Is it dependent on the initial breach's magnitude, or are there environmental factors that accelerate or inhibit cascade progression?"

"Excellent question." He begins collecting his lecture notes. "The literature suggests multiple variables..." He pauses. "But the scholars always forget one thing."

The hall is nearly empty now. He floats toward the exit, looks over his shoulder at me, a smile unhidden.

"Gravity."

I close my notebook and follow him out, already turning the word over in my mind. Adding it to the catalog of things I don't yet understand but intend to.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
chapters.content:
Kiwi and Koaltan are waiting outside the lecture hall when I emerge, leaning against the stone wall in their distinctly different ways — Kiwi with a careless slouch, Koaltan with patient stillness.

"Well?" Kiwi asks. "Did you learn how to summon demons responsibly, or was it all bureaucratic nonsense?"

"Neither," I say, falling into step between them as we navigate the crowd of departing students.

Koaltan is quiet for a moment, then: "Twenty-three thousand people. Including children. Including people who had nothing to do with the Rift or the demon. Just... frozen. Forever."

His voice carries that weight again — the moral struggle of someone who genuinely believes in good and is confronted with impossible mathematics.

"It was that or worse," I point out neutrally.

"I know. I understand the logic. I just..." He trails off, frustrated. "There should have been another way. There's always supposed to be another way."

Kiwi shrugs. "Sounds like they tried everything else first. Sometimes you're just screwed no matter what you do."

"That's bleak."

"That's realistic."

I let them debate, my mind elsewhere. Turning over Oskar's final word.

Gravity.

What determines cascade expansion rate? Environmental factors, planar membrane stability, population density as fuel for demonic spread — all the technical variables Oskar listed. But he said scholars always forget one thing.

Gravity.

Is he being literal? Does gravitational force somehow affect how Rifts expand or demons move between planes? Or is it metaphorical — what goes up must come down, cascades eventually collapse under their own weight?

Or something else entirely. Something about planar mechanics I don't understand yet.

I file it away as a question worth pursuing.

The cafeteria is chaos incarnate.

Hundreds of students crowd long tables arranged by rough social hierarchy — nobles toward the windows with better lighting, commoners toward the back near the kitchens, provisionals scattered throughout depending on how successfully they've integrated. The noise is overwhelming: conversations, laughter, the clatter of dishes, kitchen staff shouting orders.

Kiwi leads us through the serving line with the confidence of someone who's never questioned their right to take up space. She loads her plate with an alarming volume — bread, cheese, some kind of stew, roasted vegetables, two pastries.

"The food here is terrible," she announces while adding a third pastry.

I opt for balance: protein, vegetables, a reasonable portion of bread. And apple pie. The cafeteria has fresh apple pie.

Koaltan constructs what can only be described as a carnivore's fantasy — three different types of meat, barely any vegetables, extra portions of everything.

We claim a table in the provisional section — neutral territory where our mixed group doesn't draw too much attention.

I'm halfway through my meal when Kiwi leans over conspiratorially.

"You have a problem, you know."

I look at her inquisitively.

She raises her eyebrows with exaggerated concern, says nothing, but flicks her eyes between me and the apple pie.

"Ah. Fruit addiction."

"Is that admittance?" Kiwi grins.

I simply roll my eyes and take another bite of pie.

Movement catches my peripheral vision. Pierce enters the cafeteria, scanning the room. His eyes find mine and lock on with purpose. He approaches our table with the casual authority of someone who's never been told no.

"Ah, Crow! You have... a particular choice of companions."

Kiwi's head snaps up. "Crow? CROW?!" She cracks up, nearly spitting sweetened milk. "That's even better than magpie!"

Pierce tilts his head in confusion, watching Kiwi drink excessively from her mug. "I... don't believe we've met... Kiwi? Was it?"

"Yup!" She burps immediately after.

Pierce scoffs, disgust flickering across his face.

"Is there something we can do for you, Lord Battlehorn?" Koaltan chimes in, his tone polite but with an edge.

Pierce lifts his chin slightly, approving of the formal address.

"Nothing you can do, no. I do seek Crow's presence at the nobles table."

I've gotten only halfway through my food, but the logic is simple. Stay and create tension, or leave and maintain the social performance. I stand.

"I just finished. Next time."

Kiwi mutters under her breath, "Wow, you eat like a bird, too."

"Suit yourself," Pierce says with affected indifference. "Though I figured you'd want my insight. Tomorrow's lesson is with Commander Carnifex. Martials. I could teach you the basic Windsor stance for sparring."

I freeze.

Just for a moment. Just long enough for Pierce to notice.

Windsor Talon's Honor. The premier combat stance of Windsor Honor Guards. Father insisted I master it. Lucius beat it into me. I haven't practiced it since...

Pierce misreads my hesitation as consideration of his offer.

"I thank you for the offer," I say carefully. "Still, I must decline."

"Hmph." He dismisses the rejection with aristocratic petulance and walks away toward the nobles table where his usual companions wait.

"I think Lord Battlehorn might have a crush on you, Crow," Kiwi jabs, grinning wickedly.

I glare at her before turning to leave.

I can still hear her behind me: "What? It's obvious! Right, Koaltan?"

"Red?"

"Hm?"

"Eat yer damn food."

Free from the cafeteria's chaos, I take the opportunity to explore.

The Academy grounds are extensive — far larger than what's visible from the main courtyard. Gardens maintained with geometric precision. Practice yards for combat training. A small chapel dedicated to Sol and Tyrna. Administrative buildings housing faculty offices.

I walk without particular destination, just cataloging. Learning the layout. Understanding where things are.

The sun descends toward the horizon, painting everything in amber light.

Eventually I find myself in a field beyond the main campus — close enough to still see the Academy's towers, far enough to feel separate. The grass is tall here, dotted with wildflowers. A single large tree stands near the field's edge, branches spreading wide.

And under the tree, someone is already here.

A girl, maybe my age, sitting among the flowers. Common dress. Brown hair falling loose around her shoulders. She's laughing — soft, genuine, delighted by something I can't see.

Then I do see it.

Doves.

A whole flock of them, settled around her like she's some kind of saint from a temple painting. One perches on her extended hand. Another on her shoulder. She's feeding them something, scattering crumbs, and they're completely unafraid.

My mind starts racing.

Wyrm's Hollow. The stone table. Serpentmasters asking questions I couldn't answer, applying pain when I stayed silent. Hours that became days that became weeks that became months that became years.

And after each session, they'd return me to my cell. To the small cage where my dove — my sweet dove — waited ever so patiently.

The only living thing that didn't hurt me. The only companion who asked nothing. Who just existed, warm and alive and mine.

Until they took her too.

Until they made me —

Dove.

The word loops in my head.

Dove.

Dove.

Dove.

I see red.

My muscles tense. My vision narrows to the girl under the tree, surrounded by birds, laughing like the world is beautiful and kind and safe.

How dare she?

How can she sit there like that?

And she sits there with doves like nothing is wrong.

Compelled to gift her the mercy I begged for.

The flock scatters. Wings beating in panicked flight. All except the one on her hand, which launches itself away as I approach.

The girl turns, startled but not yet afraid. "Oh, hello! I'm—"

A crow caws from the tree behind me.

The sound cuts through everything. Sharp. Deliberate.

My head snaps toward it. A single black bird perched on a low branch, watching me with eyes that seem too knowing.

What am I doing?

I look at my hands. They're trembling. My vision is still tinged red at the edges.

My cheeks feel wet.

"I—" My eyes meet the girl's. She's looking anxious now, uncertain, probably seeing something in my expression that frightens her. "I'm sorry."

I turn and run.

I storm through the Academy grounds, not seeing where I'm going. Just moving. Getting away from the field, from the girl, from the doves, from whatever just happened.

I reach the dormitory and slam through the entrance. Storm down the hallway to my room. Slam that door too.

The mirror.

I flipped it around when I first got here — didn't want to see my reflection while getting dressed. Now I spin it back.

Black hair. Grey eyes.

Speer Windsor is dead. I watched her drown in obsidian water.

So who is this?

I see red again.

The scissors are on my desk — basic sewing kit provided with the room. I grab them and start cutting.

Hair falls in uneven chunks. Black strands scattering across the floor like feathers. I cut without pattern, without care, just cutting. Removing it. Removing her. Removing whoever I was or am or might be.

The roof of my mouth hurts. My head hurts. My nose is running.

Tears drop onto the desk.

I keep sniffling, keep cutting, can't seem to stop either.

More hair clutters the floor around me. I finally drop the scissors, staring at my reflection.

Jagged. Uneven. A mess.

But still those grey eyes staring back.

Wait.

For just a moment, I could have sworn — Purple?

I blink.

Grey again.

I don't hear the door open.

Kiwi appears in my peripheral vision — I catch her reflection in the mirror.

She must have opened the door in that irreverent way she does everything, probably planning some joke.

But when she sees me, her expression drops completely.

No quip. No performance. Just Kiwi, actually serious, taking in the scene: the scattered hair, the scissors, my tear-stained face, my shaking hands.

She doesn't say anything. Just walks slowly toward me, careful not to startle.

After a brief pause, she picks up the scissors.

Without asking permission, she starts trimming. Fixing what I've destroyed. Turning the chaotic mess into something intentional — a short bob that frames my face properly instead of hanging in ragged chunks.

Her movements are gentle. Practiced. Like she's done this before, though I don't know when or for whom.

When she finishes, she sets the scissors down carefully. Lets another beat pass.

Then she tenderly grabs my hand.

"Come on, Speer. Let's sit down."

I follow like a ghost. No resistance. No thought. Just movement because she's pulling me.

We end up on the couch in the common room. Kiwi settles into the corner, and without discussion, I lay my head on her lap.

She starts running her fingers through my newly short hair. Gentle. Rhythmic. Soothing in a way I didn't know I needed.

I close my eyes.

Her fingers keep moving through my hair. Steady. Constant. Safe.

I feel safe.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
chapters.content:
Kiwi and I wake up groggy, but well rested. She'd passed out on the couch, her hand still in my hair. I look toward my room, its door open, black hair scattered across the floor in the morning light.

"Oh, fuck! Speer! We're running late!" Kiwi exclaims, jerking upright.

She's right. The morning light is too bright, too angled. We've overslept.

We skip any morning ritual and bolt through the dorms. Our boots pound against stone as we sprint through the central courtyard, weaving between early-rising students who give us irritated looks.

Something catches my eye as we run.

On one of the towers, high up where it shouldn't be accessible — graffiti. A skull mask rendered in black paint or char. Stylized. Deliberate. The same symbol from the Tether pamphlet still folded in my room.

The Tether is active on campus. Which means either a student, a staff member, or someone with access to the tower.

No time to think about it. Kiwi is fast.

The North Martial Field is exactly what it sounds like — a wide expanse of packed dirt surrounded by wooden practice dummies and weapon racks. Approximately forty students are already assembled in neat rows, facing a raised platform where a man stands with military bearing.

Commander Carnifex.

I know the name from the course roster — I think he used to appear on my father's Commander Census too — but I've never seen him before. He's perhaps forty-five, built like someone who's spent their entire life in armor. Broad shoulders, scarred hands visible even from this distance, close-cropped hair. He wears Academy colors, but with military insignia I don't immediately recognize.

Every student is silent, standing at attention.

We're very, very late.

Carnifex's gaze finds us the moment we enter the field. His expression doesn't change — doesn't need to. The silence speaks for itself.

"How gracious of you to join us," he says, voice carrying across the field with parade-ground precision. "Lady... Kiwi... and Lady Corvus. I'm delighted you found time in your busy schedules to attend my lecture."

Kiwi opens her mouth — probably to make some joke that will make this worse — but I grab her wrist. Hard.

She glances at me and, for once, reads the room. Stays quiet.

"Ten laps around the field," Carnifex says flatly. "Both of you. Then you may join the other students in the bleachers."

It's not a request. There are other students who must have been late as well, mostly nobles. Embarrassingly unconditioned. Kiwi and I finish our laps with relative ease and take our seats in the bleachers. Noble section. Third row. Students around us don't look at us directly, but I can feel their satisfaction. The late arrivals got punished. Order is maintained.

Carnifex continues his lecture as if we never interrupted.

"Martial doctrine," he says, "is the systematization of violence. Every house has developed their own approaches over centuries of warfare. These stances, these forms — they're not mere tradition. They're accumulated wisdom about how to kill efficiently and survive consistently."

He gestures, and several students step forward to demonstrate. Pierce among them, eager to display his self-insisted superiority.

"House Windsor employs the Talon's Honor stance," Carnifex continues. "Developed during the First Demon War, refined over generations. Observe."

Pierce moves into position with obvious pride. His form is... good. And fundamentally wrong. Talon's Honor is an aggressive stance, prioritizing overwhelming force. His is too passive — back leg too far, sword arm in a lowered position. Is this what he was taught?

This form is diluted.

The urge to speak up comes unbidden, and I push it away immediately.

Stay invisible. Stay unremarkable. I've already invited too much scrutiny.

But my mind won't settle.

I keep seeing the girl with the doves. Keep feeling that strange compulsion. Keep remembering the purple flash in the mirror that might have been real or might have been my mind finally breaking completely.

What am I becoming?

"Lady Corvus."

My head snaps up. Carnifex is looking directly at me.

"Since you appear unable to pay attention," he says with cold precision, "perhaps active participation will focus your mind. You will duel Pierce so he may demonstrate proper form against an opponent."

The field goes quiet.

Pierce grins. "Happy to assist, Commander."

I walk toward the sparring ring on autopilot. My mind is elsewhere — still processing yesterday, still trying to understand what happened. Whether I'm too dangerous to be here. Whether connection itself is a liability I can't afford.

The weapon racks line one side of the ring. Standard training weapons — blunted but still capable of pain. Swords, axes, maces, spears.

My hand reaches for a rapier, its weight a distant familiarity — the weapon I always preferred when Lucius was bruising me like a Royal Knight in training.

"Interesting choice," Carnifex observes. "The rapier is a niche weapon. Light, fast, but requiring significant skill. Not recommended for amateurs."

Pierce selects a standard longsword. "As we can see," Carnifex announces to the class, "a rapier is a compelling choice for the lazy, given its light weight. However, inexperienced fighters will never win using a rapier. The reach advantage is negated by lack of power and the precision required is beyond most students."

"Well, Crow," Pierce says quietly as we take positions. "Looks like you should have taken my offer when you could. I like the hair, by the way." Venom in his voice.

I barely hear him.

My body moves into stance without conscious thought.

Feet positioned. Weight balanced. Rapier held correctly — Windsor technique. My left hand rises into the guard position of Mountain Patience, the Vhaldrun defensive stance I studied on my own.

A hybrid form. Windsor offense, Vhaldrun defense.

Something flickers in my awareness — brief lucidity cutting through the fog.

I look at Pierce properly for the first time.

He looks like Lucius. Kind of.

Not the face — Pierce is softer, less weathered. But the stance, the posture, the Windsor-adjacent training evident regardless of its misinterpretation.

It triggers memory like a door opening.

I'd spent all night committing the Talon's Honor sequence to memory. Not just the movements, but the logic behind them. The decision tree of each position leading to the next. Forward, backward, starting mid-sequence — I could recite it like poetry.

Lucius stood across from me, already in stance. Older. Stronger. Better trained. He'd beaten me in every duel for years.

"Again," I demanded.

We engaged.

He moved through the sequence exactly as trained. Textbook. Strike patterns designed to be unpredictable but precise to those who know the system.

But if you know the system, you can count the steps.

I watched his feet, his shoulders, the micro-adjustments that telegraphed his next move in the sequence. Strike high, parry low, counter-thrust — three moves ahead, always following the pattern.

He committed to the overhead strike.

I'd already moved, intercepting the natural counter-position he'd flow into next. My blade caught his wrist before he completed it, leaving a shallow cut.

Lucius stared at me like I'd grown a second head.

"How—"

"You're predictable," I said.

He'd beaten me harder the next three rounds.

But I'd won once. Proved I could.

I... miss him.

The memory snaps shut.

I'm back in the sparring ring. Pierce is moving — has been moving, engaged in the duel while I was mentally gone.

But my body kept fighting.

Muscle memory executing while my mind was elsewhere. Rapier deflecting his strikes with minimal movement, Mountain Patience guard absorbing the longsword impacts, Windsor footwork pressing forward, keeping Pierce on the back foot.

I blink back to full awareness.

Pierce is nearly on the ground — one more movement and he's finished. My rapier is angled for the kill position, the geometry of it inevitable, and he knows it.

He knows it.

His face is open in a way it hasn't been since I met him. Not arrogance. Not performance.

Pure fear.

The calculation is immediate and arrives fully formed: a humiliated Pierce is a hostile Pierce, and a hostile Pierce is a complication I don't need. Not here. Not yet.

I let my back foot slide.

It's a small thing. A slight overextension on my follow-through, the kind of error a student who learned from books rather than years of training might make — who understood the theory but not the conditioning. My rapier skims wide. Pierce, reacting on instinct, brings his longsword across in a clumsy counter that catches my blade and sends it clattering from my grip.

I step back. Empty-handed.

The ring is silent.

Pierce straightens slowly, breathing hard, sword still raised. He looks at me — and for just a moment, something crosses his face that isn't triumph. An uncertainty. His mouth opens slightly, like he's about to say something, and then closes again. Whatever it was, he doesn't know how to say it.

Then the crowd's attention registers, and the performance reassembles itself. He lifts his chin.

"Well." His voice carries to the bleachers. "It seems Lady Corvus finds that the theory of an unconventional weapon doesn't quite survive contact with a real opponent."

Scattered laughter. The satisfaction of a lesson confirmed.

I retrieve my rapier from the dirt without expression.

Carnifex stands at the ring's edge. He's been watching with the same unreadable quality he's had since we arrived, and he watches still as I straighten. His eyes move from my rapier to my stance to my face, and something in the assessment feels less like a teacher grading a student and more like a man cataloguing information for later use.

He says nothing.

Just holds my gaze for one beat longer than necessary, then turns back to the class.

"Lord Battlehorn demonstrates the value of patience against an overextended opponent," he says. "Mark the geometry. When your opponent commits, the counter opens."

His voice drops as he passes me on his way back to the platform — low enough that only I hear it.

"Stay after class, Lady Corvus."

Not a question.

Somewhere in the bleachers, Kiwi makes a face. Koaltan has his notebook open but his pen has stopped moving.

"Twenty laps, Lord Battlehorn," Carnifex adds, not looking back. "You ended the duel. Not the overextension."

Pierce blinks. Opens his mouth. Closes it again.

He begins his laps without another word.

I stay after.

The other students file out. The field empties. Kiwi lingers near the gate until I make a small motion with my hand — go — and she disappears with the visible reluctance of someone who will absolutely interrogate me later.

Carnifex waits until the last student is gone before he speaks.

"You made a choice in that ring," he says.

I say nothing.

"I've trained soldiers for twenty years," he continues, beginning a slow circuit of the ring's edge. "I know what an overextension looks like. I know what a deliberate slip looks like." He stops. Looks at me directly. "The question I find interesting is not whether you made the choice. The question is why someone with your evident capability would choose to lose."

The morning is quiet around us. Distant sounds of the Academy carrying on elsewhere.

"There are many reasons a student might choose to lose," I say carefully.

"Yes," Carnifex agrees. "There are." He studies me for another moment. "I'll be watching your progress, Lady Corvus. I find I'm curious about what you'll choose next."

He dismisses me with a nod.

I walk toward the gate, aware of his gaze following me until I'm through it.

In the courtyard, the tower where I spotted the graffiti this morning is clean. The skull mask has already been washed off — quickly, which means someone with authority noticed it and had it removed before most students arrived.

I file that alongside the symbol itself. Someone placed it. Someone removed it. Both facts are useful.

Professor Oskar is visible briefly at the far end of the courtyard, crossing toward the administrative wing. He doesn't look in my direction.

I watch him go.

Position is power, I think, and head toward the library.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
chapters.content:
Pierce catches me at the gate.

He's finished maybe half his laps — Carnifex let him stop early, or he simply stopped and nobody pushed it. He falls into step beside me with the studied casualness of someone who has rehearsed an approach.

"Not bad, Crow," he says.

The confidence that usually saturates every word he speaks is slightly thinner than usual. Present, but with something underneath it.

I glance at him and say nothing.

"I suspect, though," he continues, looking ahead rather than at me, "that you lost on purpose."

How astute.

I keep my expression neutral. "What makes you say that?"

"The footwork." He says it quickly, like he's been holding it. "You were moving me backward the entire duel. Then suddenly you overextend on a follow-through that you hadn't made once in the entire exchange." He pauses. "It didn't fit."

He's more observant than I've given him credit for. I file that revision alongside everything else I've noted about him.

"We're friends, aren't we?" I say.

He blinks. Whatever he expected, it wasn't that.

"I — yes. I'd say so."

"Then I was just wondering," I say, turning to look at him directly, "whether a friend who was clearly better at something would demonstrate it publicly, on the first week of classes, in front of a commander who was already watching her."

Something shifts in his face. The performance relaxes — not fully, but enough to see what's underneath it. The hunger is still there, but there's something else now. Something almost like relief. Like he's been handed permission to be a different version of himself for a moment.

He smiles. Not the sharp, calculated smile he uses on audiences.

"I knew I liked you, Crow."

We walk together through the courtyard, falling into an easy pace. He talks — about Carnifex, about the other students, about which professors are worth cultivating and which are merely to be endured. Useful information delivered as gossip, which is often the best way to receive it.

And then: "Your friends."

I look at him.

"The red-haired girl — Kiwi — and the ranger. Koaltan." He says the names carefully, like he's practiced them. "They're yours."

"They travel with me," I say.

"They're being sidelined." He says it matter-of-factly, not cruelly. "Kiwi's provisional status means she doesn't get invited to anything that matters. Koaltan's in the commoner track — he'll never see the inside of a noble seminar unless someone vouches for him." He pauses. "I could change that."

I wait.

"I host gatherings. I have standing in the social network here — not Great House standing, but enough. If I include them, others will follow. It takes one person of the right affiliation to open a door." He glances at me sideways. "Consider it reciprocity."

He wants to be seen doing something significant. Something generous. Something that someone might mention to House Windsor — did you hear what young Battlehorn did? Bridging the divide, building goodwill across the castes. He's handing me exactly what I need while believing he's negotiating.

"That's generous," I say.

"I'm a generous person," he says, with enough self-awareness to make it almost a joke.

We reach the fork where his dormitory path splits from mine. He straightens, the familiar performance sliding back into place like a well-fitted coat.

"Until tomorrow, then, Crow."

"Until tomorrow, Pierce."

I watch him go. Then I find Kiwi and Koaltan waiting for me near the library steps, exactly where I expected them to be.

Kiwi takes one look at my face and says: "You lost on purpose."

Not a question. Not an accusation. Just Kiwi, stating a fact she's already filed under things that make sense about Speer.

Koaltan is less settled. He has his notebook in his hands but he hasn't opened it, which means he's been standing here thinking rather than writing, which means he's been bothered by something since the duel ended.

"You were winning," he says. "I was watching. You were better than him."

"I was," I agree.

He waits for more. I don't offer it immediately, and I can see the patience it costs him.

"Why?" he finally asks.

I consider how to answer. The honest version — because a humiliated Pierce is useless to me, and a grateful Pierce is an open door — would trouble him in ways I don't need right now. The idealistic version happens to be true at the same time.

"Equality between the castes demands compromise," I say. I let a small smile surface. "You said it yourself. You can't change things from the inside by making enemies on your first week."

Koaltan goes quiet. I can see him turning it over — the logic is sound, the sentiment is something he could have said himself, and yet something about it sits slightly wrong with him. He can't locate the wrongness, which means he files it as his own unease rather than a problem with my reasoning.

Kiwi, meanwhile, is looking at me with the expression she uses when she's decided something about a person and is choosing not to say it yet.

"Pierce is going to extend social cover to you both," I say. "Invitations, access, a vouching presence in the noble network. He offered it."

Koaltan's expression shifts. "Why would Pierce Battlehorn do that?"

"Because I asked him to."

The silence that follows has different textures in it. Koaltan processing what this means for the project he's been building toward since before he arrived here. Kiwi processing the mechanism of it — how I asked, what I gave, what the real cost will be.

"Speer," Koaltan says slowly. "This is — this could actually work. If someone like Pierce is willing to—" He stops. Starts again. "This is what I've been trying to explain to people. That it's possible. That if someone with standing is willing to use it differently—"

"We should go in," I say. "I've been thinking about the physics text I left unfinished last night."

Kiwi falls into step beside me, close enough to speak quietly. "He's going to be insufferable about this for weeks."

"I know."

"Was that the plan?"

I push open the library door. "I just wanted to read my book."

She snorts. We go inside.

The library breathes differently at midday than it does at night. The morning quiet has given way to the low ambient hum of students at work — pens scratching, pages turning, the occasional whispered argument over a shared text.

Koaltan immediately disappears into the stacks, notebook already open, hunting for whatever map or record or historical account will feed his enthusiasm for the next several hours.

Kiwi drops into a chair across from me, produces The Duchess and the Honor Guard from somewhere in her bag, and begins reading with the focused attention she usually reserves for things worth stealing.

I find my physics text where I left it.

The passage I'd been turning over — theoretical force multiplication in enclosed systems — connects differently now after Vennick's gearbox. What the text describes abstractly, Vennick has instantiated in miniature. The gap between theoretical principle and physical application is smaller than the textbooks suggest, and larger in different places than they acknowledge.

I make a note in the margin.

Kiwi's hand settles on mine across the table.

I look up.

"How are you holding up?" Her voice has none of its usual performance in it. Just the question, direct and quiet.

"I'll be okay," I say.

"Okay." She lets the word sit for a moment. Then: "I know we haven't known each other long. But you make me feel like I have a purpose. You know?"

Something in my chest does something complicated that I don't have a clean name for. Warmth moving through spaces that have been empty for a long time.

I don't know what to say.

Before I can find words, Kiwi pulls back, puts one hand behind her head with lazy confidence, and raises her book with the other. Already reading.

The moment passes. The warmth stays.

Koaltan reappears from behind a shelf, practically vibrating.

"I had no idea the Ordo Solari had built a thirteenth citadel only a couple of years ago."

"And I had no idea House Dopsen and Windsor Talons were that... close," Kiwi says, eyes sparkling.

Koaltan looks at her blankly. "I've never heard of an official collaboration between those two."

"Oh, you have much to learn, my sweet innocent ranger." She clears her throat theatrically and opens to a page. "His gleaming armor sent shivers through my body as it fell to the ground. He held my neck. Tight. And under my dress, he impaled me with his lance — splitting me wide—" she locks eyes with Koaltan, her gaze narrowing with deliberate provocation, "—with pleasure."

I roll my eyes.

"Gah, okay Red. Enough." Koaltan staggers forward and confiscates the book. "Let's get you something more — uh — not that."

"Buzzkill." The satisfaction on her face is total.

A student appears at the library entrance, scans the room, eyes finding mine briefly before disappearing around a shelf at the far end.

Kiwi, unbothered, starts attempting chess with Koaltan — moving pieces at random with cheerful confidence. A knight like a pawn. A bishop sideways. Koaltan objects to each move with increasing desperation.

I watch them and return to my book.

Outside, somewhere on this campus, someone had placed a Tether symbol where it would be seen and removed it before it could be examined. Pierce Battlehorn had just agreed to open doors he would normally have kept shut. Carnifex had let me walk away while making clear he was still watching.

Three separate threads, none of them resolved.

I turn a page.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
chapters.content:
The cafeteria at midday is a different beast than at breakfast — louder, more settled into its hierarchies, the social geography of the first week already calcifying into habit.

We've claimed a table in the provisional section. Koaltan is finishing what appears to be his second plate. Kiwi is eating an apple with the focused satisfaction of someone who considers fruit a competitive sport.

I'm watching the room.

It's become automatic — the scanning, the cataloging, the quiet construction of a map that tells me where the power sits and where it flows and where it pools. Which tables have the most traffic. Which students people defer to without seeming to.

And then the energy in the room shifts slightly, the way it does when someone enters who the room already knows.

He's tall — a full head above most of the students he passes — with the unhurried movement of someone comfortable in any space they occupy. Tyrnosian features, darker complexion than most of the Siegmaran students, a red scarf worn loosely over his Academy uniform in a way that should look careless but doesn't. He moves through the cafeteria the way Kiwi moves through a market — reading it, navigating it, belonging to it without being owned by it.

He stops to say something to a commoner student near the back. They laugh. He moves on, exchanging words with a noble two tables over who receives him without any of the performative deference that usually accompanies interactions between castes here. Just two people talking.

"That's Margrass," Koaltan says, in the tone he uses when he's trying not to sound too impressed and failing entirely. "Third year. Top scores in every discipline they track. Tyrnosian exchange — first one they've accepted in something like twenty years." He pauses. "He's on the student mediation council. Helped three commoners appeal their scholarship reviews last term. All three kept their placements."

"He's very tall," Kiwi says.

Her voice is approximately three notes higher than usual.

I look at her. She is staring at Margrass with the focused intensity she normally reserves for expensive things she's planning to acquire, except her expression has gone slightly soft around the edges in a way I haven't seen before.

"Kiwi."

"He's very tall," she says again, as if this explains something.

Koaltan looks at her. Looks at Margrass. Looks back at her. Opens his mouth.

"Don't," she says, without moving her eyes.

Koaltan closes his mouth.

Margrass has finished his conversation with the noble and is moving toward the serving line — which takes him past our table. Kiwi sits up slightly. Her hand moves to her hair. She appears to be attempting an expression of casual indifference and producing something closer to concentrated effort.

He glances at our table as he passes.

Then he stops.

Not at Kiwi.

At me.

"You're Corvus," he says. Not a question. His Siegmaran is fluent with a Tyrnosian cadence underneath it, the kind that comes from learning young rather than late. "The duel this morning."

"Yes," I say.

He studies me for a moment with the unhurried attention of someone who looks at things properly before speaking about them.

"The overextension was a choice," he says. "Your footwork before it was too clean. You'd controlled the geometry the entire exchange." He tilts his head slightly. "The reasons are your own. But the mechanics were good." A brief pause. "Better than good."

He says it without performance — no qualification, no social calculation around whether a compliment from an upperclassman requires a particular kind of receiving. Just the assessment, stated, and then he moves on toward the serving line.

I look at Kiwi.

She is staring at the space he just occupied.

"He talked to you," she says. Her voice is very quiet.

"He was discussing the duel."

"He talked to you." She turns to look at me. Her expression is difficult to categorize. "He has a nice voice."

"He does," Koaltan agrees, apparently deciding safety lies in agreement.

"He noticed the footwork," I say.

"He noticed you," Kiwi says. Then she seems to realize what she's said and picks up her apple with sudden great focus. "Anyway. We should go. Rhys's lecture."

Koaltan is visibly suppressing something. I make no comment.

We go.

The lecture hall is filling slowly when Pierce storms in.

His face is flushed, jaw tight. He scans the room like a hunting dog searching for prey.

"Who," he says, voice sharp enough to cut glass, "stole my cloak?"

The students already seated go still. A few exchange glances.

Professor Rhys enters late from the side door, arms full of scrolls. "Lord Pierce. Sit."

Pierce hesitates—clearly wanting to continue—but eventually drops into his seat with visible frustration.

I return to my notes.

Crunch.

The sound cuts through the settling quiet like a branch snapping.

Professor Rhys pauses mid-step, turning toward the noise.

Kiwi sits three rows behind me, eyes fixed innocently on the front of the room, chewing something loud and crunchy with exaggerated slowness.

The professor stares.

Kiwi slowly—without breaking eye contact—slides the snack onto Koaltan's desk.

Koaltan looks down at the small cloth-wrapped bundle now in front of him.

Then up at Kiwi.

"…Why."

She says nothing. Just keeps staring at the professor with wide, guileless eyes.

Rhys pinches the bridge of his nose, mutters something under his breath, and returns to setting up his materials before he pauses, patting his vest pockets. Frowns slightly.

"One moment," he says, glancing at his lectern. "I seem to have misplaced—"

His notes are gone.

He scans the podium surface, then looks up at the class with mild confusion.

"Curious," he mutters. "I was certain I brought..." He trails off, then straightens. "Excuse me. I'll return momentarily."

He exits into the hallway.

The door closes behind him.

For exactly two seconds, no one moves.

Then Kiwi stands, walks calmly to her bag, and retrieves a stack of papers from beneath it. She sets them carefully on the front desk, dusts off her hands, and returns to the door with deliberate calm.

She reaches for the handle, and —

Click.

Everyone turns.

She moves behind the podium at the front of the room, picks up Professor Rhys's reading glasses from where he left them, and slides them onto her face.

She squints.

"...How does he see anything through these?"

She removes them, sets them down carefully, and faces the class with total seriousness.

"Ladies and lords," she says, voice carrying. "We are gathered here today for a matter of grave political importance."

I do not look up from my notes.

Pierce shifts in his seat. "What are you doing?"

Kiwi's expression doesn't waver. "Justice."

She gestures grandly toward the empty seats, as if addressing a full courtroom.

"House Battlehorn has suffered a catastrophic loss of prestige. As provisional authority in the professor's absence, I will be conducting an inquiry into the theft of Lord Pierce's ceremonial cloak."

Koaltan closes his book slowly. "You are not authority."

Kiwi tilts her head. "I locked the door."

Beat.

No one argues.

She motions Pierce forward with one hand. "Lord Battlehorn. Please approach the bench."

Pierce hesitates, clearly torn between outrage and the deeply ingrained noble instinct to never refuse an audience.

The audience instinct wins.

He stands, straightens his shirt, and walks to the front of the room.
