The company was my sanctuary. In those blueprints, in the steady hum of construction sites and the satisfaction of projects completed, I found control. My father’s voice was a distant echo there, lost in the noise of progress. I knew every project by heart—every foundation, every steel beam. It was my domain, not his.

I exhaled slowly, turning off the water. The early morning light began to seep through the bathroom window, painting soft shadows on the tiles. I caught my reflection in the mirror—ice-blue eyes staring back at me, a mix of my mother’s ocean blue and my father’s steel gray. For a moment, I saw too much of him in that reflection. My jaw tightened, a vein ticking in my forehead. But I forced a deep breath, calming myself as I reached for the towel.

Wrapped in it, I padded into the bedroom, pulling on my black three-piece suit. The cool fabric settled against my skin, a protective layer between me and the world I was about to face.

The smell of fresh coffee greeted me as I entered the kitchen, its warmth already working to clear the lingering fog from my mind. I poured myself a cup and sank into one of the leather chairs, letting the heat seep into my fingers as I held the mug.

The silence of the penthouse pressed in around me, broken only by the distant hum of the city below. I rarely had visitors—just the maid who came twice a week and Sandy, when he wasn’t busy with business. The vastness of the space, though luxurious, felt hollow. Solitude clung to the corners, a constant, like the ticking of a clock.

I took a slow sip, savoring the warmth as it slid down my throat. The coffee was a brief comfort in the stillness, but it wasn’t enough to shake the sense of isolation that seemed to hang in the air. I finished the cup, setting it down with a quiet clink, and grabbed my keys from the counter. The cool metal rested reassuringly in my palm as I moved toward the door, the echo of my footsteps barely a whisper against the polished floor.

The penthouse, with all its sleek, pristine surfaces, often felt more like a gilded cage than a home. But as the door clicked shut behind me and I stepped into the hallway, a brief sense of freedom washed over me. I was ready to face the day ahead, the familiar pull of work beckoning me to the only place where I felt truly in control.

chapters.title: Lukas
chapters.content:
The building’s glass and steel exterior rose sharply against the soft dawn, casting cold reflections that mirrored the empire my family had meticulously crafted. As I pulled up to the security checkpoint, I lowered the window, and the brisk morning air washed over me, crisp and grounding. From outside, a faint ripple of laughter drifted in, surprising against the strict formality that usually hung over this place.

The guards were relaxed, exchanging a few easy jokes that broke the silence. For a fleeting second, their laughter cut through the polished emptiness surrounding me, reminding me of something I couldn’t quite grasp.

One of the guards, a solidly built man with lines of silver at his temples, stepped out of the booth, his stance easy and open—until his gaze landed on me. Recognition flickered, and in an instant, his relaxed posture stiffened, shoulders squared, the trace of a smile slipping into a curt, respectful nod.

“Good morning, Mr. Karpov,” he said, his tone steady but now stripped of the warmth he’d shown just seconds ago. He took my ID with mechanical precision, each movement efficient, practiced. Around him, the other guards snapped to attention, their casual ease replaced by rigid formality.

The shift was immediate, a silent acknowledgment of who I was—or rather, who they thought I was. It was a routine I’d seen countless times, yet each time, it hit the same. A reminder of the shadow that followed me, the reputation I’d inherited and could never quite outrun.

“Morning,” I replied, watching him slide my ID under the scanner, the faint beep punctuating the silence between us. We both knew it was unnecessary—there wasn’t a single person here who didn’t know my name or face. But in a place like this, appearances and formalities were the foundation, woven into every interaction.

He handed the card back with a brisk nod, his demeanor meticulously professional. “You’re all set, sir. Have a good day.”

I took the ID, pocketing it without a word. His eyes held a flicker of something—respect, maybe, or the guarded awareness people wore around me.

“Thank you,” I muttered, rolling up the window as the gate groaned open, the noise fading into the background as I drove past the checkpoint and into the parking lot. I pulled into my usual spot near the entrance, the closest I could get without attracting too much attention. For a moment, I sat there, fingers drumming absently on the steering wheel, eyes tracing the towering silhouette of the building.

It loomed above, all polished glass and steel, hiding a network of secrets in the shadows beyond those pristine walls. Out here, it looked like any other office complex, an architectural testament to success. But I knew better. Inside, under the sterile hum of fluorescent lights, the real work thrived in dim corridors, in coded conversations, in deals made off the books and off the radar. I took a deep breath, steeling myself for the day ahead, knowing I’d soon be stepping back into that world—a world that demanded as much from me as I’d ever taken from it.

Stepping out of the car, I tugged my jacket into place, running a hand over the fabric to smooth any creases—a habit drilled in from years of keeping up appearances. The sharp, rhythmic click of my shoes against the pavement broke through the morning’s stillness, each step echoing in the empty space around me. The air was crisp, carrying the faint scent of asphalt and steel, reminders of a city that never truly slept. As I neared the glass doors, my reflection stared back—composed, unreadable, the mask slipping into plaThe doors slid open with a soft whoosh, and a rush of cool, conditioned air greeted me as I stepped inside. The polished floors stretched out before me, gleaming under the stark, artificial lights, reflecting the pristine lines and calculated elegance of the lobby. The faint aroma of freshly brewed coffee drifted over from the café nestled to the side, a small comfort that was gone almost as soon as it reached me. As I moved deeper into the lobby, my path clear, I passed the security checkpoint without a glance from the guards. No one dared stop me here; my presence alone was an unspoken threat.

I kept my gaze fixed ahead, pretending not to notice the sudden hush that followed me through the lobby. Conversations cut off mid-sentence, laughter stopped short, lively chatter dissolving into tense murmurs.

It was the same every time—an unspoken ritual I’d grown used to, each pause and quieted word a reminder of the weight I brought with me. The air thickened whenever I entered, charged with a subtle deference I’d come to expect, yet it never failed to bring with it the same reminder.

The elevator doors slid open as I approached, and I stepped inside, the polished metal reflecting back an image I hardly recognized some days. The ride up was quick, and as I reached the executive level.

As I strode toward my office, the calm of the morning was interrupted by one of the employees stepping into my path. He was nervous, his hands shaking slightly as he extended a folder toward me. A brief glance upward revealed one of the HR staff, already sweating under the pressure of our encounter.

I raised an eyebrow, my annoyance clear. “What is this?” My tone was sharp, the unspoken reminder that wasting my time wasn’t an option.

The employee swallowed hard, his fingers trembling slightly as he adjusted his grip on the folder. “It’s the background check you requested, sir… on your new secretary.”

His nervousness did nothing to alleviate my irritation, though I took the folder from his hand, flipping it open without breaking stride. The details inside were expected—thorough, precise—but my mind was already on the meetings and the challenges ahead.

The weight of the day already felt suffocating as I stepped into my office, hoping for a moment of calm before the usual barrage of demands. But instead of the stillness I craved, I was greeted by an unexpected sight.

A figure was bent over my desk, her fingers moving quickly, rearranging my scattered papers with precision. The early morning sun streamed through the large windows, casting a warm glow over the room and illuminating her movements. Her focus was intense, her lips slightly pursed as she worked, unaware that I had entered.

“What exactly are you doing?” I asked, my voice cutting through the quiet, tinged with amusement.

She straightened up so fast that she nearly knocked over a stack of reports. Her cheeks flushed a delicate pink, her hands freezing midair like a child caught in the act. “Good morning, sir,” she stammered, blinking rapidly as if trying to reset herself. “I didn’t mean to barge in like this. I just saw that your desk was… well, a bit disorganized, and I thought I’d tidy it up for you. First impressions and all…” She trailed off, tucking a loose strand of hair behind her ear, her fingers trembling slightly.

I raised an eyebrow, taking in the sudden transformation of my workspace. My desk, usually a battlefield of scattered documents, now had a strange sense of order to it. The chaos I had grown used to was replaced with neatly stacked papers and organized files.

A rare sight.

“I appreciate the initiative,” I said, a slight edge of amusement softening my tone. “But next time, ask first.”

Her eyes widened, and she nodded quickly, almost too eagerly. “Of course, sir. It won’t happen again.” She straightened her blouse and adjusted her glasses, clearly trying to reassemble the professionalism she had lost in her flustered state.

Bemused, I watched her scramble to regain control, her movements fast, her nervous energy evident. She was trying to present herself as composed, but it was obvious she was still rattled. As I settled into the leather chair behind my now-neat desk, I allowed the moment to pass, shifting into the day ahead.

“Now, what’s on the schedule?” I asked, leaning back in my chair and crossing my arms, my tone sliding back into the sharper, more familiar edge of business.

She cleared her throat and quickly opened her notebook, her fingers flying over the pages. “You have a meeting first thing with the head of the Calido Group,” she said, handing me a neatly prepared folder.

I took it from her and flipped it open, the words barely registering before I let out a low, involuntary groan. The glossy images of the proposed nightclub stared back at me, accompanied by pages of overly optimistic financial projections. Ramirez Calido was always the same—he’d paint grandiose pictures of his ventures, all designed to dazzle investors, while hiding the true cost underneath layers of charm and deception.

The new secretary had enough tact to pretend she hadn’t heard my groan, though I noticed her lips twitch slightly as if she had to force herself not to react.

I scanned the documents, taking in the bold, slick presentation. The site was just a few blocks away from here, a prime location for a nightclub—if that was really all Calido wanted to build. My instincts told me otherwise. Beneath the polished facade, I could already sense the hidden angles, the shady side of the deal he wouldn’t dare put in writing.

I snapped the folder shut and sighed, the sound filled with the weight of yet another headache waiting to happen. “Wonderful,” I muttered under my breath.

The secretary shifted awkwardly on her feet, still standing by the desk, waiting for further instruction. I rubbed the bridge of my nose and closed my eyes for a brief second, trying to push the irritation away.

“Get me the numbers on his last project,” I said finally, leaning back and glancing at her. “And coffee. Strong.”

She nodded quickly, scribbling a note before hurrying out of the office. The soft click of the door closing behind her was the only sound left in the room. The sudden quiet brought no comfort—it was just a temporary pause before the day’s demands piled up again.

I sat there for a moment, staring at the closed folder, my fingers drumming lightly against the desk. The brief sense of peace I had hoped for had slipped away the moment I stepped into the building. The calm I craved, like always, was out of reach, drowned by the relentless noise of business.

He’d been circling my company like a vulture for months, desperate to have us back his latest endeavor. We both knew what it really was—a thinly veiled front for his illegal operations, just like all the others. This time, he was offering a forty percent share in the profits, as if that would make his underhanded dealings more palatable.

The sheer audacity of his demands was exhausting. Each proposal he sent my way was more absurd than the last, filled with grand promises and vague threats that did nothing to shake my resolve. His arrogance, while infuriating, was nothing new. I’d learned long ago that showing my frustration would only give him more satisfaction.

I glanced up at the secretary, standing there with her clipboard and an air of quiet professionalism. “When is this meeting?”

My voice remained steady, but there was no hiding the tension threading through each word. She flipped through one of the folders in her arms, then checked her watch. “In fifteen minutes, sir.”

Her tone was composed, though I caught a flicker of sympathy in her eyes. Everyone knew dealing with Ramirez Calido was like trying to wrestle a snake without getting bitten.

I sighed, glaring down at the folder one last time before standing up and making my way to the conference room. The weight of another round of negotiations with Calido sat heavily on my shoulders, pressing down as I walked through the quiet hallways. My footsteps echoed off the polished marble floors, each one a reminder of the confrontation to come.

When I stepped into the conference room, Calido was already there, lounging in his chair like he owned the place. His bright, cocky smile flashed across the room the moment he saw me. The tailored lines of his expensive suit and the casual way he leaned back spoke volumes. He was confident—no, overconfident, like always.

“Well, if it isn’t the mini-boss,” he sneered, his voice dripping with mockery. “Have you finally decided my proposal is good enough for the Karpov empire?”

His words hung in the air like a taunt, the smirk on his face practically daring me to rise to the bait. I knew better. Ramirez loved pushing buttons, testing limits, seeing how far he could go before getting a reaction.

I took a slow, measured breath, sinking into the chair across from him, forcing myself to remain calm. This was going to be a long exchange, and I’d need every ounce of patience I had to get through it. His arrogance filled the room, and I could already tell he had no intention of making this easy.

***

After nearly three grueling hours of verbal sparring with Calido, I finally managed to escape back to my office, my body and mind drained from the exhausting negotiations. While I’d succeeded in pushing through some of my demands and tempering his, the smug satisfaction on his face as he left the conference room lingered in my thoughts, gnawing at me. Calido had walked away thinking he had the upper hand, and that alone made the deal feel like a pyrrhic victory.

I leaned back in my chair, staring at the piles of reports that awaited me, their edges spilling over the desk like an avalanche of obligations. The once neatly arranged papers, courtesy of my new secretary, had reverted back to chaos, each document screaming for attention. The thought of diving into monthly reports after the marathon with Calido made my head pound, a dull throb already spreading behind my eyes.

This wasn’t where I should have been. My focus needed to be on cleaning up the mess Carpathia had left in his wake. His latest project had spiraled into disaster, and now the fallout was mine to manage—more collateral damage that my father would, no doubt, be eager to remind me was my responsibility. I rubbed my temples, feeling the weight of it all pressing down harder.

I reached for the damage report, flipping it open without much thought, but the numbers hit me like a punch to the gut. My fingers tightened around the paper, and I could feel my pulse rising, the thudding in my temples intensifying.

“You’ve got to be fucking kidding me!” The words burst out, sharp and bitter, as I scanned the figures. The damage was far worse than I’d imagined—staggering losses that would cripple some of our operations if not addressed immediately. I tossed the report back on the desk, my frustration flaring hotter as the implications sank in.

Millions lost. Equipment destroyed. And the delays—the delays alone would set us back months. Every page of the report was a fresh blow, each figure another reminder that the cleanup wasn’t just a logistical nightmare, but a ticking time bomb.

I slammed my fist onto the desktop, the force rattling the papers, pens, and everything else cluttering the surface. The impact reverberated through my arm, but the frustration inside me barely lessened. Out of the corner of my eye, I saw my secretary jump at the sudden noise. Her eyes widened, and I caught a glimpse of alarm flicker across her face as she stood frozen, uncertain.

I ignored her and glared down at the chaotic stack of papers, my mind racing. Loose ends—missing pages, incomplete reports, careless work. It infuriated me. I hated having to clean up after people who couldn’t be bothered to do their jobs properly, especially when I was already juggling more than enough. My father had taught me to value control above all else, and seeing things fall apart like this was intolerable.

With a sharp exhale, I stood up, feeling the heat of my anger rising. One last look at the pile of papers—the latest burden thrown onto an already overwhelming day—sent a surge of frustration through me. Before I could think, I grabbed the stack and hurled it across the room. The pages fluttered wildly before scattering across the floor, a disorganized mess reflecting the storm inside me.

Helplessness hit me like a wave, sharp and bitter. It wasn’t a feeling I was used to, and I hated it. It reminded me of what had happened a few days ago, of the mess Carpathia had created. He knew how to get under my skin, how to play the game better than most. Worse, he seemed to know exactly which buttons to press, and I couldn’t stand the thought of losing control, of being a pawn in whatever sick game he was playing.

The thought gnawed at me, twisting in my gut, making my hands tremble slightly at my sides.

“Sir?” a cautious voice cut through the fog of my thoughts, pulling me back into the present. I turned, my eyes narrowing as they landed on my secretary—what was her name again? Lydia? Lisa? I couldn’t remember. She stood at the edge of the room, her gaze flickering from me to the scattered papers on the floor, then back again. She shifted nervously, her hands clasped together, clearly unsure how to approach me in this state.

“What do you want?” I snapped, the frustration spilling over without restraint. The last thing I needed right now was another interruption. Another demand for my time, for my attention. My patience was hanging by a thread, and every new intrusion felt like another weight, dragging me down.

She looked briefly startled by the venom in my tone, but to her credit, she recovered quickly, straightening her posture with a nervous swallow. “Um, Mr. Artem Karpov is on line one for you,” she said, her voice wavering slightly but still maintaining a veneer of professionalism.

My scowl deepened, an involuntary reaction at the mention of his name. The last person I wanted to hear from right now was my father. Just the thought of him made my blood pressure spike. I toyed with the idea of ignoring the call, letting it go unanswered, but I knew better. Dismissing him would only invite more trouble later, and the tongue-lashing I’d receive at home was something I couldn’t afford right now—not on top of everything else. His constant anger was a shadow over my life, always lurking, always ready to smother me at the slightest misstep.

With an irritated wave of my hand, I dismissed the secretary. As soon as the door clicked shut behind her, I snatched the office phone, jabbing the button for line one. “Father.” My greeting was clipped, any hint of respect carefully stripped from my voice.

Our relationship had been strained for years, and the tension had only worsened in recent months. Every call, every conversation felt like a battleground, each word loaded with the potential to spark another argument. His overbearing nature and relentless interference were the main sources of my frustration, the reasons I felt trapped under his thumb, even in my own office.

“Lukas, turn on the news. Right now,” he barked, skipping any semblance of pleasantries. His voice carried the familiar harshness of a command, laden with the authority he wielded so effortlessly, and it struck the same defensive chord in me that it always did.

I clenched my jaw, glaring at the remote sitting on my desk. The 72-inch screen on the wall loomed over me, a silent reminder of the constant surveillance I felt under my father’s gaze, whether he was physically present or not.

“Why?” I shot back, unable to resist the small act of rebellion. I knew it would piss him off. My father hated being questioned, and the rebellious streak in me, the part of me that resented his control, relished these small moments of defiance.

“You’ll see,” he snapped, his tone brimming with impatience. I could hear the barely concealed annoyance seeping through the phone, and I smirked inwardly, knowing I’d gotten under his skin. His voice always had that edge, a mix of impatience and frustration that never failed to drag me back to my childhood, to the days of endless pressure and expectations I could never quite meet.

It had shaped me—this constant battle between us—but he would never understand the weight of it. He only saw what I wasn’t, what I should have been by now.

I bit back the snarky reply sitting on the tip of my tongue. It would have been satisfying to push him further, to see how much I could rile him up, but I knew the repercussions that would follow. I’d dealt with them plenty of times before, but right now, with Carpathia breathing down my neck and the pressure building on every front, I didn’t need my father’s wrath on top of it all.

As I flicked on the news, a bitter taste rose in my throat. The TV came to life with a flicker of light, and for a moment, I hesitated. It was always the same—an order barked through the phone like I was a dog he could command at will.

But then the image on the screen came into focus, and I felt the familiar knot of dread tightening in my stomach. I barely stopped the groan from escaping, keeping my face impassive despite the urge to curse aloud. My father thrived on pulling the strings, waiting for me to jump whenever he snapped his fingers.

A reporter stood outside a warehouse that I knew too well. Her face was composed, but I saw the cracks beneath the surface—the slight crease in her brow, the tension in the way she tugged her hair behind her ear, as though every word she spoke was a battle to remain composed. Behind her, the scene was a chaotic mess of flashing lights, cop cars, and forensic vans, their lights painting the warehouse in harsh reds and blues. Officers moved with a grim purpose, combing through the wreckage. My stomach churned.

The warehouse wasn’t just any building—it was one of ours. A vital hub in our logistics network, and the fact that the police were swarming all over it like flies made the situation far more dangerous than I wanted to admit. The reporter’s voice carried an edge of urgency beneath her professionalism, every syllable adding weight to the disaster unfolding in front of me.

“Last evening, authorities were alerted to this location after an anonymous tip-off. Details are scarce, but it appears there was a confrontation between two notorious gangs, the Serpent Kings and the Chain Vultures, just hours before police arrived.”

The camera panned over the scene: shattered windows, scorch marks licking the walls, debris scattered across the lot like the remnants of a war zone. Police officers sifted through the wreckage, their movements methodical and heavy with the weight of yet another crime scene to process.

I clenched my jaw, eyes narrowing at the footage. I knew where this was headed. The inevitable responsibility would fall on me like it always did, but I still had to ask, if only to delay the moment. “What about it?” I asked, forcing my voice to stay neutral even as tension coiled tighter inside me.

“This has gone too far,” my father snapped, his voice sharp, biting. “Fix it.”

Of course. Fix it. As though that was all it took to erase whatever mess Carpathia had stirred up. My fists curled into tight balls at my sides. “Why do I have to fix it?” The frustration bubbled up, slipping through my control. “Carpathia’s the one behind all of this, and yet I’m the one—”

“Lukas.” My father’s voice sliced through my words like a knife, cold and dismissive. “You will fix this. If you plan on ever running the business—on ever being worthy of being called my son.”

The line went dead with a click, the dial tone blaring in my ear before I realized he’d hung up. His words were still ringing in my head, the sting of them sharper than I cared to admit. I slammed the phone down into the cradle, the force of it rattling the desk as I muttered through clenched teeth.

“Un-fucking-believable.”

I stared at the phone, the anger boiling beneath the surface, every muscle in my body tight with tension. Of course, he would dump his dirty work on me again. Of course, he’d expect me to clean up this disaster without hesitation.

I pushed myself away from the desk, my movements sharp, barely controlled as I paced across the office. My hands dragged through my hair, pulling at the strands in frustration. The walls felt like they were closing in, my thoughts racing with no clear direction. With every step, the weight of his expectations bore down on me, pressing harder and harder.

In a burst of frustration, I kicked the trash bin next to my desk. It spun across the floor, scattering its contents and leaving my office even more disheveled. The mess on the floor mirrored the mess in my head. The room felt smaller, more suffocating with each passing second. Control—something I thrived on—was slipping further from my grasp.

I took a deep breath, fighting to keep my temper in check. The urge to punch something, to let the rage boil over, was almost overwhelming. Damn it. How does he expect me to fix this? It wasn’t my fault that Carpathia had thrown everything into chaos, but somehow, my father always managed to shove the fallout into my lap. Always.

Shaking my head, I stalked over to the floor-to-ceiling window that overlooked Brooklyn’s business district, the city sprawling beneath me in neat grids. I leaned one arm against the glass, pressing my forehead against the cool surface as I let out another long, frustrated sigh. The city buzzed with life below, oblivious to the storm brewing in my world, the chaos that Carpathia had unleashed.

He wanted this—wanted his rivals to crack, to slip into disarray. And damn it, so far, he was getting exactly what he wanted. The more chaos he stirred, the easier it became for him to tighten his grip. I’d been helpless to stop him so far, and that burned worse than anything.

But that had to change.

I pushed the anger down, burying it beneath the cold calculation I knew I needed right now. This was going to take everything I had—every favor I could pull, every ounce of leverage I could muster. I would need to control the narrative, manipulate the media, and keep our name from getting dragged through the mud. Failure wasn’t an option. Not if I wanted to prove myself—to my father, to myself.

I pulled away from the window, reaching into my pocket and pulling out one of the burner phones I kept on hand. The familiar weight of it in my palm was a strange comfort amid the chaos, a reminder that I wasn’t entirely powerless here. The number I dialed was one I knew by heart, each press of the buttons almost automatic.

It rang once before a voice picked up, low and steady. I didn’t wait for pleasantries.

“Sandy, I need you to send someone to do a deep clean,” I said, letting my Russian accent slip through, thickening each word. Old habits. You never knew who might be listening. The code phrase had been used before, and Sandy wouldn’t need any more explanation.

The line went quiet for a beat, long enough that I wondered if Sandy hadn’t heard me. Then, his voice cut through, laced with a familiar hint of exasperation. “I’m guessing you got a call from daddy dearest. Who needs to be dealt with this time, and why?” He knew the routine all too well.

I let out a slow breath, my gaze drifting back to the television, where the warehouse footage still dominated the screen—police officers, crime scene tape, and evidence bags. It was a mess, and it was my mess to clean up, courtesy of my father’s grand expectations. “You didn’t catch the news?” I asked, my tone dry. “Looks like our visit to the warehouse attracted some unwanted attention.”

“Nah,” Sandy replied with a dismissive snort, though I could hear the concern edging into his voice. “You know I don’t watch that depressing shit. It’s too much.”

I chuckled under my breath. Of course, Sandy would try to brush it off with humor, even now. “Well, it’s all over the news. Seems like the boys in blue got curious about our little warehouse escapade.”

The line went silent for a moment before I heard Sandy let out a long, resigned sigh. “Alright, who needs the money? The Boys in Blue? The media? Or those who sit on the judgment seats?” His tone shifted, all business now, ready to mobilize the resources we’d need to put out this fire.

I smirked, though it barely reached my eyes. “All of the above, apparently.” I ran a hand through my hair, the weight of it all pressing heavier by the second. “My father’s convinced I have to fix this.” My voice held more frustration than I intended, the words tasting bitter on my tongue.

Sandy chuckled, the dry sound on the other end of the line. “Of course he is. That’s the price you pay when the King of Brooklyn is your old man.”

“Self-proclaimed king,” I muttered automatically. It didn’t matter if it was true—if he was the king. To me, he was nothing more than a figurehead with an iron grip on my life, leaving me to do all the dirty work behind the scenes. The bitterness in my voice was unmistakable, even to me.

Sandy was quiet for a moment, and when he spoke again, his voice was more serious. “You want this mess to go away, right? Not for him—but for your own plans.” He understood the stakes, the long game I was trying to play. This wasn’t just about damage control. This was about my future, about stepping out of my father’s oppressive shadow once and for all.

“Exactly,” I said, my voice tired but firm. I leaned back against the glass, the cool surface grounding me. “I’m not doing this to clean up his messes anymore. This merger is supposed to be my ticket. I’m done playing the janitor in his empire.”

“You can make a lot of things disappear with a few thousand bucks.” Sandy’s voice was steady, reassuring in the way only he could be. “Leave it to me. We’ll take care of it.”

“I hope so,” I muttered, running a hand down my face. “This is the third time this month we’ve had to pay them off.” The incidents were happening too often, and each one chipped away at my patience.

“Money’s never been a problem for you,” Sandy replied almost cheerfully. “We’ve got it covered. You just focus on your wedding—oops, I mean your merger.” The line went dead before I could respond, leaving me alone with his parting jab hanging in the air.

For a moment, I wasn’t sure whether I wanted to laugh or curse him out. Sandy’s flippant attitude, while usually a welcome distraction, felt sharper today, like a reminder of just how much pressure was bearing down on me.

I slipped the burner phone back into my pocket and leaned my forehead against the window, the cool glass fogging slightly as I exhaled. My breath left small, clouded patches on the pane as I stared out at the city below. Brooklyn stretched out before me, vast and indifferent.

This merger—this wedding—was supposed to be my way out, my chance to finally prove myself without my father’s shadow looming over every move I made. But every day, it felt like that shadow grew heavier, more suffocating. I pressed my fist against the glass, jaw tight.

Failure wasn’t an option. Not this time.

This was my chance, and I’d be damned if I didn’t reap every single benefit it promised.

chapters.title: Jayna
chapters.content:
I stood in the center of the bustling room, my hands resting on my hips as I watched the workers meticulously drape the soft, flowing fabric across the stage. The material billowed gently, catching the light as it created a cascading, elegant backdrop for the event. Around me, the steady clink of cutlery and the rustling of linens filled the air, blending with the hum of quiet conversations and the occasional burst of laughter from the crew. The space buzzed with a mix of concentration and anticipation, each person intent on their task.

In the corner, the rolled-up banner for Angela’s Angel Foundation in partnership with Sheltered Kids waited to be unveiled. Its bold, vibrant lettering promised hope and change, a visual testament to all the work that had gone into this moment. The bright colors and uplifting message felt like a beacon, a reminder of what we were here to accomplish. The transformation of the space, from an empty hall to a room brimming with potential, made me smile.

I took in the scene, my heart swelling with pride. This wasn’t just another event—this was special. It was a tribute to my mother’s legacy, something she would have been so proud to see. The foundation’s work meant the world to her, and today, as we prepared to make a real impact on the lives of these kids, I felt her presence more than ever. It was as if, through every draped piece of fabric and polished table setting, her influence lingered.

I was pulled from my thoughts by the sound of someone clearing their throat. Turning, I saw Wanda and Lauren approaching. Wanda, with her calm, steady presence, always brought a sense of order to the chaos, while Lauren’s bright energy was like a spark that kept everything moving.

“Jayna, everything is coming along wonderfully,” Wanda said, her voice reassuring, as it always was.

I smiled, feeling the weight of her words settle over me like a balm. “Thanks, Wanda. I’m really pleased with how it’s turning out,” I said, my gratitude for her and the team overflowing.

Lauren stepped forward, holding a clipboard close to her chest. “We just need your approval on the final schedule and a quick walk through of the setup,” she said, her excitement evident even in her professional tone.

I took the clipboard from her, scanning the well-organized schedule with a sense of quiet satisfaction. Every detail, every timeline was accounted for, each element designed to ensure that the event would flow seamlessly. This was more than an event—it was the culmination of months of planning, a reflection of our collective dedication to these kids and the cause we held dear.

“Everything looks perfect,” I said, handing the clipboard back to her with a nod. “Let’s do the walk through.”

As we moved through the hall, inspecting each detail, I couldn’t help but feel a renewed sense of purpose settle over me. The tables, carefully arranged with floral centerpieces, glowed under the soft lighting, and the backdrop, now fully in place, made the stage feel inviting, like a place where something important would unfold. This was more than just another charity gala; it was a testament to everyone’s hard work and commitment, a chance to bring real, lasting change.

Just as we were about to wrap up the walk through, the soft patter of footsteps echoed across the hall. I turned, catching sight of two children—a boy and a girl—bounding toward me, their faces bright with excitement and curiosity. They couldn’t have been more than eight or nine, their energy filling the space like a ray of sunshine cutting through the last of the morning preparations.

“Miss Jayna!” the girl called out, her voice bubbling with enthusiasm. Her wide smile was infectious, her eyes sparkling with a sense of wonder that instantly drew me in.

I knelt down to their level, my smile mirroring hers. “Hello there! What are your names?”

“I’m Lily,” she said proudly, beaming up at me. “And this is my brother, Max.”

Max, more reserved, gave a small, shy wave. His eyes darted around the room, wide with awe as he took in the decorated hall. “Hi,” he said softly, his voice almost lost in the buzz of the activity around us.

“It’s so nice to meet you both, Lily and Max,” I said, my heart warming at their presence. “Are you excited about tomorrow?”

They nodded vigorously, Lily’s enthusiasm leading the charge. “Yes! Very excited!” she exclaimed, bouncing slightly on her toes. “We just wanted to say thank you for everything you’re doing. It’s really nice to have people who care about us.”

Max, finding a bit more courage in his sister’s energy, chimed in, his voice a touch louder. “Yeah, thank you, Miss Jayna. We don’t get to go to events like this very often. It’s really special.”

Their words hit me straight in the heart, and I felt a lump form in my throat. I reached out, gently taking their hands in mine, feeling the warmth of their gratitude radiate through the simple touch. “Thank you for telling me that. It means so much to hear. I’m so glad you’re both here, and I hope you have the best time tomorrow.”

Lily’s eyes gleamed with gratitude, her small hand squeezing mine. “We will! And thank you for making it so fun!”

Max nodded beside her, his smile growing a little wider, his earlier shyness fading. “Yeah, thank you.”

I stood up slowly, watching as they ran off, their laughter echoing across the hall as they joined the other children already exploring the space. Their joy, so pure and unguarded, sent a wave of emotion through me. It was moments like this—moments of connection and unfiltered gratitude—that made all the late nights and meticulous planning worthwhile. It wasn’t about the logistics or the grandeur of the event—it was about the happiness we could bring into their lives, even if just for a day.

Wanda, who had been quietly observing, stepped closer, her calm presence grounding me. “Moments like that make it all worth it, don’t they?”

I nodded, still watching Lily and Max as they disappeared into the flurry of decorations and excited voices. “Yes, they really do.”

As the final touches fell into place and the event came to life around us, a deep sense of fulfillment settled over me. This was what it was all about—more than the banners or centerpieces. It was about creating moments of joy and hope for the children, giving them a sense of belonging, even if only for a little while. Each smile, each bit of laughter, was a reminder that we were making a difference, one child at a time.

The night had been a blur of restless tossing and turning, my mind unable to quiet. The events of the day replayed over and over in fragments—flashes of excited smiles from the children, the pressure of final details, the lingering anxiety of what could go wrong. Sleep, when it came, was shallow, each moment of peace shattered by the whirlwind of thoughts swirling in my head.

When morning finally arrived, it felt like no time had passed at all. My body felt heavy as I dragged myself out of bed, exhaustion clinging to my every move. The soft light of dawn filtered through the curtains, but it did little to ease the fog in my head. I shuffled into the kitchen, the promise of a hot cup of coffee the only thing pulling me forward.

The familiar aroma of freshly brewed coffee greeted me, offering a small comfort as I leaned against the counter, my fingers wrapped around the warm mug. The rich, earthy scent grounded me, reminding me that I had faced challenges like this before, and somehow, I had always pulled through. Still, the knot in my stomach refused to loosen completely.

As I took my first sip, my phone buzzed on the counter, pulling me back into the moment. I reached for it, my thumb swiping across the screen to reveal a message from Wanda.

Wanda: Morning, Jayna! Just a quick reminder about the final walk-through at 10 AM. Let me know if you need anything else. We’ve got this!

Her words, filled with her usual calm and reassurance, brought a small smile to my face. Wanda had this uncanny way of grounding me, her steady confidence acting as a counterbalance to my racing thoughts. I quickly typed out a response.

Jayna: Thanks, Wanda. I’ll be there. Let’s make today amazing!

I set the phone down and took a deep breath, letting the warmth of the coffee flow through me, slowly pushing back the cloud of exhaustion. Wanda was right—we did have this. The excitement and anticipation of the event still bubbled just beneath the surface, but now there was a sliver of calm edging its way in.

After finishing my coffee, I headed for the shower, the hot water helping to wash away the last remnants of sleeplessness clinging to my skin. I had picked out the perfect dress for today—an elegant, full-length red gown that radiated confidence. As I slipped into it, I caught a glimpse of myself in the mirror, feeling a spark of determination light inside me. This event was more than just an obligation; it was a reflection of everything we’d worked for.

Grabbing my bag, I cast one final glance around the apartment, my eyes sweeping over the scattered papers on the coffee table and the half-drunk cup of coffee on the counter. With a sigh, I stepped out the door, my heels tapping sharply against the hardwood floor. Each step felt purposeful, my pace quickening as the weight of the day settled on my shoulders.

The drive to the venue blurred by in a whirlwind of mental checklists. My fingers drummed impatiently on the steering wheel at every red light, my thoughts running faster than the car could move. The centerpieces still need tweaking. Have the programs arrived? I hope the AV team is ready…

When I pulled into the lot, the event hall loomed ahead, its glass façade reflecting the busy flurry of movement inside. I could already hear the hum of voices before I even stepped out of the car. The moment I entered, the buzz of activity washed over me. Volunteers hurried past, some balancing floral arrangements while others adjusted banners along the walls. The catering staff moved like clockwork, setting up the food stations with practiced precision, trays of pastries and steaming coffee filling the air with warmth.

Across the room, I spotted Wanda, her curly hair bouncing as she gestured animatedly to one of the volunteers. Her bright red lipstick stood out against her soft smile, even from a distance. The moment our eyes met, she waved, her expression lighting up as she weaved through the crowd toward me.

“Morning, Jayna!” she called out, her voice cutting through the chatter. “How are you holding up?”

Her gaze searched my face, a mix of concern and anticipation. I let out a breath, offering her a smile that I hoped conveyed more confidence than I felt. “I’m alright,” I said, straightening my posture as if that could chase away the exhaustion clinging to me. “Just a bit tired, but I’m ready. Let’s get this show on the road.”

Wanda nodded, her playful smile slipping into a more focused expression. “We’ve got everything under control. The kids are starting to trickle in, and the media crew is getting their equipment set up by the main stage. All we need now is your final approval on the schedule, and we’re ready to roll.”

She handed me the clipboard, the smooth surface cool against my fingers as I flipped through the neatly organized pages. Every slot was filled with careful planning, each activity set to flow seamlessly into the next. The names of volunteers and presenters were written in sharp black ink, their roles clear and precise. I could see the months of preparation condensed into this one sheet of paper, and a wave of pride swelled inside me. Our team had pulled off something special.

I glanced back up at Wanda, her eyes searching mine for reassurance. “Looks perfect,” I said, a smile tugging at my lips as I handed the clipboard back. “Let’s make this happen.”

With a quick nod, Wanda turned on her heel, already relaying the go-ahead to the rest of the team, her voice a blend of calm authority and excitement. I lingered for a moment, standing in the center of the bustling hall. The air buzzed with energy—children’s laughter echoed from one side, the clatter of trays from the catering team on the other. The decorations we’d painstakingly designed shimmered under the soft overhead lights, and the scent of freshly brewed coffee mingled with the sweet aroma of pastries.

This was it. Months of late nights, endless meetings, and careful planning had all led to this day. It wasn’t about the recognition or the flawless execution of the event—it was about the kids. Their wide-eyed wonder as they explored the space, the joy that would light up their faces during the activities we had lined up. That was the heart of it all.

I closed my eyes for a brief second, letting the moment sink in, feeling the weight of it settle in my chest. My hands tightened around the strap of my bag as a familiar warmth washed over me.

This one’s for you, Mom. Every step, every decision—I hope you’re watching. I hope I’m making you proud.

As I stepped into the event hall, I was immediately struck by its sheer beauty. The room glowed under the soft lighting, casting a warm, inviting atmosphere. Delicate shades of pinks and blues cascaded across every surface, blending together like a pastel dream. The decorations were exquisite—floral arrangements of hydrangeas and peonies lined the tables, and elegant streamers hung from the ceiling, their soft hues blending into the walls. It felt as though the entire room was bathed in a gentle, otherworldly glow.

A soft hum of jazz played in the background, the gentle notes curling through the air as the orchestra set the perfect mood, their music rising and falling in an effortless rhythm that filled the room with sophistication. It was mesmerizing.

Glancing around, I noticed some of the kids had already taken their seats, their eyes wide with wonder as they whispered excitedly to one another. Others, braver and filled with energy, had wandered onto the dance floor, twirling around with infectious laughter. Seeing their joy, the light in their eyes, made every late night, every stressful moment, worth it. This was why we worked so hard—to create moments like this, where they could feel celebrated and free.

The hum of voices quieted as Lisa’s voice echoed through the room, her words carrying easily over the soft music. “Good evening, everyone. Thank you for joining us here today to celebrate the kids and everything they’ve achieved with our support. Tonight, we honor not only their accomplishments but the journey they’ve taken to get here. And none of this,” she paused, glancing my way, “would have been possible without the tireless efforts of Jayna. Without her, this organization wouldn’t be where it is today, and we wouldn’t be able to make a difference in these kids’ lives.”

The room erupted into applause, the sound reverberating off the walls. I felt the weight of dozens of eyes turn toward me, and for a moment, a flicker of nerves crept up my spine. But as I looked around at the smiling faces, the warm, grateful eyes of the children and their families, I couldn’t help but smile back. I gave a small nod, a quiet gesture of thanks, and a sense of contentment washed over me.

This was a moment to cherish, and even though the spotlight felt unnerving, I knew this was where I was meant to be.

“Well, don’t let me stop your fun. Let the party begin!” I exclaimed, raising my voice above the excited chatter. The room shifted in an instant, like a switch had been flipped. The music transitioned into an upbeat rhythm, and the lively beats pulsed through the speakers, energizing the room. Laughter and cheers echoed as the kids jumped onto the dance floor, their carefree joy filling the space. Sponsors mingled with the children, talking and laughing, while Maisy, our photographer, moved stealthily through the crowd, her camera flashing as she captured moments for our social media pages.

“Well, I can see you know how to throw a party,” a familiar voice called from behind me.

I turned to find Frederick Glass standing there, his sharp suit perfectly tailored as usual, a hint of amusement in his dark eyes. I couldn’t help but offer him a small, knowing smile. “I didn’t think you’d actually come. Didn’t you say these events were just ‘innovative ways to scam people out of their good money’?” I raised an eyebrow at him, my tone teasing.

He chuckled, shaking his head. “Yeah, well, there’s that.” His grin softened as he shifted his weight, glancing around the room. “But I can’t exactly say no to you, can I? Plus, I stumbled onto your Instagram page the other day. I couldn’t resist those photos of the kids. You might as well sue me for getting soft,” he muttered, a playful edge to his voice.

I rolled my eyes, a scoff escaping me as I crossed my arms. “Well, I’ll keep the lawsuit on hold for now. What’s more important is that you’re here, and trust me, I’m grateful for that.” I grinned, a lightness in my tone. “Besides, it doesn’t hurt that you’re loaded. Your presence alone bumps up our credibility,” I added with a laugh, nudging him lightly.

He smirked, his eyes narrowing in mock offense. “Always hitting me where it hurts, huh? My wallet.”

The two of us had met back in business school, and for a time, we’d been inseparable. But life had a way of pulling people in different directions, and we’d drifted apart when my personal struggles took over. Recently, though, we reconnected, and I was reminded of why we’d been such good friends in the first place. Frederick was running his own company now, making waves in the industry, and despite everything, he had shown up for me tonight. That meant more than he probably knew.

His expression shifted suddenly, his features softening as he asked, “Where’s Abby?” There was a slight hesitation in his voice, and I noticed the way his eyes softened at the mention of her name.

Ah, Abby. She was a dear friend and, for as long as I could remember, the object of Frederick’s unspoken affection. They had danced around each other for years, and despite his usual confidence, when it came to her, he seemed a bit unsure.

I noticed the way Frederick’s cheeks flushed slightly, a hint of pink rising along his sharp cheekbones. “I’m sure she’s around here somewhere,” I said, glancing toward the catering section. “Probably giving one of the chefs an earful about how the hors d’oeuvres aren’t perfectly arranged or something.” My voice was light, but I wasn’t laughing like he was. His chuckle came easily, but I just stared at him, raising an eyebrow.

“Why am I not surprised?” he mused, shaking his head. “At least I see she’s still the spitfire I remember.”

“Yup, same old Abby,” I said, a grin tugging at the corners of my lips. “Now, go on. Enjoy the food, the music, and have some effortless fun for once. You’ve earned it.”

Frederick gave me one final smile, warm and genuine, before resting his hand on my shoulder for a brief, comforting squeeze. His touch was familiar, but brief, and before I could say anything more, he turned and blended into the crowd, disappearing into the throng of guests.

I stayed back, hovering at the edge of the room where I could watch the event unfold like a silent observer. The gentle hum of conversation filled the air, mixed with the occasional burst of laughter. The kids were getting comfortable, I could tell. They had started to warm up to the donors, their initial shyness melting away as they were drawn into animated conversations or guided toward the dance floor.

Seeing them like that—carefree, happy, their faces lit with excitement—it filled me with a sense of quiet contentment. This was exactly what I had wanted for them. A space where they could feel important, where they were seen and celebrated. Watching them, I couldn’t help but think back to when I was their age. The ten-year-old girl who had been terrified, uncertain of her place in the world, and desperate for someone to notice her. I hadn’t had something like this, a moment where I felt like I truly mattered.

But tonight, these kids did. And that was enough.

I should have known better. All good things come to an end.

As I made my way toward the refreshment table, weaving through the pockets of laughter and easy conversation, something caught my attention. Near the far wall, standing still while the rest of the room moved around him, was a man. He didn’t blend in, despite the suit that fit his broad shoulders perfectly. There was something off about him—the way he stood, the way his eyes scanned the room without really seeing it. His suit may have been tailored, but it wasn’t his true uniform. He looked like someone who belonged in dark alleys and backroom deals, not at a charity event.

The air around him seemed colder, like a chill creeping in through a crack no one else noticed. I stopped mid-step, my smile fading as a knot of unease twisted in my stomach. Nope. I wasn’t sticking around to find out what he wanted. I turned on my heel, my eyes darting through the crowd, searching for Wanda. I had a sinking feeling about who had sent him, and whatever it was, I wanted nothing to do with it.

But before I could slip away, I felt it—him—moving with me, shadowing my steps. His presence loomed behind me, and then his voice, low and firm, confirmed my worst fear.

“George has requested your presence.”

I froze. That voice, flat and unyielding, was like running into a brick wall. I sighed, closing my eyes for a brief second before turning to face him, hands planted firmly on my hips. “Do I have a choice?” I asked, though I already knew the answer.

“No,” he replied, his tone devoid of emotion, just cold efficiency.

I let out a bitter laugh, anger flaring inside me. “Then it’s not really a request, is it?” My voice sharpened, the old frustration bubbling to the surface. “What does he want this time? Found a new way to fuck up my life?”

Just saying my father’s name left a sour taste in my mouth. George. He wasn’t a man you could just walk away from. Control, manipulation, and endless battles—that was my childhood. Leaving had been my only escape, and the last thing I wanted was to be dragged back into his orbit.

The man shrugged, indifferent. “You’ll have to come and find out.” His eyes darkened, a subtle gleam of threat behind them. “We can do this the easy way or the hard way. But I doubt the kids would enjoy watching me drag you out of here.”

His words hung heavy between us, a clear threat that made my skin crawl. I could feel the tension building in my muscles, my fists clenching at my sides. Men like him—they didn’t ask twice. They were the kind my father always surrounded himself with—hired hands to enforce his power, to keep everyone in line.

I looked around the room, at the kids laughing, their faces bright with joy. This was their day, their moment, and I wasn’t about to ruin it for them. Not because of him. My jaw tightened as I swallowed my frustration, the weight of my decision sinking in.

“Fine,” I muttered, the word laced with venom. “Lead the way.”

The man’s grip on my arm was firm, guiding me forward with a quiet insistence, each step pulling me further from the life I’d carefully built.

As we approached the exit, I cast one last glance over my shoulder, letting my gaze linger on the laughter, the bright smiles, the world I was leaving behind—if only temporarily. At least I hoped it was temporary. The warmth of the room seemed to grow dimmer, the cheerful hum of voices a faint echo, receding as though it belonged to another life.

In the crowd, I caught a glimpse of Wanda, her face turned away, too caught up in the celebration to notice my departure. A pang of regret settled in my chest. I could only hope she’d keep the day running smoothly, keep the joy alive for the kids. They deserved a day uninterrupted by my past.

We stepped outside, and the sharp evening air hit me like a slap, prickling my skin and filling my lungs with a bitter chill. The sounds of the party were muffled now, as though a heavy door had closed between me and the warmth inside, sealing me off. Everything seemed colder, the shadows stretching long in the dimming light.

At the curb, a sleek black car waited, polished and ominous, its tinted windows concealing whatever lay within.

The man released my arm, stepping forward to open the door, his silent gesture an invitation—or a command. I hesitated for a moment, my heart pounding, the weight of every choice I’d made pressing down on me.

The threshold of that car felt like a line drawn in sand, one I couldn’t cross without consequences. But there was no turning back now. Taking a steadying breath, I stepped forward, slipping into the dark interior. The door closed with a heavy finality, sealing me in, and as the car pulled away, the warmth of the party faded into a distant memory, swallowed by the encroaching night.

data.title: Modern Day Martial Arts
data.author: TheeRaven
data.summary:
He died the day the sky turned red.

He woke up on Earth. No qi. No clans. No war. Just a second life in a world that should have nothing to do with the one he lost. For years, Blue lived quietly—training in secret, holding onto a power no one else could see.

Then the gates opened. Monsters poured through. Cities fell. Humanity awakened powers to survive. But Blue didn’t awaken, he had something else. Something this world wasn’t meant to understand. Now a porter in modern-day Ohio, he keeps his head down— Until a golden gate appears. One only he can enter.

On the other side… Murim still exists. But everything is wrong. His name is gone. His power is sealed. And something is watching him. Guided by a system that hides as much as it reveals, Blue is forced onto a new path— joining the Silent Edge Corps in a world already on the brink of collapse. To survive, he must abandon the path that once defined him… and become something far more dangerous.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.content:
[Welcome back, Tang Jiung.]
Before I returned to Murim, before the system called me home, before my sister became someone who looked at me like a stranger… I died.
I remember the sky turning red.
I remember the gates opening.
I remember the blade.
Cold. Black. Final.
And then—nothing.
Before Murim fell… before the system called me home… there was my grandfather.
They said my grandfather once stood against the Heavenly Demon himself.That for three days, the sky trembled.That neither of them yielded. Inever saw that battle.I only saw what came after.
Before I came along... my father also had his own problems.

───

Inside the Tang great hall, a storm awaited."You will marry the daughter of the Sword Saint of Namgung!" Yoryeon's voice shook the walls. "You cannot simply run off with a woman you met at a bar!"
Jinho remained kneeling, head lowered. "I love her, Father. I will not marry a woman I've only met twice."
"You would discard an alliance that strengthens this clan for her?"
"She is the woman I love," Jinho said.
An elder stepped forward. "Young Master, you shame—"
"Silence!" Yoryeon's word struck like steel. He rose, fists clenched. "Is she worth exile?"
"She is pregnant, Father."
Gasps filled the hall.
"Everyone out. Now."
As the elders filed from the great hall, Yoryeon's hands slowly relaxed. "I am going to be a grandfather." His face softened. "I have met this woman. She refused my gold. She refused my anger. And she chose you anyway." He looked at his son. "You have chosen well."
"Father?" Jinho looked at him, confused.
"Do you know why I am strong?" Yoryeon asked quietly. "It is for you. For your mother. For this clan. So that you may be happy and choose your own path." He exhaled slowly. "You will be removed as young leader. Shunned. Cast out. But I will always love you. And I will protect you, no matter what." He gestured toward the door. "Go. I will have a house arranged outside Chengdu."
Jinho left the clan that day.

───

For ten years, he worked as a caravan escort, protecting merchants through dangerous roads. His wife stayed home with their five children. Yoryeon visited when he could, training and sparring with Jinho in secret.Only one set of eyes ever watched.Mine.
I was ten years old, pressed against a storehouse wall, absorbing every movement. That was the night my dream of martial arts was born.
"Grandfather! Please — teach me!" I dropped to my knees, hands flat on the floor.
"I cannot, my grandson," Yoryeon said.
"Why? Why will no one allow me?" The anger in my voice surprised even me.
"You are not affiliated with the Tang Clan. If that day comes, I will train you. Until then, it is your parents' wish that you not step into this side of Murim."
And so I watched. Copying movements in secret — crude, unrefined, but alive.
The knock came at dawn.Not from Yoryeon. A stranger in a merchant's crest, stained with blood.
"There were no survivors," the man said.
I didn't understand.
My mother fell to the ground. "Jinho… your father… he is dead."
The words didn’t make sense at first.They just… hung there.
Weeks passed. She searched everywhere—townspeople, merchants, even bandits.Every lead ended in silence.Every day, hope bled a little more.
One evening she returned, face pale and trembling."They burned the body," she whispered.
Each day grew heavier after that. I started sleeping with one eye open, keeping watch over her. I began to follow her through alleys and markets, silent, learning what desperation looked like from the outside.Then one evening, Yoryeon arrived.His face was grave. His eyes were heavy.
"Grandfather? Why are you here?" I whispered.
"I'm sorry, Jiung," he said. "Your mother she's...dead. He swallowed. "Murdered." "I will do what I can to protect you and your siblings."
Something inside me went quiet after that.
Grandfather stepped down as patriarch that same night, taking responsibility for the grandchildren and the mistakes of the past.

───

Years passed without a word about the clan.I worked — cleaning dishes, cooking meals, keeping the younger ones fed and clothed. At night, I snuck out and watched Yoryeon train the way I always had. The old man moved like a ghost, faster than my eyes could follow.
"Old, my ass," I muttered often.
I thought if I could mimic even a fraction of what I saw, I might carve a path of revenge for my mother and father.When So-Yeon. Ny younger sister, begged to attend a martial academy, I understood. I couldn't have what I wanted — but I would not deny it to her. Together, with Yoryeon's help, we enrolled her.For months I watched her come home from the academy each day. I watched her train and spar and grow. And I said nothing.Yoryeon saw it on my face.
One night he found me outside. "Tonight, after the others are in bed — come find me."
I stood under the willow tree while he stared at the stars.
I didn’t know it then…but everything I would become started that night.
"There is much I regret," he said. "I couldn't change the rules for your father. And now, watching you take his place raising his children…" He paused. "Perhaps this is how I atone."
"You've done enough, Grandfather. You owe me nothing."
"Even so." He placed a hand on my shoulder. "I will teach you what I can. The Tang breathing technique. The basics passed through our bloodline — daggers, poisons, hidden weapons. The foundation. The rest will be up to you."
For a moment I felt something like joy. Then reality settled back in.
"I know nothing. I'm responsible for my siblings. I'm not even affiliated with the clan." My voice came out quieter than I intended. "Maybe this dream came too late for me."
"You are my grandson," Yoryeon said. "The son of Jinho — a man of the Tang Clan. Take pride in that." He squeezed my shoulder once. "My time is short. But this much I can leave behind."
From that night onward, we trained under the stars. He taught me to breathe, to feel the flow of qi within my body, to mold it, to sharpen it. I learned what it meant to be third-rate. I read manuals late into the night and practiced stances until my legs gave out.He never called himself my master.
"I'm just a grandfather," he said once, laughing. "Fulfilling a promise before I go."
He passed away months later.The Tang Clan held a grand funeral. Lanterns stretched across the streets of Chengdu. Warriors of every sect came to pay their respects. I watched from the crowd, hidden, knowing we were still exiles despite our blood.My siblings and I mourned in our own way. But life continued. It had to. Death had become too familiar.I kept training. So-Yeon advanced quickly in her school. The younger ones found their own paths.
By the age of twenty, every day seemed to pass like the one before. Molded by grief. Taught by sorrow. I had become the head of my family without ever choosing to be — and I believed, foolishly, that the worst was behind us.That was until the day the sky turned blood-red.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 - Rebirth on Earth
chapters.content:
The screams didn’t fade when I died.
They followed me. Murim was already collapsing when the gates opened.
 
The sky split open like torn flesh, a jagged wound of crimson light. Screams tore through the land as gates of black and gold erupted from the earth. Sect houses crumbled. The great clans fell one by one.
 
In the distance, a masked figure stood at the heart of it all…serene amidst the carnage. Then a blade flashed—
and my head rolled across the ground.
 
A flash of light. Blinding. All-consuming.
 
And then...silence.
 
I opened my eyes.
 
I woke to the sterile smell of disinfectant and the hum of machines. My body felt strange young, fragile, untested. Around me were strangers calling me “Blue.” At first, I thought it was a dream. Then a punishment. A chance to start again...or a cruel trick from the heavens.
 
I was ten years old. My parents claimed I’d collapsed from pneumonia. No signs of martial trauma. No qi deviation. Nothing to suggest the warrior I had been. The world I woke into was Earth. No qi. No clans. No monsters. No Murim.
 
For weeks, I lay in silence.
Watching. Listening. Learning how this world worked. The ceiling blinked with lights. Machines beeped beside me. People wore white coats and masks instead of robes and armor. They spoke quickly, kindly, but I couldn’t understand most of it. The energy of this world was different. Dead. The air held no weight. No tension. I felt like I’d drowned and surfaced in a mirror of reality where nothing resonated.
 
I wanted to hate them...David and Mary, the parents who called me “son” and wept at my bedside. But they were kind. Honest. And slowly, over months, their warmth softened something frozen inside me. Still, I couldn’t forget who I had been.
Tang Jiung. A brother. A warrior. A protector. And the last thing I remembered before dying—So-Yeon, screaming as monsters poured through the red gate. A flash of poison. A burst of qi. Then darkness.
 
The dreams came often. Fire. Screams. Blood. Sometimes it was the moment I died—pierced by that black blade, the monster in the horned helm looming over me. Other nights, I saw So-Yeon again. Standing in the burning courtyard. Crying out. Reaching for me. Always just out of reach.
And then there was the voice. It didn’t speak often. But when it did, it echoed through the dreams like thunder in a canyon.
"When you get to where you belong… we’ll begin."
 
The first time I heard it, I thought it was my grandfather. The second time, I thought I was going mad. The third time, I stopped thinking about it at all. Just my imagination, I told myself. A relic of the past.
 
Earth was bizarre. The streets were loud and wide. Steel beasts rolled by on black roads, honking and coughing smoke. Glass towers rose into the clouds, and lights blinked from every corner. There were no sects, no guards at the city gates, no martial houses or sparring courtyards. Just stores. Machines. Screens that shouted at you from walls.
 
The first time I took a shower, I nearly jumped through the wall. The water came from a silver serpent’s neck with a twist. I thought it was enchanted. I called it a spirit pipe. David laughed until he cried. Mary showed me how to use it, again and again, patient and warm. She taught me how to brush my teeth, how to open food containers, how to use something called a microwave. I watched her carefully. I copied her. But inside, I felt lost.
 
The doctors told them I’d been in a coma for weeks. That I might not remember anything—names, routines, even parts of myself.
“Be patient,” they said. “Let him find his way back.” So they waited. Gently. Painfully. Treating me like fragile glass that might crack if pressed too hard.
They thought I was lost. But the truth was worse. I wasn’t the boy they’d raised. I was someone else entirely. And yet… they loved me anyway.
 
School was awkward. I barely spoke. I watched everyone. I listened. I learned quickly, but I was different. My posture. My gaze. The way I carried myself. One boy asked if I was a foreign exchange student. Another called me “Blue-bot” because of how quiet I was. I didn’t care. I kept to myself.
Until I met her.
 
She had purple hair and purple eyes. Quiet. Always sitting by herself. There was something about her—like she didn’t belong here either. Her name was Eve. She noticed things. She understood things that others missed.
 
One day, a boy tried to trip her in the hallway. She didn’t react. Just kept walking. That same boy came after me next. Called me a freak. He swung. I moved without thinking, sidestepped, twisted his wrist, and dropped him. No injuries. Just a soft thud. Everyone stared.
 
They left me alone after that. Eve started walking with me. Sitting near me at lunch. Watching me train behind the school. She never said much, just copied my stances, breathing when I breathed. I never told her about Murim. Never shared who I truly was. But we fell into rhythm. Pizza after school. Long walks through the suburbs. Quiet evenings playing video games she insisted I try. She became my best friend. My anchor.
 
My parents—David and Mary—did their best. I never called them Mom and Dad out loud, but I thought it once, quietly, after Mary stayed up with me during a fever. After David built me a wooden dummy so I could practice, he converted the basement into a proper training area for me. The dummy sat in the center. Mary watched with bright eyes, telling me to always follow the path that made me happy. That night, I said it for the first time:
“Thanks, Mom. Thanks, Dad.”
 
At night, after homework, after the house grew quiet, I trained. I moved the coffee table aside and rolled out the old yoga mat Mary had given me. It wasn’t much, but it was space—and that was all I needed. I stood in the center of the room, breathing slow and deep, the way Grandfather had taught me. Inhale. Draw the energy inward. Visualize the meridians. Focus on the dantian, just beneath the navel. The qi was barely there. A spark. Smaller than a pea. But it pulsed. Real. Alive. It responded when I called.
 
I flowed through basic stances—low, deliberate movements that burned my legs. The air around me grew still, heavy with silent focus. Each motion aligned breath and intent. Each breath drew a little more strength. Sometimes, Eve watched from the porch. She never said much...just leaned on the railing, purple hair tucked behind her ear, curiosity in her gaze. I knew she had questions. I always knew.
 
“What are you doing?” she asked one night, her voice low.
“Breathing,” I said.
“That doesn’t look like breathing.”
I gave a small shrug and shifted into the next stance.
“Is it a martial art?” she asked another time.
“Sort of,” I said, not looking at her.
“Just something my grandfather taught me.”
 
She accepted it, like she always did. Never pushed. Never pried. But she kept coming back.
 
 
By high school, I was stronger than anyone my age. Faster. More precise. Reflexes beyond natural. All thanks to the small amount of qi i had been absorbing through the years. But I never showed it. Never needed to. At least I thought.
 
The hallway smelled of sweat and cheap cologne. The chatter of students faded as he stepped into the middle of it.
The quarterback—a mountain of a kid with a sneer and shoulders like boulders—grabbed Eve’s backpack and shoved her against the lockers.
“Hey, freak girl. Why not come hang out with a real man instead of that douchebag,” he laughed.
 
Something inside me stirred. The memory hit like a strike to the chest: a boy reaching for So-Yeon, that burning anger, the red gates, the chaos… and me, standing between her and danger.
 
The world slowed. My hands clenched. My legs moved before my brain caught up.
 
“Let go,” I said.
 
The words barely left my lips. The next moment, he flew ten feet through the air, landing on his back with a thud. The hallway fell silent.
I stood over him, heart pounding, fists clenched. I could feel the surge in my chest, my dantian pulsing faintly—but strong enough that anyone could see I wasn’t joking.
 
The kid’s eyes widened, terror written across his face. He realized—too late—that he had underestimated me.
Eve stepped forward, hand on my arm. “Thanks… Blue. Let’s go,” she said quietly, pulling me back as whispers spread down the hall.
I exhaled, letting the tension fade. Calm returned. No one ever bothered her again.
 
That night, I stood in my room, breathing slowly. Calm. Still. My dantian pulsed faintly. The qi was growing.
Maybe Earth didn’t have Murim—but I carried it inside me all the same.
And soon, this Earth would resemble Murim more than I could ever imagine.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 - The Awakening
chapters.content:
After graduation, everyone asked the same question: Where are you going next? College? A trade? Something, anything?
I told them I needed time to figure things out.
 
David nodded like he understood. But one night, he pulled me aside. “You’re strong, Blue. That’s not something to be ashamed of. Ever think about joining an MMA gym? Just for the discipline, maybe? Could be good for you.”
 
I thanked him, but I never went. What would I even learn there? What could a cage teach me that death hadn’t?
 
I spent my nights downstairs—moving through silent forms, sharpening my breath, feeling for qi. It was still faint. Still small. But it was mine, and that was enough.
 
During the day, I took up part-time jobs. Grocery store stocker. Warehouse runner. Delivery boy. Places where I could move, lift, disappear into the noise.
Every paycheck went to savings. Every night ended in the basement. Same breathing. Same fire behind my ribs.
 
The day I turned eighteen, it happened. The same monsters I had seen in my dreams. The same chaos. The same red eyes and jagged teeth.
Cities burned. Highways collapsed. Families ran through the streets as the sky split open and gates tore into the world. Dimensional rifts bled creatures that didn’t belong—abominations with bone armor and molten breath.
 
The media called it “The Awakening.” And just like that, Earth changed forever.
 
The System revealed itself to the world. Not through dreams, but screens. Interfaces. Stats. People began awakening—gaining powers never before seen. Mana. Aether. Flux. Spirit. They weren’t martial artists. But they became something else entirely.
 
Hunters. Rankers. Gate divers. And for the first time, Earth fought back.
 
Guilds formed overnight. City governments collapsed under the weight of their influence. The United Nations assembled what remained of the world's leaders and birthed the Awakened Association, a global body tasked with monitoring awakened individuals and maintaining some semblance of control.
Behind closed doors, though, their job was simpler: keep the guilds from gaining too much power. To keep the world from falling into another war.
The gates weren’t all the same. Red ones brought death. But two golden gates appeared—one in Seoul, the other in Paris.
 
Unlike the others, these gates didn’t bring monsters. They led to other worlds. Entire civilizations on the other side. Most of the world fixated on the red gates—because they brought death. But those who paid attention knew the real secret wasn’t in the horror. It was in the gold.
They shimmered like starlight, humming with a warmth that pulled at the soul. Unlike the red gates, they didn’t pulse with hatred or bleed corruption.
Instead, they sang…softly, like a memory long buried.
 
Golden gates didn’t unleash monsters. They offered passage. But only to a chosen few.
The Association called them Resonants…individuals whose inner energy aligned with the frequency of the gate. Less than one in a million even qualified. For those who did… they vanished from Earth and stepped into entirely different worlds.
The Seoul gate led to Thalorin—a realm of spirits, druids, and wild beasts. A place of towering groves, whispering winds, and living mountains. Beings who spoke not with words, but presence.
 
The Paris gate connected to Nytherra, a kingdom of arcane might, floating spires, ancient tomes, and magic woven into every breath. Mana flowed like blood, knowledge carved reality itself. A world straight from fantasy novels and manwha pages.
Entry wasn’t free.
 
The Association stationed rift-walkers—licensed awakened individuals capable of opening stable paths—at each major guild and city worldwide. Airports were too dangerous. The skies, littered with flying beasts. Travel was regulated. Restricted. You needed approval. Status. Power.
And Eve had it.
 
The evening started like most others.
 
I got off my shift bagging groceries, met Eve at the pizza parlor down the block—same booth, same two slices, same quiet rhythm we’d fallen into over the years. Then we headed home. Down to the basement. My sanctuary. Tonight, though, things would be different.
I sat cross-legged in the center of the room, shirt clinging to my back from the walk. The air was still. Familiar. The wooden dummy David built stood in its corner. The old mats Mary bought lined the floor. Sacred. This was the space where past and present blurred.
 
I closed my eyes. Drew in a breath. Focused. Visualized the meridians. Pulled the qi inward. Guided it to the dantian. Slower. Deeper.
I was just beginning to feel the faint stirrings…like a whisper of warmth in my core when Eve gasped.
My eyes snapped open. She stood frozen by the door, wrapped in golden light.
 
“What’s happening?” she whispered. “Something… popped up. A blue box. The System. It says something about… choosing a path.”
