I didn’t respond right away. That word—System. The thing that had whispered to me in dreams, the thing that said I wasn’t where I belonged… it hadn’t spoken since the gates appeared two years ago. And now… it was here. But not for me. For her.
 
Her eyes darted through invisible prompts. Hands moved through nothing I could see. Then one word: “Spirit.”
The golden hue pulsed, then faded into her skin. She looked stunned…then overjoyed.
 
“I awakened!” she whispered.
 
I forced a smile. “That’s… incredible.”
 
It was. But it wasn’t for me.
 
She ran to me, nearly knocking me over. “Blue! I awakened! I awakened!”
 
Her voice shook. Her eyes gleamed. She didn’t know what it meant yet…not fully. But I did. I’d seen what awakeners became. Hunters. Heroes. Protectors.
 
“You always said I’d be strong one day,” she whispered.
 
I nodded. Gently. “You will be.”
 
We celebrated that night. Shared leftover pizza. Watched old cartoons. Talked about what her ability might be. She didn’t notice the quiet edge to my smile. The weight pressing against my chest like a dull blade. No matter how much I trained—I hadn’t awakened. Not by Earth’s terms. And the System, the one I thought was waiting for me, chose her instead.
 
The next morning, we headed to the Association building in downtown Columbus. Hunters filed in and out, flashing badges, shouldering massive weapons, laughing like gods among men. Eve looked so small next to them. But she held her head high. The registration staff confirmed her class: Spirit User. High compatibility. Rare affinity. They smiled like they were looking at a future star. I stood in the back. Watching. Silent.
 
She turned once to look for me. I waved. She beamed. I didn’t need the spotlight. I’d lived that life before. But seeing them look at her—like she was a gift from heaven—still stung.
 
A month later, she showed up at the pizza place holding a white envelope. She didn’t sit. Just stood there, grinning like a kid with a secret.
“They chose me,” she said.
 
I blinked. “Who?”
 
“The Buckeye Guild.” She slid the letter across the table. I opened it.
 
Official sponsorship. Travel approval. Gate authorization. “They want me to represent them… in Thalorin.”
 
My breath caught. Seoul. That’s where the golden gate was. One of only two on Earth.
 
“You’re… leaving?” I asked.
 
She nodded. “I have to.”
 
We sat in silence for a moment.
 
Then she chuckled. “When I get back…” Her eyes met mine. “I’ll be stronger than you.”
 
She meant it as a joke. A promise. But it still sank like a stone in my gut.
 
“Good luck.”
 
I smiled anyway. But inside, something twisted—a quiet fire that had nothing to do with the Basements, the qi, the training. It was the taste of being left behind, of watching someone else step into what I had trained for all these years.

data.title: Rare Medicine
data.author: Wolf_Bandit
data.summary:
Alvin Lennon is completely and positively sick of the sinister 'Obsidian Syndicate.' So once he finds his way out, he doesn't look back, though adjusting to life in the witness protection program is harder than it seemed. Harper is an up and coming photographer. But when tragedy strikes and she is left choosing between an opportunity in Pinecrest, Oregon, and her apathetic parents, she chooses to leave Fort Worth and never look back. What happens when the curious photographer and the hardened ex-con discover a string of disappearances in their newfound home? Join Alvin and Harper on their investigation into the darkest part of Pinecrest State Park.

A Wolf Bandit Production

chapters.title: In the Dead of Night
chapters.content:
“Sad Case/Happiness, Missouri” – EL VY

“All’s Well That Ends” – Rainbow Kitten Surprise

“Downstairs” – Matt Maeson


They don’t tell you when they’re coming. The day, the hour, or the minute. They don’t tell you they’ll break into your home. It would’ve been nice to at least have had some notice. Maybe I could’ve put a tarp down in the kitchen so it would be easy to clean the apartment up for Tony, my landlord. I don’t suppose he was too happy about having to clean up this mess.


I fought my way through at least four before they pinned me to the floor. Before they placed the bag over my head. Before I was hog-tied and thrown in the back of some vehicle. Didn’t have any time to think or process what was happening.


But the witness protection program requires a completely blank slate, even if they have to shatter the slab to get it clean.


They tossed me around, felt like they were having fun with it, too.


At first, I didn’t think it was the government; I didn’t think it was the U.S. Marshals. It felt like, once again, Hadley had his hand wrapped around my throat, dragging me back into our dark world with no other choice, no way out this time. It was get with it or get gone, and I…


I didn’t want to die.


——


We switched cars at one point, them pulling me out and carrying me over by my hands and legs. I felt like a spit-roasted hog.


It was bright when they pulled the sack off my head, splashing a little water on my face. They handcuffed my hands behind the back of the chair.


One with an ugly mug came up, with his wiry, ‘tough-guy’ chevron mustache, stepping up like he owned the very chair I was probably pissing in.


“Alvin Lennon, the United States Government is allowing you to enter the Witness Protection Program for your own safety.”


“You fucking dragged me outta my apartment!”


He stepped closer, towering over me, his brows furrowed. I felt the spit cover my face as he yelled at me.


“And you knocked out five of my guys!”


Got more than I thought. I got angry too, leaning as far forward as my cuffed arms would allow, nearly tipping me and the chair over. I felt the warm liquid running down my legs. 


How embarrassing.


“Only because I thought they were Hadley’s men, Marshal!”


He held the bridge of his nose as he tried to contain his obvious disdain for me. 


“Just shut it for a minute. Calm down, and maybe we can talk about getting you out of those cuffs for the paperwork.”


I sat back down, my head feeling dizzy once the adrenaline wore off. It took a few minutes to get my breathing under control, just to look around the room and take it in.


It was big. Looked like a garage. The van I assumed they had kidnapped me in or moved to was sitting there, just a few feet away from me. Gray concrete with various oil stains peppering the floor. Or was it blood? I couldn’t tell. 


The man came back over to me, positioning himself behind me. I heard the jingle of keys.


“You gonna try to take us out again?”


I shook my head.


“No.”


“Good. The name’s Frank.”


And he unlocked my handcuffs. My wrists were red, sore from the rope and the metal. I looked down at my pants, soaked through and stinky as hell.


“Any chance I could get a change of clothes? And use the bathroom?”


He nodded and waved for me to follow him. I did. Into the house and through the living room, where the other U.S. Marshals were sitting around watching T.V.


He led me past them and to the first full bathroom.


“Wait here,” he grumbled as he exited the room. A minute passed, and he came back with a set of clothes, just some nondescript sweatpants, a new pair of boxers, and a t-shirt. He set them on the sink counter.


“Thanks.”


“Towels,” he pointed to the cabinet, then to the shower, “Shampoo, conditioner, body gel, all that. If you have tats, shave over them.”


I nodded as he closed the door. And there was silence, stillness for the first time since I had laid down to sleep just seven hours ago.


Silence…


I locked the door. As much as they claimed to be keeping me safe, I didn’t trust them.


——


Off with the clothes. I stuffed them in a trash bag; they smelled bad and would need to be washed.


On with the shower, letting the water get hot before I got in.


I closed my eyes and just let the water wash over me. It was like one of Huron’s bad stories, stranded on an island with his friend, the Admiral. They didn’t seem true, but he told them like they were, and that was entertaining enough to pass the time.


What was this mess that I had gotten myself into this time? Of all the things.

chapters.title: Safe House
chapters.content:
“Cringe” – Matt Maeson

“Subliming” – Richy Mitch & The Coal Miners


Frank sat across from me at the long wooden table in the dining room. The other marshals were cooking something up in the kitchen. At least it hadn’t been a lonely month.


I was reading a novel they had in this prim and proper-looking prison. The author’s name sounded like a spice, Cormac McCarthy. And while every paragraph felt like a workout, the ashes of America pulled me in. Replacing silence with the weight of a shopping cart and a tired father.


Frank tapped the table with his pen, his unspoken way of grabbing my attention when I was engrossed in those pages.


“Gonna have to do something about those tats you’ve got.”


He had a point. ‘Rugged By Bond - Polished By Fire’ was scrawled across my collar bones, my pledge of loyalty to the Obsidian Syndicate. It was meaningless now. After my testimonies, the trials.


Ten convictions. And that’s just the ones I appeared in person for. With my recorded statement… I’m not sure how many people were tried and convicted. Maybe not the Pack… At least not Wren and Colt. I know they flipped.


“Like… Get ‘em removed?”


“Nah, that’s too expensive, the state wouldn’t swing for that.”


Frank went back to his laptop, writing on a notepad that he soon slid over to me.


“Figure out what you want to cover ‘em up.”


Oh…


“Oh, alright.”


Cover them. These testaments I’ve had for years.


“All of ‘em?”


Frank simply nodded, not even bothering to look at me. I thought of all the bones I had broken in my life, the reason I wore those words on my collar. Mine. Other people’s. The lives I held in my hands, the ones I spared, and the ones I sent off.


“Bones. Broken bone, one on each side. Blackout job.”


“That’ll work. We’ll get someone in by the end of the week.”


New tattoos, new home… new man.


The other marshals finished their cooking and brought us grilled cheeses. Eddie, one marshal, sat with me and Frank and ate with us. 


“Need a better name, too.”


“Whattaya say about Jeremy Rodgers?”


“Does he look like a Jeremy? Jeremy’s are born in New York, somewhere civilized.”


I chuckled.


“Mama said Nicholas was a close second for me.”


“Anyone know that?” Frank asked.


I got quiet. It hurt to think about.


“No. No one knows that.”


“Nicholas, it is then. Nick, Nicholas… Owens?”


“Wilson.”


Frank looked at me like the name was a good idea.


“Wilson works,” I replied. “Nicholas Wilson.”


The tattoo artist came just two days later to cover the ink on my collar bones. And nearly as quick as I had branded myself a member of the Obsidian Syndicate, I was born into Nicholas’ body.


New look. Couldn’t keep the redneck outlaw thing I had going on. A full beard looked better with the cropped buzz cut. I decided Nicholas would look better if he looked like a military nut. Maybe people’d leave me alone if I looked like the letter of the law.


I watched as the hair fell from my head and into the sink. At first, nearly completely bald. My stubble grew slow. Days passed like a blur of mornings and evenings. Wake up, eat, read, eat, T.V. and even that was limited, eat, sleep.


Months like this. Months.


Months of this droning repetitive nonsense. I was kicking to get out. I had never had cabin fever until then. I could go outside, with supervision, of course. But never off property, never to the city.


A month before I was placed, they sat me down. 


“Pick three places. If you could live anywhere in the U.S., where would you live?”


So I get to pick where I would be living?


“Anywhere?”


“Anywhere.” Frank nodded. 


“Texas, New York, Florida.”


He wrote them down on his notepad and disappeared for a few days. That weekend, they took me to the Goodwill a few miles away. They didn’t let me see outside the van. They didn’t want me to know how to get to the safe house.


The Goodwill had some decent stuff. I got a few things for mild temperatures, subtle heat, and mild cold. A couple of flannel jackets, a pair of boots. There was a nice canvas backpack, green and black. It was nice enough that you had to wonder why someone would’ve thrown it out. 


We also went to a small department store so I could get new underwear and socks.


Everything I owned fit inside my new backpack and a few ‘Pruitt’s Food’ grocery bags. My life, reduced to three bags, a new tattoo, and a new haircut. All packed and ready for my new life somewhere far from Missouri.


I knew where I was headed. Down to the oil fields in West Texas, or out to the Floridian naval ports like Dan, or up to New York to become some low-income train driver in the subways.


Somewhere far from here. Somewhere new, where I got to choose my future for once. Far from the Syndicate, far from the Hadleys, far from the blood I’ve spilled and far from the bodies I’ve buried. 


A fresh start.

chapters.title: As Requested
chapters.content:
“No Complaints” – Noah Kahan

“Dirty Love” – Mt. Joy

“Part of Me” – Noah Kahan


It was a brand new year, a cheap flight at the beginning of the week, Tuesday the 14th of January, 2020. Frank didn’t tell me where we were headed until we got to the gate. Oregon.


“Hey, I didn’t ask to go to Oregon-”


“You tell anyone how much you like Arizona? Florida? New York?”


“Yeah, but-”


“But nothin’. Once those Black Glass motherfuckers start lookin’ for you, those are the first places they’ll check.”


What was I supposed to do? Fight the marshal?


“Oregon in the middle of winter. You’re dropping me into the middle of a blizzard.”


“Weather’s nice this week out there. Get your head outta the clouds. You wanna keep your neck? You come with me to Oregon.”


He looked at me, his head half cocked to the side like a father would look at a stubborn child, too preoccupied with throwing a fit in the aisle than with walking with him. I looked at him, him who was old and hard and slightly irritated with me.


I took a breath and then a step. A step towards one more thing that I didn’t get to choose.


The plane was packed. People upon people, mothers and their screaming babies, incels and their horrid funk. At the very least, I had a window seat, with Frank between the nasty man who smelled like piss and me.


“Fly like this often, Marshal?”


I cracked a sly smirk, and Frank just groaned.


“Just try not to irritate me the whole way, Wilson.”


Wilson… My smirk faded, and I turned to look back out the window. I missed my name. Lennon. Six letters, but it made people whip around and ask, ‘Are you related to the Beatles’ John Lennon?’


Now I was Wilson. Nicholas Wilson.


“Nicholas Wilson,” I muttered, still bitter. “Still doesn’t sit right in my teeth, Frank.”


“Shut up.”


So I did. And we both spent the five-hour-long flight in silence. 


When we arrived, he had a taxi pick us up at the Portland airport, muttered some address to the driver, and from there we drove nearly two hours down to the coast. The wooden sign on the side of the highway said ‘Pinecrest,’ and the road was lined with frosty pines. A blanket of snow covered the landscape. Nothing was safe, not even the squirrels. 


A few minutes after that, we hit downtown. Some quaint little square, with a stunning view of the ocean.


“This the place?”


“Pinecrest, yep. Plenty of work here, houses and apartments for sale. Lots of nobodies live here, you’re one of ‘em.”


It was small, homey, and downtown felt like it had stolen the architect of 1960s San Francisco. When the taxi finally stopped, we were at a motel. I scoffed and chuckled bitterly as I saw the sign.


The Emerald Star Lodge.


“You gotta be fuckin’ kiddin’ me…”


I could imagine what Cass would’ve said, ‘Are we sure Huron’s stories aren’t just his fucking noir benders?’


“There’s gotta be a different place to put me up in this town.”


Frank shook his head, already irritated again.


“This is the only motel in Pinecrest, and Pinecrest is where we’re sending you.”


I resigned myself.


Frank checked me in and told the clerk the card was good for a month. After that, I was on my own. He walked me to the room, and I set my bags down on the bed.


It was small, a little dingy. The color scheme was emerald green and forest brown, and somehow it worked. Somehow.


“Alright. This is where I tell you the gist. You get an allowance for seven months. $10,000 a month, okay? The state is covering the room for the first month, so start figuring out a job, housing, and the rest. After those seven months, you’ll get nothing else from us. New birth certificate and social will come in the mail in the next couple of weeks.”


“Got it…”


I didn’t ask any more questions; I understood. The government I had risked my life to help put the bad guys away was going to throw me to the wolves with nothing after seven months. Real nice.


“You don’t tell anybody your old life. You do that, it gets out, anyway, and you’re out of the program. And you won’t be eligible again. You got that?”


“Yep.”


Frank looked around. I couldn’t quite make out his face. Irritated. Tired. Worried?


“Look, kid… I know this is disorienting.”


“Damn straight-”


“Just… Listen for once, yeah? Just listen.”


I glared through my brows, crossing my arms. I nodded at him for him to continue. He spoke with that hardened Texan voice he had.


“Who you tell is up to your discretion. But the more people you tell the easier it’ll be for Hadley’s bastards to find you. Some folks never come out of WitSec, just ‘cus they feel safer. It’s up to you.”


He paused for a moment, looking around the room like he was trying to decide on something. Then he took out his wallet and handed me a business card.


“My home phone is on there. You get into any trouble, want advice, or hell… just need to talk to someone who knows who ‘Alvin Lennon’ is… You call me. Day or night, okay? You. Call. Me. Got that?”


I took the card with a bit of hesitance. 


“Why?”


He sighed. Put his hands on his hips.


“My son’s name was Alvin. They killed him during Operation Desert Storm, over in Iraq. Talked a lot like you ‘fore he left.”


I nodded, and an awkward silence fell over us before Frank moved to head out of the motel room.


“Call anytime, kid. Got it?” He asked me, sternly, like a father making sure his son understood him.


I nodded. “Got it.”


“Good. Alright. Take it as easy as you can.”


And just like that, Frank was gone.

chapters.title: The Start of a Breath
chapters.content:
“Freakin’ Out On the Interstate” – Briston Maroney

“God Put a Smile upon Your Face” – Coldplay


Pizza Maker, Cosmo’s Pizza, Tillamook, Oregon.

Store Cashier, Aldi, Tillamook, Oregon.

Package Handler, UPS, Tillamook, Oregon.


I must’ve scrolled through thousands of job listings in Tillamook County. All of them were boring, and none of them were decent-paying jobs. I hadn’t had a legit job for a while, but even so… The Syndicate kept me flush.


Grocery Clerk, Fred Meyer, Tillamook, Oregon.

Delivery Driver, Uber, Pinecrest, Oregon.

Road Maintenance Tech, City of Pinecrest, Pinecrest, Oregon.


I scrolled through more. Nothing jumped out at me. Not a single application.


State Park Ranger, Pinecrest State Park, Pinecrest, Oregon.


A park ranger…


For the first time, a job didn’t sound like a total bore. I clicked apply. Filled out my very vague background. And waited.


Went for a walk. Checked my email. Went to the Crescent Joint, got a drink. Two. Three. Four. Took a jog. Then went back to the hotel.


A day passed. Then two. Then a week. A week and a half of this monotony. A week and a half of the same popcorn ceiling. A week and a half of the same half-paneled wooden walls and emerald green wallpaper. A week and a half of powdered eggs and half-frozen biscuits at breakfast.


Ding!


I checked my email. Pinecrest State Park. An interview date and an address.


So I put on my best jeans and the cleanest shirt I had. Cleaned up the beard, buzzed my hair again, and then jumped in the truck. 


The park wasn’t too far of a drive from the motel, maybe fifteen minutes down a winding road through the mountains. The cool air filtered through the old vents of this 36-year-old hunk-o-junk that the government decided was worthy of a criminal like me. At least it ran like butter, no stuttering, no puttering. Just the pure roar of Ford engineering.


I parked in a space next to a blue Subaru SUV and made my way inside, tugging at my shirt to make sure all the wrinkles came out before I opened up that front door.


“Welcome in!”


A cheeky thing piped up from behind the front desk, way more chipper than I’d expect from a park ranger.


“What can I help you with?”


“Name’s Nicholas Wilson. I was supposed to have an interview today?”


“Oh yeah! I know you. You’re an hour early.”


“Yeah, I try to be early.”


“Well, so far you’re already doing better than half the applicants.” She reached out her hand for a handshake, her grip firm. “Sarah Lewis.”


“Nice to meet you.”


“Same here.” She peered across the small welcome center towards a set of couches around a coffee table. “Let’s sit there. You can tell me more about yourself.”


More about myself…


Right. 


We sat opposite each other, the coffee table between us, where she propped her feet up. She held a clipboard and a pen in her left hand. 


“So, tell me about yourself? Where are you from, family?”


Right into the deep end, huh? I sighed, took a breath, and did my best to look friendly.


“Uh, yeah… Yeah, I’m from Missouri, Springfield, actually. I’m the only one, no siblings, and my folks aren’t, uh, they aren’t really around.”


“Oh, I’m sorry to hear that.” She tapped the end of her pen on the paper, wrote something, then looked back up. “What brings you to Pinecrest?”


“Change in scenery. Seemed like a nice, quiet place. Still working on getting an apartment, I-I hope that isn’t a problem.”


“Pinecrest is the city of fresh starts, at least in the locals’ opinion. I’m from New York myself. Most of the locals aren’t actually from Oregon.”


“Oh—”


“Well, anyway, what qualifies you to be a park ranger?”


I straightened up my back. 


The interview didn’t take long. I gave vague but convincing answers, carefully fibbing and building my backstory like how I had learned.


She hired me on the spot. Wasn’t sure if Sarah had been that desperate for help in the park or if I was actually a good fit for the job. It didn’t feel like it. 


The trails were on rotation. Walk a certain route every day, make sure the trails are up to par, that the rests along them were still usable, and that they weren’t blocked. It was peaceful. A different level of peace.


It wasn’t peace in the sense of hiding out in a safe house, knowing the people trailing you didn’t know where you were, but could find out. That nagging feeling at the back of my neck, telling me to keep running.


I was tired of running. For once, I just wanted to relax, find peace in something real. Not fake or made up, no playing pretend.


I wanted something real. And Pinecrest was real. A chance. Maybe, in time, it could be a home.

chapters.title: At the Break of Dawn
chapters.content:
“Helplessly Hoping” – Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young


My alarm woke me at 5:00 sharp, and I, groggily, pulled back my covers and sat up. Legs dangling off my bed, the cold chill hit my bones quickly, and goosebumps littered my skin.


It was a cool summer morning, a rarity in June, especially in 2021. A nice break from the triple digits of the Texas heat. No classes that day, and no work. But my older sister had to testify one last time. Neither of us were looking forward to it.


I dragged that morning, slowly getting dressed, slowly gathering my things, slowly leaving my room. Quinn was still sound asleep, which didn’t surprise me one bit. She’d been sleeping more and more ever since the police returned her to us. It didn’t help that she refused to go to the psychologist that Mama and Papa paid for. 


She needed to talk to someone. I don’t know how many times I begged her or tried to convince her to go. Even to just talk to me. She refused. Just kept to herself, slept more, and talked less. Every day it seemed more and more clear that whatever she was carrying, she would not hand to anyone.


Anyone except for the courts, that is.


I put my hand on her shoulder to lightly shake her.


“Quinny, hey… Gotta get up sweetheart…”


She always woke with a start now, but if you did it gently enough, it wasn’t as jerky.


“Harper?”


She grabbed my hand tightly.


“Yeah, it’s me, I’m here. You gotta get up, or we’re gonna be late.”


“Oh… Right,” she nodded, “last trial…”


“Yep, just gotta get through today. Come on, up and at ‘em.”


I helped her get up. She was even more tired than me.


Dark colors for her, no more bright pinks and yellows. It made me a little sad. Squash Blossom yellow used to be her favorite color. Maybe it still is. I wouldn’t know.


I remember when we got to choose the color of our rooms. She was 10, and I was 8. Mama and Papa let us pick out colors from the Behr paint chips. She picked ‘Squash Blossom’ yellow, and I picked ‘Park Bench’ green.


I knocked on her door gently.


“You ready?”


She came out of her room and put on that semi-fake smile she had learned to use so well. It fooled our parents, it fooled the cameras, but it didn’t fool me. I smiled half-heartedly, matching her melancholy vibe as we walked down the stairs and out to the car waiting for us in the horseshoe driveway of our house.


The drive to the Tarrant County courthouse wasn’t long for us, with the Rhodes mansion just a few minutes away from downtown. Our driver dropped us off in front of the Tim Curry Criminal Justice Center. I told him we’d meet him at the Razoo’s on Sundance Square, and he just nodded, flicked down his sunglasses, and drove away.


Getting into court was routine now. How many states had we flown to? At least the last one was here at home. No late-night flights and early court dates. No struggling with TSA or arguing with American about our tickets.


No more stress for my sister. 


They took her away from me, and I went into the courtroom like I always did. Her support, her rock. I will always be there for her, like she was for me.


And I sat. I listened to the same horrid testimony she had given hundreds of times before. Only minor deviations, new lawyers, new questions, new circumstances.


“And when you were there at the halfway house run by the Obsidian Syndicate, did you ever see this man?”


“Yes.”


“In what nature did you see him?”


“He was one of the guards; he would go with the other guys. Be gone for hours. They’d always have more girls with them when they came back.”


This line of questioning always went on longer than necessary. But soon it was finally over, and the courts would release her back to me.


Her smile was genuine when she saw me, and I pulled her into a tight hug once we got close. 


“Hungry?”


She simply nodded.


“We can walk down to Razoo’s, get you some tchoupitoulas. Sound good?”


“Sound’s delicious.”


Lunch was a little loud, but worth it to see Quinn smile and laugh again. The things that were causing her pain were all finally over. And the sooner she could forget what happened, the sooner she’d recover.

chapters.title: Dear Quinn,
chapters.content:
“Sugar Water” – Gigi Perez


But things like this sneak up on you. The darkness is almost never obvious. It hides itself in a mask. Behind your loved one’s forced smile, so practiced and so rehearsed that it looks real. And all the things that seemed so normal become things you missed the most. 


You were born in San Antonio on September 17th, 1996. Mama and Papa moved you to Fort Worth, and two years later, on April 12th, I was born. The things we got up to, the adventures we had.


Braiding each other’s hair. Stealing Mama’s makeup. Sneaking into each other’s rooms to play dress up in the middle of the night.


That summer in 2005, when we both ‘ran away’ into the woods of the park near our house. We built a fort out of sticks and told Papa we weren’t ever leaving. 


You cheered me on in my swim competition in 2007. I won.


Your yellow bedroom, filled with Barbies and posters of the Hoh National Rainforest. You wanted to visit it so badly, all the girls at school teased you for wanting to go. 


You said Texas was so yellow, you just wanted to run in the green. Washington, Oregon, California, Colorado, the Carolinas, you wanted to see them more than anything. Their greens and vibrant blues, no sickening yellow grass for you there. You were the reason I got into photography, the reason I wanted to go to college for it.


The summer of 2008, when everything changed. The day you went missing, I searched all over the neighborhood. I skipped school to find you. I never could.


Fall of 2010, I still couldn’t forget you. I looked for you in everything. Papa bought me my first camera. I took pictures of everything that reminded me of you. 


2015. Grandpa died, and everything else fell apart. The house grew still and silent. I barely saw Mama and Papa. We didn’t speak with Abuela, or Tío Raúl, or Tía Isabel anymore.


He was gone. And everyone tried to tell me you were gone too, but I couldn’t believe them. I knew you were still out there. 


You were.


2019… I remember the way the knock on our front door sounded when the police came. When they said they had found you. And when you came back to us. Broken.


Exhausted and slow and weak and dull. The yellow disappeared from your sky and left us with nothing but a black and gray expanse of clouds and gloom.


Mama and Papa faked their happiness in front of the press, but went right back to their silence as soon as they crossed the threshold into our house. I took you to the trials so you could tell your story, tried to get you to talk to me about those missing years, and I was always denied.


You seemed so happy. The week before, after the last trial, you practically begged me to skip classes to hang out with you. I did, of course. We went shopping, and you barely let me get you anything. 


But that yellow bracelet with the sunflower charm. And once I bought it, you never took it off.


The last thing I wanted was to see that yellow bracelet, with the sunflower charm, without the movement that made it yours. 


Now all I have of you are these memories, this bracelet, this crumpled piece of paper I was too arrogant to keep pristine. I balled it up and threw it away at first; I didn’t want to see what it said. I still don’t.


If I don’t read this, I’ll wake up from this nightmare, and you’ll be waiting for me by my truck, just waiting for our next adventure. We’ll go to the Hoh Rainforest. We’ll go and never leave. We’ll tell Papa we’re never coming home, and build a house out of sticks.

----

“This Is What Remains” – Some Are Lonely


I took the letter from my trash can and straightened it out as best as I could. Still in the envelope, unopened. I put it on my nightstand. I was too scared to open it, to read the words Quinn had written for me.


Mama and Papa read theirs and cursed her instantly. I said nothing to them.


I didn’t come out of my room for a week. When I did finally come out of my room, I sat vacantly in the living room, mindlessly scrolling through job sites. I needed to be busy.


Friends gave empty apologies, then went about their business. After a month, everyone around me forgot Quinn.


I didn’t. I couldn’t. 


“Stop being so mopey.” “You need to put on a smile.” “What will the investors think?” “Get out of the house.”


My parents wouldn’t let up. They wanted so badly to push past it, to speed through grief like it was optional. Their attitude seemed to be a near-permanent thorn in my stay.


I burrowed myself in blankets on my bed, blinds closed and curtains drawn, the darkness creeping in like a hug from the aether. I tried to calm down, to rest my eyes.


Ding!


Lazily, I picked up my phone and held it over my face, squinting at the bright light. A notification from Indeed. 


Subject: Pinecrest Tourism—Photographer Position


Hi Harper,


I came across your resume and wanted to reach out personally. We’re currently looking for a City Photographer here in Pinecrest, and your experience really stood out to us.


I know we’re far, but if you’re open to it, I’d love to talk more about the position and what life in Pinecrest looks like.


Looking forward to hearing from you,

- Ada Reece


A job offer. From Oregon. And they wanted me. Me…


What reason did I have to decline? 


I didn’t really have one. Not one. Nothing was keeping me here, so why did I feel like I was chained to my bed?


My parents showed their true colors. How much they didn’t care. How little Quinn meant to them. My sister was gone, my friends weren’t real…


Hello Ms. Reece,

I’d love to talk about the position. The distance doesn’t bother me, as I’ve been needing a change of scenery recently. 

When can we talk?

Thank you, 

–Harper Rhodes


It was really a dream job. Managing the social media accounts for a city on the Pacific coast, all those trees. The sort of green Quinn wanted to see…


So I took it. I took the job. I only packed the most important things, my favorite clothes, papers, and a few knick-knacks. I knew my parents would blow up once they found out. 


I only stayed for her funeral. I made myself busy, not letting myself have a moment to let it land. A bird can’t fly once it’s sat in the tar. I’d learned that.


My parents didn’t do much for Quinn’s funeral, either. Mama hired a pastor to give the eulogy. We didn’t go to church. They had her cremated and put her in the family plot at Greenwood Memorial Park. They didn’t even ask me if I wanted to keep some of her.


I had never done anything illegal. Never. I never jaywalked or littered, never ran a red light or skipped school. But the night after her funeral, I waited for the maintenance crew to leave and jumped the fence of the cemetery. I found the plot and used a screwdriver to pop the lid to her in-ground-urn.


My sister was going to come with me to Oregon. We were going to see the green leaves together. I was not going to leave her behind, even if it meant stealing her ashes in the middle of the night.

chapters.title: Off the One
chapters.content:
“Paul Revere” – Noah Kahan

“Sierra Vista” – Richy Mitch & The Coal Miners

“Rhiannon” – Fleetwood Mac


“Where are you going?”


“I’m moving out.”


I had loaded the last small box into my new truck. I bought it with the bonus Papa put into my trust fund last year. Brand new Toyota Tacoma with all the features in bright candy-apple red.


“Moving out?!”


Mama was furious.


“When the hell were you going to tell us you were ‘moving out?!”


There was a lot of screaming. Lots of cussing.


“Your father has worked very hard for you to have a future here-”


I had started to tune them out. But-


“Are you really going to jeopardize your father and Xanthic Oil?!”


Something snapped in me. Her tone, the way it felt like she was yelling at an intern instead of her own daughter.


“Yes, I am!”


She was practically clutching her pearls, taken aback like no one had ever talked back to her in her life. Was it bad that I enjoyed seeing her afraid? Scared that her picture-perfect life was in jeopardy?


“I have had it with the facades and the lies. My sister is dead! She is gone, and neither of you cares. You didn’t like her when she was alive. You certainly didn’t like the scandal that followed her fucking SUICIDE-”


I slammed the truck door. I closed my eyes, huffed a breath through my nose, before inhaling deeply.


“I got a job in another state. No, I am not telling you where.”


“If you do this, Harper, you will have no more financial support from us-”


“You can stop that thought right there.” I pulled out a receipt. “All the money in the trust fund is already gone. Legally transferred. It’s mine. You can’t take that away from me.”


“Harper, this is a mistake!”


“No, mama… this is the best decision I’ve ever made.”


I walked around to the driver’s side door. I tuned her out. She was just a mess of screaming garbage. Rolling down the window, I chucked my phone out at her feet.


“I don’t need that either. Stay out of my life.”


And I left. Nothing but a few boxes and my sister in an expensive urn.


The drive was long. It took me almost three days to get there, 30 hours from Texas to Oregon, and that’s before pit stops and naps. It felt like it might never end. 


But soon enough, I was driving through the downtown area of Pinecrest. It was beautiful, one of those towns you’d expect Hallmark to shoot a Christmas movie in. Classic storefronts, old brick streets.


I parked at City Hall. Locked the truck as I walked in. Adeline was waiting for me.


“You must be Ms. Rhodes! Let me be the first to welcome you to Pinecrest!”


She came up to me and gave me a great big bear hug. My arms hung awkwardly by my sides.


“You must be Ms. Reece?”


“In the flesh,” she released me, and I straightened out my red jacket and black dress shirt. “I must say you are more professional in person. But don’t worry, we’ll beat that out of you real quick!”


She was very energetic.


“Come, walk with me. How was the trip up?”


We started walking through the halls, leading to offices in the back.


“It was alright. A long drive.”


She whipped around, looking at me in disbelief. 


“You drove here?! From Fort Worth?”


I nodded. 


“Wasn’t thinking about it.”


“Do you even have a place yet?”


I shook my head. 


“If I’m being honest, I wasn’t thinking that far ahead.”


“Guess you really needed to get the hell outta Dodge, huh?” 


She looked me up and down, then wiped her brow and eyes with her hand.


“I think,” she began scrolling through her phone furiously, “the Harlans have a property they’ve been trying to sell. They might be open to renting.”


“The Harlans?”


“Yeah, I texted you the address. That’s Harlan Mercantile. Talk to… James, yeah, talk to James. He’s the one I was discussing this with last week.”


“Got it…”


“Go get settled in and then come back Monday! I’ll get you started then.”


She smiled at me and gently shooed me away. It was oddly comforting.


So, on to the general store.


The sign on the front read ‘Harlan’s Mercantile,’ a square-front shop. An older gentleman was working out in front, planting something in the big standing flowerbeds. 


“Hello, are you Mr. Harlan?”


The man turned slowly, holding onto the wooden box for stability.


“Yes, I am he. Don’t mind me, I’m just planting some wildflowers!” He puttered around some, going back to his planting. “You can go in and shop, uh- Richie’s workin’ the counter.”


“I- I’m actually here to see you? My name is Harper- Harper Rhodes. I’m the new city photographer. Adeline told me you had a house for sale?”


He laughed heartily.


“A house? She’s a generous girl. It’s more like a shack in the woods. Could you hand me that trowel, dear?”


“Of course-”


He took it gently, making small holes in the soil. I had seen our hired gardener, Liza, do that before, though I had never had time to ask her why.


“What’re you planting?”


He looked at me with such joy, his face lit by the widest smile.


“Oh! Well, I’m mixing Bee Balm and Uthadiums in these pots. They’ll be blooming come the first day of spring!”


“Uthadiums?”


A younger man stepped out of the store, holding a little Ziploc baggie of what looked like various seeds.


“Dad, you left this on the counter.”


“Oh, well, thank you, Richie- oh, have you met my son yet?”


“Um- no, sir, I just got here-”


He nearly pushed us both inside.


“Let’s get out of the biting wind, come on now, come, come-”


They had nearly everything you would ever need: repair supplies, auto parts, electrical, cleaning supplies, tech, and more. It was the Pandora’s box of small-town general stores.


A jingle bell clanged on the door as we walked through it. Coming in, a woodsy, dusty smell assaulted me. Not old dusty, more like how your abuela’s house would smell because she couldn’t reach the tops of all the cabinets. 


“Ms. Rhodes was just asking me about the cabin.”


“Is it possible we finally have a buyer?”


I nodded.


“How much are you asking for it?”


Richie looked at me like I shouldn’t be serious.


“Are you kidding?”


“The young woman looks quite determined.” Mr. Harlan snickered.


“I’m quite serious, Mr. Harlan-”


“James-” he turned to me. “Please. Call me James.”


“James… I am serious about buying the cabin. I moved up here kind of hastily.”


Mr. Harlan looked at Richie and shrugged his shoulders. 


“We weren’t even going to charge for the cabin. My father here wanted it gone so bad we just were going to sell the land it’s on.”


I stepped forward.


“How much?”


Mr. Harlan just chuckled.


“Eighty-thousand.”


“Deal.”


“Don’t you wanna see it first?”


“Uh-”


I had a headache. It was all so much.


“Richie,” Mr. Harlan nudged him. “I’ll watch the store, go show her the cabin.”


He sighed and set down the papers he had in his hands. Then he started toward me with a hint of urgency.


“You something that can go off-road?”


I nodded.


“Good, let’s go-”


It didn’t take long to get there. Pinecrest was a smaller city than I was used to. The square faded into residential, then the residential faded into forest. Close to twenty minutes later, Richie had me turn down onto a long dirt road. I was grateful to have gotten the supped up suspension.


“This little truck drives like a dream.” Richie said to me.


It was a small little cabin. Two bedrooms, one bath, open concept kitchen and living room. It had a fireplace too, which would be good for winter.


“All this for just eighty-thousand?”


Richie nodded.


“Dads had this for forever, but it was too small for us when I was born. He always said he was gonna rent it out, but he never did.”


“Any issues?”


He nodded, walking around to the kitchen.


“There’s a couple leaks in the roof, should be easy repairs. The cabin has been around for a bit, so there are a few hairline cracks in the drywall, but you can fix those with plaster and a can of paint.”


“Sound’s relatively easy.”


He looked at me.


“If you still want it, I can give you the contact info to a couple handymen around town who do roofing.”


“Yeah, I think… I think I’ll take it. It’s nice.”


“Alright well, we can do a down payment and then-”


“No, I can pay the total. $80,000. Just… Point me to a contract.”


He seemed surprised.


“What?”


“I just… we didn’t think anyone would want to buy it outright.”


“Why wouldn’t you? Buy it outright, I mean. That’s how property management works.”


“Most people do a down payment, but if you want to pay for it all outright, I won’t stop you. Like I said, Dad has been trying to sell it for a while.”


So… that was that. We drove back to the store, and the Harlans called their realtor, who brought the contract that I signed. A simple money transfer later, and I was the proud owner of a shabby cabin in the woods.


My home.

data.title: A Kingdom of Cards: Spade Dynasty
data.author: Counting Sheep
data.summary:
In a fragile alliance between the fae-ruled Diamond kingdom and the predominantly human Spade kingdom, peace is more performance than truth.

Phoenix, a Spade princess, has always lived by duty, instinct, and the quiet certainty of what her world demands of her. But when the Diamond royals return, a certain prince turns her world upside down. Orion, a boy from her past who no longer feels like one, comes back more snarky and arrogant than before.

Old bonds resurface. Loyalties blur. And beneath the surface of diplomacy and tradition, something far more dangerous begins to stir.

chapters.title: Prologue
chapters.content:
The halls were eerily quiet, each step echoing like a drumbeat in a crypt. The sharp tap of Flint’s heeled soles struck the polished marble floors, reverberating down the corridor with each trembling step. He kept his chin lifted, back straight, and eyes locked on the towering double doors at the end of the hall. The servant boy passed beneath heavy tapestries and jeweled relics proudly held on display as he neared the Queen’s quarters.


With every step, the air thickened and his palms grew clammy. His fingers trembled around the letter and the tiny branches sprouting from his knuckles shook with them. Flint held the parchment with the same care one might handle the royal crown, cautious of his every move.

The Spade Kingdom’s royal seal stamped the missive shut, its black wax winking in the candlelight as if daring the boy to break it open.

Twin doors dwarfed him in size as he came to a halt. Flanking the doors were two knights, hardly acknowledging his presence as their indifferent glances offered no comfort. When he reached out to knock, he felt his limbs stiffen. His body felt rooted to the ground as his pulse drummed in his ears.
 

What in the high divinities' names was he even doing here? Delivering royal correspondence wasn’t part of his duties, it had been thrust upon him without warning. He should have refused. But refusing meant no job, and no job meant no money.


He rapped the door gently, his branches scratching the door quietly, then he stepped back. Swallowing wasn’t enough to ease the dryness in his throat.


A muffled voice called from within and the guards opened the doors without a word.


The room was dark and faintly lit by a single candle. A large bed sat against the far wall, and across from it, a vanity with rows of cosmetics arranged with unnatural precision. A single painting hung above the bed: a depiction of war, brutal, gory, and burning.


The Queen was nowhere to be seen.

Flint’s stomach churned with unease. The stillness of the room pressed in on him and he unconsciously held his breath. Rumors spread through the castle staff about the cruel woman the Queen could be.


“What is it that you desire of me?” came her voice, cold and flat.

She stepped from the shadows without a sound, gliding to the balcony with unnatural grace. Her gown of black satin shimmered faintly under the moonlight as she pushed the glass doors open and let the breeze in.


“F- Forgive me your majesty…” he stammered, his dark hair falling over his shoulders as he bowed his head and held the letter up with both hands.

Slowly, she turned. The Queen’s venomous green eyes locked onto him, sharp as blades. Her lips curled into a faint, displeased frown. Her silky raven colored hair was pulled back into one long braid, absorbing the moonlight rather than reflecting it. Her eyes flicked to the letter and lingered on the seal before she snatched it from his trembling hands causing him to flinch.

Her gaze pierced his large, brown eyes, forcing him to lower his own as he stepped back.


“I hold a missive… from the Kingdom of Spades, I- I was informed it was of utmost urgency..” he mumbled.


In the moonlight, she was nothing more than a black silhouette, her ebony skin glowing faintly. Her green eyes burned fiercely against the darkness, like a creature out of legend or nightmare.


“Well. That is obvious…” she retorted, glancing at the wax seal. “Take your leave.”
She flicked her hand and the doors flew open.


Flint bowed once more before scrambling out of the room, not daring to look back.

data.title: Archangel
data.author: Pheonixstreem
data.summary:
Vesper, is a cybernetically enhanced mercenary trying to pay off crushing debt while searching for answers about her missing brothers. During what should be a routine theft, she steals a mysterious serum called Project Archangel and discovers that her experimental AI-assisted armor is beginning to override her free will.

At the same time, Hamish, a mage working as a mercenary, is sent to investigate a series of abandoned towns. What he finds is far worse than anyone expected: a spreading techno-organic plague that twists people, machines, and cybernetics into something monstrous.
When powerful forces place a bounty on Hamish and begin hunting anyone connected to the outbreak, Vesper and Hamish are forced into an uneasy partnership. Together they must uncover the truth behind Project Archangel

chapters.title: Prologue
chapters.content:
It was a cold evening, the kind of cold that slipped through layers of clothing and settled deep in the bones. A steady wind swept across the city rooftops, carrying the metallic scent of rain and the distant hum of traffic below. The sky hung low beneath a blanket of heavy clouds, swallowing the last traces of daylight and hinting at the fast-approaching winter.  

    I knelt on the roof of a warehouse, tucked behind the bulky frame of a generator. Its constant mechanical rumble vibrated through the concrete beneath me, offering a thin veil of noise to mask my presence. The metal casing was cold against my shoulder, even through my armor and I could feel the dampness of the evening air gathering on every exposed surface. 

From my position, I had a narrow view over the edge of the roof and across the maze of industrial buildings beyond. Their windows glowed faintly in the growing darkness, scattered islands of pale yellow and sterile white among endless stretches of steel and concrete. Exhaust vents coughed steam into the cold air. Cargo drones drifted silently between distant towers, their navigation lights blinking like wandering stars.

Somewhere in the city, a bell tolled mournfully, its deep notes carrying farther than they should have through the night. One. Two. Three. 

Almost midnight. Another hour was added to the mental clock that never stopped running in the back of my mind. 

Five years, two weeks, three days, seven hours, and forty minutes.

That's how long it had been since my brothers vanished. 

No bodies. 

No answers. 

No final message, no ransom demand, no trace worth a damn. 

Just a clock that never stopped counting, and me filling the empty space between its ticks with things I never thought I'd do. 

Smuggling. Theft. Corporate espionage. A few jobs that sat in the gray area between legal and criminal, where the rules were flexible and the consequences weren't. 

The kind of work that paid well enough to keep searching. The kind of work that slowly changed a person. 

I pushed the thoughts aside and slowed my breathing until even my enhanced hearing barely registered it. The city faded into the background—distant engines, humming power lines, the rhythmic clatter of machinery several blocks away. 

My pulse settled. Muscles loosened. One tap against the control port on my hip. The blue-green glow of my cybernetics vanished instantly. Darkness swallowed me. The augmented overlay that usually painted the world in thermal signatures, threat markers, and targeting data winked out, leaving only shadows and moonlight. For a brief moment I felt naked without it, stripped of the artificial senses I'd relied on for years. 

Blind and exposed to the night. Just the way I needed to be. 

Across the street, the target building stood silent. Security patrols followed their predictable routes. Cameras swept through their programmed arcs. 

Behind reinforced walls sat a prize worth more credits than I'd earn in a decade of honest work. 

One more job. 

Get in. 

Get out. 

Pay off the last chunk of debt from the Ghost-Class armor I'd upgraded to. A couple steps below Wraith-Class, but still capable of stopping a rail round and outrunning a turret's targeting solution.

Expensive as hell. Worth every credit. 

Pain hurts more than guilt ever did. 

My fingers brushed the armored plating beneath my jacket. I could still remember signing the loan agreement. Remember the interest rates. Remember realizing I'd just sold years of my life for a chance to survive a little longer. 

But survival had a way of becoming addictive. 

Almost free. The thought lingered in the darkness. 

Almost.

Gravel shifted below me. I froze. Every muscle locked in place. Even the wind seemed to vanish. 

For a heartbeat, the only sound was the low growl of the generator at my back and the distant pulse of the city beyond the warehouse district.

Another tap. Emerald vision flared to life. The darkness shattered. Heat signatures bled into the world like coals in a furnace, painting every living thing in shades of amber, gold, and white. Night vision layered itself beneath the thermal feed, outlines sharpening as targeting software quietly synchronized the two streams. Distances. Angles. Movement vectors. 

Five figures. Two baseline humans. Thin silhouettes wrapped in heavy coats, moving with the nervous energy of people who knew exactly what kind of company they kept.

Their hearts fluttered visibly through the thermal overlay, rapid flashes in their chests like trapped birds beating against a cage. 

Three Fomori. The giants stalked between them. Slab-built monsters, broad enough to block an alley and tall enough to make ordinary men look adolescent by comparison. 

Their Aegis-Class dermal plating caught the faint ambient light in dull metallic ridges where synthetic armor merged seamlessly with flesh. The thermal feed showed heat pouring from them in waves, each one radiating like an industrial engine. 

Fuck their armor. 

Aegis-Class wasn't protection. It was a philosophy. 

Become the wall. Become the tank. 

Let the other bastard run out of ammunition first. 

They traded speed, stealth, and comfort for raw survivability. Small-arms fire bounced. Explosives annoyed them. Most people faced with a charging Fomori discovered exactly how fragile the human body really was. 

Corporate muscle. The kind companies deployed when they wanted a problem solved publicly. The kind built to break doors and people with equal efficiency. 

One of them turned its head, scanning the rooftops. My targeting suite immediately highlighted threat probabilities, escape routes, and estimated engagement outcomes. None of them looked good. 

I held perfectly still. My lungs burned as I resisted the urge to breathe. 

Don't move. Don't twitch. Don't give the sensors anything to catch.

The group continued down the alley below, boots crunching over loose gravel and discarded debris. The humans talked quietly among themselves. One of the Fomori laughed—a deep metallic rumble that echoed between the warehouse walls. 

Seconds stretched. Then they kept walking. Good. Let them pass. Let them disappear into the night. And for once, this job might actually finish clean. 

Job was simple enough. Get in the building, grab the goods, and get out. 

Experience didn't buy simple. 

It never had. 

The patrol rounded the corner, boots grinding against the gravel below. Their voices faded into the maze of warehouses and loading yards. 

I stayed motionless, counting the seconds in my head. 

Five. 

Ten. 

Fifteen. 

The heat signatures dwindled at the edge of my HUD, shrinking to distant embers before vanishing entirely. 

Silence reclaimed the rooftop. 

I rose from my crouch. My knees protested immediately. Hours spent perched on concrete and steel had left them stiff despite the reinforcement braces woven through my armor. 

The city wind swept across the rooftop, tugging at my jacket and slipping through the seams of my gear. It carried the familiar scent of the industrial district—ozone from overloaded transformers, rust from aging metal, and the faint chemical bite of exhaust from the street-level generators. 

Then the world lurched sideways. 

Frag!

Pain exploded through my skull.

It felt like someone had driven a white-hot spike through my right eye and buried it deep in the center of my brain. 

The pain hit so suddenly that my vision went white for a fraction of a second. My balance disappeared with it. My vision fractured. 

I staggered. One hand shot out and slammed against the generator housing before I could fall. Cold metal bit into my palm. The world refused to stay still. 

My night-vision feed shattered into emerald static. Thousands of bright green pixels danced across my vision like a swarm of insects. Diagnostic windows erupted across my HUD faster than I could process them. Warnings, system checks, error codes. Half of them vanished before I could read them. The other half dissolved into corrupted symbols. 

The rooftop flickered. 

One moment I was staring at a rusted ventilation duct twenty feet away. The next it was gone. Replaced by darkness. Then the darkness vanished and the rooftop snapped back into existence. 

Then darkness again. 

Then color. 

Then black. 

The transitions came so quickly my stomach rolled. 

A high-pitched whine began somewhere deep inside my skull. At first I thought it was coming from the generator. Then I thought it was coming from my comms. Then I realized I wasn't hearing it at all. I was feeling it. 

The vibration crawled through my teeth and jawbone, rattling the tiny implants buried along the base of my skull. 

Every cybernetic component in my body suddenly felt present. The ocular replacements behind my eyes. The neural jack at the base of my neck. The reinforcement mesh threaded through my spine. 

I became aware of all of it at once. 

Every piece of machinery. Every foreign component. Every gram of metal living inside me. The sensation was nauseating. 

My right eye twitched violently. The HUD tried to recalibrate. Failed. Tried again. Failed again. 

Thermal imaging flooded my vision without warning. Heat signatures smeared across the rooftop in brilliant oranges and whites. 

A heartbeat later the thermal layer vanished and low-light optics took over. Then both systems attempted to run simultaneously. 

The result looked like someone had poured molten glass over reality. 

I squeezed my eyes shut. That somehow made it worse. The pain intensified instantly. A tremor raced down my neck and into my shoulders. My muscles locked. 

For a terrifying moment I couldn't tell if my body was shaking or if the rooftop itself was vibrating beneath me. 

My pulse hammered in my ears. Too fast. 

Far too fast. 

I tasted copper. 

Blood. 

I had bitten down hard enough to split the inside of my cheek. The metallic taste spread across my tongue. 

The whine climbed higher. 

Higher. 

Higher. 

My implants felt hot. Not physically hot. Not enough to burn. Just wrong. Like circuitry operating beyond tolerances. Like a machine trying desperately to do something it wasn't designed to do. 

I dropped to one knee. The impact jarred through my armor.

Even that felt distant. Muffled. As though my body belonged to someone else and the pain was arriving through a damaged connection. 

"Not now..." I hissed through clenched teeth. 

The words sounded strange. Distant. Like I was hearing someone else speak. 

My hand tightened against the concrete until the armored glove creaked and the concrete cracked beneath it. 

Seconds dragged by. Each one felt hours longer than the last. 

Then, as suddenly as it had begun, the pressure eased. The whine faltered. The static thinned. The fractured layers of vision slowly drifted back into alignment. 

Diagnostic windows stabilized. 

The rooftop stopped spinning. The pain retreated from a screaming inferno to a dull, familiar throb behind my eye. 

I stayed where I was, breathing hard, waiting for another wave. It didn't come. 

One breath. 

Then another. Long enough for the pain to retreat behind my eye and become manageable. Long enough for the rooftop to stop pitching beneath my feet. 

Not long enough to trust that the episode was over. 

Good enough. 

It would have to be. 

I stepped to the edge of the roof and jumped. 

Air rushed past, cold and electric.

The city rose to meet me in a blur of concrete, steel, and fractured neon. Wind clawed at my jacket and roared in my ears, drowning out the distant hum of traffic and machinery. 

For a brief moment, gravity owned me. 

Mid-fall, I triggered the reinforcement servos in my legs. A fraction later than I should have. Part of it was habit. Part of it was distraction. Part of it was the lingering question of whether the implants would decide to eat themselves again before I hit the ground. 

My HUD apparently shared the concern. A small amber warning appeared in the corner of my vision. 

OPTIMAL ENGAGEMENT WINDOW EXCEEDED. 

"No shit," I muttered. 

The ground rushed up. I hit in a crouch. The shock dampeners ignited through the armor, dumping the impact into the reinforcement frame. Heat flashed through my knees, hips, and lower back as the system dispersed the force. 

The landing drove a dull jolt up my spine. Still better than shattered ankles. 

I straightened carefully. A faint tremor lingered in my hands.

Whether from the jump or the episode, I couldn't tell. The street was empty. 

Silent, save for the distant buzz of neon billboards and the low rhythmic pulse of a rooftop drone somewhere overhead.

chapters.title: Vesper
chapters.content:
Everything felt on edge.
Breaking in had been too easy the service door’s lock barely put up a fight, the security keypad still running factory firmware. No alarms rang out. One soft, click and the door swung inward like it had been expecting me. Never a good sign
Inside, the halls felt wrong — too clean, too empty. Fluorescent strips buzzed overhead, their light thin and clinical as a surgeon’s lamp. It bounced off sterile walls and polished concrete that refused to hold a fingerprint. No foot traffic. No drones careening through the vents. Not even a bored rent-a-corp seated in a chair doom scrolling the net.
My camera loop ran perfect, a seamless feed of empty corridor after empty corridor. It should’ve calmed me. It didn’t. It made my nerves itch like static under a sock. The air tasted of recycled vent output left running too long: stale and metallic, with a faint chemical tang I couldn’t place.
I paused and pulled up the intel packet. Schematics flickered in the corner of my vision: access routes, maintenance shafts, redacted sections that made my teeth grind. Target: sub-basement. Floor tag: 7. I’d have to drop five, maybe six floors if the corp architects got cute with extra unlabeled floors. They loved burying secrets deeper than they hid ethics.
A low vibration hummed through the floor plating under my boots — heavy machinery somewhere below, cycling in a slow, steady rhythm. It was almost comforting, that mechanical heartbeat. Almost. My reflection ghosted across the HUD for a second: green eyes rimmed in dark, tired lines, a faint crawling static dancing across the overlay. The static felt personal, as if something inside me wanted attention. I scrubbed it away.
This should’ve been a team job: sweep, breach, extraction. Divide the risk, divide the fire. Instead someone had insisted a single Kinzan could slip in clean. Or that a single Kinzan was expendable. Either way, I was solo, and my mouth tasted like iron because of it.
I moved fast. The service stairs were concrete, the handrail polished slick with oil and anonymous fingerprints. My boots ate the descent in three even sets of two; the echo of my steps was the loudest sound in the building. Sub-level six opened like an artery: narrow hallways, service doors every few meters, labels that meant nothing and everything. Still empty. The building was breathing around me, and I felt like the only foreign body inside it.
I eventually hit the floor I needed to be on. And it was short work reaching the door. I glanced over my shoulder, then set my back to the cold steel door. The lock was reinforced: mag-hold with a tiny diagnostics strip blinking amber. I fed a bypass spike into the access port, felt the relay click under my glove, then a hiccup. The spike met resistance, microscopic pins catching on an unseen latch.
I cursed softly and worked the spike. The strip flickered amber, then green. The door clicked open. Relief was thin; it tasted worse than the cheap synth-coffee I’d been living off of.
I slipped inside and eased the door shut behind me. The latch clicked soft as breath.
The HUD flickered once, then again. Overlay symbols crowding my vision as it tried to tag every surface in sight. Power conduits. Heat signatures. Unknown compounds. A mess of pop-ups, all bright and eager, all noise.
“Not now,” I muttered, blinking twice to suppress the AR flood. The system hesitated like a sulking dog before dimming to a minimal display.
I took a step forward. The air felt heavier here, filtered but stale, with that faint antiseptic bite labs always have, like someone had scrubbed away something worse.
It was a lab, all right. Not what I was expecting, but somehow not a surprise either. Long counters lined both walls, cluttered with sealed sample canisters, spent diagnostic cartridges, and shattered glassware that no one had bothered to sweep up. The lighting was too bright in places, too dark in others, half the strips flickering, half burned out.
A row of suspended monitors hung from the ceiling, cycling through frozen data screens. Whatever they’d been working on, the process had been interrupted mid-step. Cooling fans still whined somewhere deep in the room. A faint hum under the floor suggested active systems—life support, containment, something.
I moved further in, careful where I placed my boots. My reflection ghosted across a glass panel, warped by some fluid behind it. For a second, the HUD picked up a heat source where there shouldn’t have been one. An outline, vaguely human, curled in on itself. Then it vanished. Glitch or not, it made the back of my neck prickle.
I shook my head, dismissing the floating overlays until the room went quiet again—just the muted glow of night vision and the slow bloom of heat from the machinery around me. Clean. Controlled. Manageable.
Then I brought back the info packet, a thin strip of data scrolling across the corner of my vision. I flicked through encrypted notes and redacted lines until a description popped up—small glass vial, six centimeters long, steel cap, cryo-stamped label reading Project: Archangel.
That was all I needed.
I set my internal scanners to active search mode. A soft pulse rippled through the space—short-range sweep calibrated for compound density and temperature variation. The HUD painted faint wire-frames over the lab benches, highlighting shapes and containers. Most registered as empty or inert. A few flagged volatile, a couple still cold enough to mist the air when I passed. None matched the pattern yet.
The pulse returned faint echoes—metal, glass, composite. But under it, something else. A deeper thrum, like a second signal bleeding through the scan, just out of sync. My sensors glitched, flickering once before stabilizing.
I ignored it. Or tried to. My head buzzed for half a second too long, like a mosquito inside my skull. I gritted my teeth and pushed the thought aside. The mission came first. Always first.
I started moving between workstations, scanning shelves, drawers, containment trays—each click of my boots sounding way too loud even above the machinery hums.
I traced the edge of the table, metal cold under my fingertips. Every minute pulled at me like thick syrup. Too slow.
Finally, my HUD picked it up. A faint thermal signature in the cold storage fridge a few meters ahead. of course. Nothing worth a damn ever sits in plain view or easy access.I edged around the table, careful not to kick scattered glass or forgotten tools. Each step precise, measured. Night vision painted the room in green, thermal outlining every object like a blueprint. The vials came into view, shimmering with clear liquid slightly warmer than the cold air. My sensors hummed faint approval. My HUD flagged six of them.
I scanned the area for a carrying case. There had to be one. My HUD flicked through overlays, highlighting shapes, edges, potential containersnothing useful. A dozen sealed drawers, a few shattered trays, and a single overturned cart leaking coolant across the floor. No transport unit. No containment box.
I clenched my jaw, pulse ticking behind my teeth. I didn’t have any means of moving the vials safely. No one told me I’d need to. Typical. They send me in blind, expect me to improvise, and act surprised when things burn down.
I crouched beside a counter, rifled through a drawer. Empty. Another—just brittle gloves and a cracked data-pad still looping a corrupted boot screen. The third offered a sliver of hope: insulated tubing, a fragment of foam packing, and the stale smell of ethanol. Useless. I tossed them aside and glanced back toward the fridge. Frost was creeping across the glass in delicate, spidering veins, each breath of the machine louder than the last.
I switched to just thermal for a moment—clean lines, cold air pooling low around the floor, heat shimmering faintly from the vials inside. That faint warmth again, just enough to register wrong. Something about the temperature discrepancy clawed at me, but I pushed it aside.
I felt the tickle of static crawl up my spine—HUD interference bleeding through my implants. My vision shimmered for half a second, outlines bending, text flickering in languages I didn’t know. The glitch passed, leaving a faint hum in my skull like a leftover migraine. Not again. I took a slow breath, forcing my pulse back down. Not the time. Not the place.
I scanned the lab one last time, eyes lingering on a half-collapsed containment unit in the corner. Metal casing. Sealed edges. Maybe, if I could jury-rig it…
The clock in my HUD ticked down another minute. I exhaled. No one told me I’d need to bring a carrying case. No one ever tells you the details until you’re already in the dark, staring at something you shouldn’t be touching.
I grabbed the containment unit and hauled it onto the nearest counter. The casing was dented, one hinge half-broken, but it would do. I tore out the inner racks, lined the bottom with the foam packing I’d scavenged earlier. It wasn’t much, but it would keep the vials cold long enough to get them topside. My hands moved fast, more muscle memory than thought—cut, repurpose, reseal. The soft hiss of coolant escaping the cracked tubing filled the air.
I kept glancing back toward the fridge, measuring seconds in the rhythm of its compressor. The temperature differential on m HUD was already fluctuating; those vials weren’t meant to stay exposed long. I forced my breathing steady. Fast was fine. Sloppy was fatal.
Almost done. Just needed to re-seat the power coupling and I could lock the temperature loop. I leaned in, fingers working the makeshift seal, then the HUD spasmed. A sharp, jarring flicker across my vision. A yellow alert glyph blinked in the corner: MOTION DETECTED — SECTOR ENTRY POINT.
“Shit.”
I killed the display instinctively and shoved the half-fixed containment box under the table. The metal scraped against the floor, too loud in the silence. I winced, slid it deeper, and straightened just as the door’s magnetic locks disengaged with a soft thunk.
The air pressure shifted—subtle but unmistakable. The door cracked open, spilling a thin slice of sterile light into the lab.
I launched myself upward, servos in my legs kicking with a muted whine as I caught the ceiling’s edge and pulled myself into the corner. The metal framework groaned under my weight before settling. I braced there, one hand hooked around a support pipe, boots pressed flat against the junction where wall met ceiling.
My systems adjusted, compensating for the shift in balance. I killed the last traces of active HUD light—darkness swallowed everything but the soft pulse of thermal outlines bleeding through my optics. Breath slow. Muscles locked. Motionless.
The door opened fully beneath me. A sliver of white light sliced across the lab floor, scattering reflections off broken glass and metal trays. Shadows moved in that beam—tall, armored, careful. Whoever they were, they knew enough to keep their weapons low and their steps measured.
A faint hum reached me through the air, like the soft tuning whine of a comm unit. One voice, then another. I recognized it, it was the group from earlier.
One of them swept a handheld scanner across the room. The beam passed inches from my position, painting everything below in soft UV glow. I felt the sensor pass over me, the hairs at the back of my neck prickling as the device cycled through frequencies. My armor’s active camo modules adjusted automatically, dampening my thermal signature until my body heat barely registered.
One of the Fomori muttered something to the other. A reply, muffled. Boots scuffed. A shadow moved closer to the fridge—their focus was on the open door, the exposed vials glinting inside.
My fingers tightened around the pipe. The sound of my own pulse filled my ears, too loud, too human. I forced myself to stay still, to wait, even as the itch of adrenaline burned under my skin.
One wrong twitch, and they’d look up.

chapters.title: Hamish
chapters.content:
“I go no further.”

I paused mid-scribe, my pen hovering over the half-finished rune I had been working on. The sigil dimmed, its pale cyan glow guttering out as the mana-thread collapsed

The guide had already killed the engine. Silence rushed in to fill the space it left, broken only by the soft patter of rain against the vehicle’s shell. Outside, the road ended in rot and weeds, the old mag-lanes cracked and half-swallowed by mud. A single flickering lamp leaned crooked at the roadside, its light sickly and weak, barely pushing back the fog.

The guide twisted in his seat to face us. His coat was synth-leather, patched and re-patched, the collar threaded with warding wire. A chrome implant replaced one eye, its iris scrolling faint diagnostic runes. He held out his hand, palm up, fingers twitching once.

“No,” Cameron said from the back seat. He leaned forward, the glow from his wrist-rig casting sharp lines across his jaw. “We agreed fifty percent up front, fifty percent after we get back.” He craned his neck, peering past the guide through the rain-streaked windshield. “And aren’t we still, like, two miles out?”

The guide’s smile didn’t reach his eyes. “Town close enough.”

“Just pay him.” our healer said softly. She sat with her hands folded around a mana crystal at her throat. Her dark brown hair fell in waves around her shoulders, accentuated by the soft blue glow of the crystal “We’ll be okay.”

Cameron gritted his teeth. “Fine. But he leaves the vehicle here.”

For a moment, I thought the guide might argue. Instead, he shrugged, the motion loose and careless, as if none of this mattered to him anymore. Cameron slapped a pre-loaded cred-stick into his waiting palm. The guide didn’t even look at the balance before pocketing it.

“Fine by me,” he said, opening the door. Rain and cold flooded in. “Where you go is death.”

I arched an eyebrow as he left.

“Yeah, frag you too,” Cameron muttered, watching the guide’s silhouette vanish back the way we’d come.

I looked down and reactivated my work. Mana bled back into the lines as I finished the sigil, the ink flaring briefly before settling. I leaned close and blew across the page, drying it with a faint shimmer of residual energy.

“Don’t know why you don’t just use a tablet,” Cameron said, leaning over my shoulder. The glow from one of his augments washed the paper in pale blue light. “Would be faster.”

I folded the paper carefully, edges aligned, creases pressed flat with my thumb. The warmth lingered, a soft thrum pulsing through it like a heartbeat. I held it out to him.

“Can’t give it to you if it’s on there,” I said. “Also, you know tech and magic don’t mesh well.”

He took it, turning the folded sheet over in his hands, brows knitting as if he could feel the spell through the paper. “What is it?”

“Protection ward,” I answered. “We don’t know what’ll be out here.”

He shrugged, easy, like we were gearing up for a routine guard job instead of a run into a dead town. “Cool.”

“It should stop an attack from someone about your strength,” I continued, meeting his eyes, “but only once. After that, it’ll break.” I tapped the folded paper with two fingers. “I can’t keep throwing mana around. Need to conserve what I’ve got.”

“Did you do one for Milyah?” he asked.

“I’m good,” Milyah said, shaking her head slightly. “I may be specialized in healing, but I know a few defensive spells.” She glanced down at the folded ward in Cameron’s hands, then back up, offering a small smile. “And a couple offensive ones, if it comes to that. But I appreciate the thought.”

“Anyway, we came all the way out here for reconnaissance,” I said, pushing myself upright and tucking my notebook away. “All the client wants to know is why towns out here keep getting abandoned. We find the reason, get out and they’ll send a specialized team in.”

“Hey, y’all done chit-chatting up there?” a voice crackled over our Nexus comms. “It’s kinda cramped back here.”

“Oh, right.” Cameron laughed, the tension bleeding out of his voice. “Sorry, guys.”

We climbed out of the vehicle and circled around to the rear of the transport. Cameron popped the latch and hauled the door open. The seal hissed, and the remaining three members of our recon team spilled out as they stretched and swore in unison.

Jason was the first to straighten, rolling his shoulders as his Genesis armor crackled and whined, plates shifting to compensate. “Crikey,” he said, flexing his hands. “Hope this goes smoothly. I need the cred from this job if I’m ever gonna afford an upgrade.”

Dallas, our local locksmith, snorted and slugged Jason’s shoulder hard enough to make the armor thump. “Damn straight. Your rig’s, what, three generations behind now? I’ve seen museum pieces with better response time.”

“Still kept me alive,” Jason shot back.

“Barely,” Avery said, rolling his eyes.

Avery was probably the least augmented one of us, not counting Milyah and me. No visible augments, no glowing interfaces, no obvious hardware. Just muscle. Thick, dense muscle, packed onto a frame built like a bunker. He looked human enough, but everyone who met him for more than five minutes swore he had to be half-orc.

“Pay off the Sharks first,” He added flatly. “Upgrades don’t mean much if you’re dead in an alley.”

“Yeah, yeah,” Jason grouched, adjusting the tension of one of his shoulder plates. “Can’t go five minutes without someone reminding me about my debt.”

“If you’d stop gambling, we would stop.” I said, deadpan.

Jason shot me a look, at the same time scrubbing a hand through his sandy hair. “It’s not gambling if I’m good at it.”

Dallas barked out a laugh. Avery just shook his head, unimpressed.

“Statistically,” I added, “you’re not.”

That earned me a groan and another round of muttered complaints as Cameron sealed the transport back up behind us.

“Alright,” Avery said. “Eyes up. Focus. No more horseplay.”

He gestured toward the dark stretch of road leading into town. “We move in teams of two. Keep visual contact with your partner at all times. No heroics, no wandering off.” His gaze lingered on Jason for half a second longer than necessary.

“We split to cover ground faster, sweep outward, then converge on the town center. If anything goes sideways, you fall back to your partner first, then the rally point.” He nodded once, decisive. “Comms stay open. If you see something that doesn’t belong, you call it.”

He jerked his chin at Jason. “You’re with Cameron.” Then he nodded toward Dallas. “Dallas, take Milyah.” Finally, his eyes landed on me. “Hamish, you’re stuck with me.”

I shrugged, rolling one shoulder under my coat. “Sure. Just… no one get flattened, yeah? We’ve only got one actual healer, and I’d like to keep it that way.”

“You know healing spells,” Dallas said, pointing at me like he’d caught me trying to dodge responsibility.
