In a minute, she was standing beside me, examining the hinge, closing and opening the door with varying amounts of force while I covertly plucked bits of wood off my tongue. The surprise in her eyes made my chest puff out, and I beamed as she nodded in approval.

"Alright, then," she said, "a tray of my iced rolls for you."

The reward was enticing, but felt awkwardly misplaced now. My excitement was muted.

I followed her downstairs, where I watched her pull about a half dozen iced rolls off a sheet and wrap them in tika cloth. I debated in my head how fast I could eat all of them. Three children instantly materialized around me as I accepted the reward like a sacred offering. I was swarmed with questions, then fierce negotiations for the desserts, and I barely escaped with my life and my six rolls.

I noticed a little kitchen timer on the floor on the way out. Just sitting there, waiting to be stepped on. Thrown. Broken—and its components, a beautiful concoction of springs and gears and ratchets, wasted.

I jerked my tail, and my hammer thudded on the floorboards.

"Oops."

I crouched to scoop both it and the timer up, and I left the house.

chapters.title: Chapter III
chapters.content:
Leaving Master's house, the sun shone even warmer than before, hot against my bare arms like the air at the forges. The surfaces of the streets rippled like the air was dancing. Hounds barked and livestock brayed in the distance.

I stuffed my hammer back into its sleeve, and the timer into a pants pocket. Suki was still waiting outside, sniffing around the ground; the position of where the staff lied marked how far off she'd wandered from where I'd seated her. I couldn't blame her for getting bored. I had no idea how long I'd been in there for.

I whistled, and she perked and bounded over. Her nose worked furiously when she came into proximity with the wrapped bundle in my arm. I angled it away from her.

"Mine."

I rode her back to the forges. I guided her between them to the storage shed in the middle, where I dismounted. I left her to chew on the staff as I approached the shed door, held ajar by a stone, and slipped inside.

It felt delightfully loftier on the inside. Each breath was flavored with coal, cold iron, dusty wood, leather. Its walls were lined with shelves and crates crammed with billets and ingots ready to be shaped; broken tools and scrap likely to be remelted; spare tongs and hammers and files and fullers and swage blocks. The opposite wall was stacked nearly to the ceiling with sacks of coal.

They didn't look that low on coal. I wondered if Toad took his father's habit of exaggeration literally. Or maybe he'd made his clan comment purely to test me.

Irrelevant now. I put my bundle of wrapped pastries on a barrel, lifted my tail by my hip to pull Grunt's pliers out of the tool sleeve, and found his toolbox was in a different corner now. I opened it and stuffed the pliers back in.

I heard a gruff noise like the grunt of an old hound. I turned.

Grunt was standing by the door in that one corner the window light didn't reach. I'd gone right past him.

"What're you doing with my tools?" he grumbled, sour and gravelly.

"Toad took them and asked me to bring them back," I said.

"Why would he take 'em?" the stocky man growled.

I shrugged. "Ask him." I turned and my tail extended out behind me for balance as I crouched between two crates, where a tarp was spread over sharp, irregular shapes. I heard low, rough grumbling with heavy shuffling that transitioned from cobblestone floor to distant dirt. The shed breathed again as Grunt left, and I settled into the intimate embrace of solitude.

I pulled the tarp up, which greeted me with a cloud of slack dust and the smell of oil.

This was my little space I'd earned for myself. In whichever corners they'd fit, I snuck in my own mechanical projects. My current pile was two half-formed rifle bodies, a wind-up pencil sharpener that broke a lot, an experimental spring coil mechanism with a functionless pulley thing, two springs bolted to a spoon for reasons that had long since escaped me, and my current project.

I'd copied the body of a speargun. A speargun was as it sounded; it shot spears like a crossbow shot arrows. It'd been invented for soldiers who couldn't throw spears anymore.

I was most fascinated by controlling energy and movement, potentials and kinetics. This did enter the range of weaponry, but only because I was fascinated by their function, not by the results of their use.
But all that projectile weapons did was exert a burst of outward force, and that energy simply blew away in the wind afterward. No other function. Frankly, boring.

I wanted to create a multipurpose tool out of a one-use weapon.

I wanted to make my speargun shoot rope, and then reel the rope back in automatically. Like a fishing rod, but without the retrieval mechanism relying on manual force—the human arm was too slow, and stood no chance if the spearhead was lodged into a surface like stone.

But if I ever got it to work, and if the chief ever recovered, he would surely name me Artificer. I didn't want Fling-Husekai-Fighter-Artificer to be a fantasy anymore.

I took the timer out of my pocket and inspected it. It was a nice, shiny brass, with a cream wooden clockface and black, spindly hands. Its maximum counter notch went to fifty minutes. I traced a scratch on its casing. I shook it. I wound it partially—clickclickclickclick—and it rang hysterically in my hand.

"You sound quite healthy," I assured it. "I hope you don't mind." I grabbed my chisel off my tail and started prying off the timer's rear case.

The casing popped off, revealing a belly full of little metal innards. Tiny, intricate gears of steel and copper I paused to admire. The ratchet wheel, the bell hammer, the escapement gears. The mainspring was half coiled, about to burst free. I pinned it down with my thumb as I debated how to get it out without it exploding.

I fell into my natural rhythm of wiggling and muttering. It helped me think. Very slowly, very carefully, I wiggled the mainspring out of its little compression chamber. Freed, it laid slack and content in my palm.

"I'm impressed by whoever was patient enough to get you to behave," I told the spring.

It occurred to me that this entire machine was designed around the slow, measured release of this one spring. It fascinated me so completely.
Because most people weren't built like this. Even I wasn't. I exploded under pressure. My escapement system must have been trash.

I wondered when the city would explode, too.

I poked at the ratchet wheel. I wound the timer again to see the ratchet spin and hear it click through its rotation, though that was all it did with the mainspring missing. Its only energy source was manual... which was my current problem with my project. Spinning alone was useless.

I tried to spin the ratchet wheel the opposite way. It gave one click before obstinately locking in place against my finger.

"Controlled direction of force," I observed aloud, as if voicing the discovery made it more prestigious.

I looked at my gun prototype. I had a drum installed that acted as a spool for the rope. If I shot the harpoon, the drum would spin rapidly as the rope unspooled. My current problem was trying to recycle that energy, or get it to produce more energy, to spin the drum the opposite way so that it would reel the rope back in.

I heard footsteps approaching outside. Too light to be any worker I recognized—and slightly uneven. Toad?

I didn't look up, and spun the drum as I pondered. The rope tangled, and I spun it the other way. I'd been stuck on this for about a week now.

My blueprint parchment was still folded under my belt, and I fished it out and unfolded it. It was a rough, smeary diagram of the gun. I had been trying to map out the size ratios of potential mechanism pieces for the rope retrieval system, but I didn't even know what pieces to start with.

"Why in the world did you tell Grunt Saluk I took his pliers?" said a familiar youthful voice, strained with impatience.

I glanced up. Toad—now clean. He had a smooth, creamy complexion lighter than Master's aged tan, but the same black waves of hair.

"He believed it," I replied, leaning over to look back into the open interior of my gun. I held the timer's mainspring over it, hoping it might whisper to me all the answers of the universe. Then I got distracted trying to scrape dirt out from under my thumbnail with it.

I vaguely registered Toad balking at me.

I looked back at the gutted timer. It functioned by creating, storing, and releasing energy. It was already doing exactly what I needed my gun's retrieval system to do. That ratchet held the timer mainspring's tension and released it only one way. I knew that was important.

"Ratchet," I mumbled to myself.

Could this exact set of components work on a grander scale? Perhaps I could make a compression chamber for a large spring? A force, maybe the fired gunshot, maybe a crank, could compress the spring; a ratchet could hold that tension so the drum wouldn't spin the rope back out. And then—

"Is that—why do you have that?!" Toad squawked, jumping at the timer. His silver eyes were wide at the gaping hole in its front. "You took my mother's kitchen timer?!"

"Rescued," I corrected, tapping my knuckles against my lips as I tried desperately to cling to the thought I'd just had before he spoke.

Ratchet. Hold the tension. Release... how? A button, a lever?

"Is this what people mean?" Toad said in a tone that challenged my impression of his seemingly quiet nature. "Everyone says you steal and you lie. I didn't believe it. And you kept saying you'd stopped. But you took those tools in front of me, and then you took something out of my own house?"

Would that one burst of energy be enough to get the entire rope's length back in? No, controlled release so that the energy release lasted for the rope's length. Just like the timer. I jittered inside. I was so close to something! Why did I have to be interrupted now?

"Rescued off the floor with babies who throw things. You'd be crowing at someone no matter what," I ground out, setting my blueprint on the floor. I heaved a sigh. "I just needed it for something."

"For what?"

"For this." I gestured to the body of my prototype and the bits and pieces scattered around it. "It just gave me an idea."

Toad stared at it. I couldn't tell if that look meant incredulity or curiosity. I arrogantly assumed the latter and clarified.

"It's a line-throwing harpoon gun that I will design with a retrieval system," I said. I couldn't deny the pride in my voice. "Think about it. This could be a grapple gun. That could save your life in a bad situation. Or it could save you travel over precarious terrain. Rescue device. It could transport cargo over geographical gaps. It could retrieve objects or game over long distances. It's the feathers to your wings!"
I tapped the barrel with my chisel to make a nice click. "The chief would name me Artificer for sure if he wasn't ill. And your little kitchen timer just inspired me."

Toad stared a minute longer. I pursed my lips to one side as I waited for him to unfreeze.

"So I'm supposed to tell my mother her baking timer is gone because you wanted to make a weird gun?" he asked with genuine confusion in his voice. I groaned in anguish.

"For the love of the Carriers, I can put it back together," I relented, then glanced at my paper. Immediately I scrambled for something to write with. "After I write it down."

My hand groped furiously at my little cup of tiny screws and gears and tools. Charcoal... where? Pencil? Pen? Did I have anything in there to write with?

"Fling Husekai-Fighter, you don't get it," Toad pleaded, his pitch rising. "Father let you in his house because I had told him I thought you didn't steal anymore. This puts me in a very strange position!"

I felt my backstripe stiffen under my vest. Why would Toad care whether or not I still stole? I didn't even know his name until today.

"You don't get it." I finally found a piece of vine buried under all the other little pieces in the cup and started scratching down a sketch of the timer's internal composition. I had to remember it. "This is important. I needed this to understand how it worked. And I didn't steal it. I'll—"

I paused, licking my lips as my eyes flicked between the timer's ratchet teeth and my charcoal mimicking its notches on the parchment.

"—I'll give it back."

A beat of silence. I imagined the expression Toad was making—probably that bug-eyed stare again—as I muttered at my sketch. It was so... flat. Two-dimensional. The thought of relying on this instead of the original subject pained me.

"If I didn't come in here, you wouldn't ever give it back, would you?" Toad asked. My charcoal paused, then continued scratching down its crude replication.

I didn't care to answer. I was busy. I nudged the timer's ratchet to mark down which direction it spun in.

"If I tell Father, you won't get the scrap bin," Toad said.

I raised my head and looked up at him in disbelief. He now had my attention in a way I did not like.

"You'd tattle like one of your baby sisters?" I jabbed.

Toad frowned. It was that soft, blank sort of frown he'd had when he'd been complaining about the forge slack blowing in his face. Back when I thought he was a more passive type.

"I said I'd give it back!" I snapped.

"Put it back together," Toad insisted. I squirmed with the surge of exasperation.

"Fine!"

And so Toad stood there the entire time, watching me as I begrudgingly reassembled the kitchen timer. I yelped as I sliced my thumb open trying to slip the spring back into its place, then made sure its chamber connected to the ratchet gear properly, and then I bolted the casing back on.

I shoved the timer at Toad with force just short of throwing it at him. "I hope your mother is very fond of—"

It fell.

It hit with a sharp metallic impact. I looked down. The timer had exploded on the stone floor, its components scattered around Toad's feet.

I stared.

It'd just... slipped between our hands. I thought he'd had it.

"That wasn't—why didn't you—"

I crouched, hand hovering over the pieces. The casing had split open and spilled its gears, the bell... the ratchet wheel. It wouldn't fit back together. My bleeding thumb left red smears on the brass.

Toad stood there staring down at me. I stood up, sucking on my bloody thumb, tasting iron and oil as my tail lashed.

He inhaled. Then said nothing. He crouched to scoop up the pieces one by one, and walked out with the kind of silence that told me he didn't like me anymore.

I didn't like him anymore, either. Filthy little goody dove. It would never have broken if all the variables involving him hadn't existed. It would never have been a problem if he hadn't came in—

He'd came in because I lied to Grunt. Blast it all!

And out with him went the answer to my retrieval system.

The answer to my next name.

I growled and ran my hands through my curls, looking in disdain at my crude sketch, and then my gun.

I'd been so close to something!

I spent an hour staring at my blueprints. I had the idea for the retrieval system, but not the execution. Everything I had built that functioned had been off of a base or a reference. Everything I built from imagination had been useless. Like the springs bolted to the spoon.

The timer could have been my reference, my base. But now all I had was a rushed two-dimensional sketch.

I could find another timer.

I needed to find another timer.

Maybe there was one in my house somewhere. I had to trust it would be built the exact same way.

At some point I was just sitting between the storage crates, angrily stuffing cold pastries in my mouth to get the aftertaste of blood out. Their presence felt entirely undeserved now, but they took the edge off my irritation. Sweaty smiths lumbered in and out of the shed, taking or adding items, and casting me odd looks.

Eventually I felt a little sick from the sugar and realized I'd accidentally eaten through all six rolls. I balked for a moment, then licked my fingers, compacted my things into the smallest pile they could be, threw the tarp back over them, and left the shed.

I squinted and shielded my eyes as I stepped into the sunlight. The sun was high. Near noon. I had to meet my ts'una soon—my tutor—but there was still time to get to my house first.

Except Suki was nowhere in sight. I looked around, slowly circling in place. The knucklegrass crunched under my boots. Suki wouldn't be by the forges; she didn't like the heat. She wouldn't go past them; she was trained better than that. I saw the guiding staff lying ahead and picked it off the ground. There were fresh wet spots and splinters in it from her teeth.

I whistled. She didn't come.

After a few more paces, I realized she was beside the shed, squatted down. I jogged to her, to find she was mid-defecation.

I threw my head back with a long groan. "Suuukiii—"

She glanced at me with no urgency whatsoever.

I waited.

She was taking so long that I was starting to sweat under the sun. It was as if her bowels had froze to spite me. Eventually I gave up, and ran towards the hill of my house on my own two feet, staff still in my hand.

Building placements guided me onto the main road that cut straight through the city. I flew through the traffic, swinging my tail to weave around people and animals without losing speed despite the disgruntled cries following in my wake. I made it about halfway until I realized I had just downed far too much sugar and dough to get away with this. Five seconds later, I was leaned against a wall, panting, pressing my elbow into the sudden cramping in my gut. It felt like it'd been stabbed.

"You're being terribly dramatic," I muttered to it. It tightened like a fist as if to argue back. I made a pitiful little noise on accident, and carefully pushed off the wall. I would just walk. That was fine.

This was embarrassing. Six rolls. Why had I eaten all six?

I walked five more paces. Then froze.

I heard something.

I wouldn't have heard it if I'd kept running.

There were spaces between some of the taller buildings that made enclosed alleyways because the roofs were so wide. It wasn't the alley I was passing, but the one ahead, wherein I heard a distant bark of voice.

Then a thud against stone as I drew nearer. Another impact.

A second voice. Not just any voice—I knew it. I knew that curse. I knew whose favorite curse that was.

The last building I passed had a yellow banner, Husekai crest, half torn off a pole. I peeked around the corner, into the alley. I couldn't immediately compute what I saw.

There were two youths grappling deep within the alley. One of them was visibly of the head family of Clan Bajul; rust-brown hair, grey horns, backstripe that went down the entire tail. The other—

Rock.

The Bajul boy had a fistful of Rock's shirt. Rock shoved and slammed the boy into a wall, knocking dust loose from the stone. The boy cursed and darted sideways to evade, towards me, and arced around Rock without noticing me.

I saw a bloody nose. Heaving chests. Backstripes bristling like razors.

The boy punched Rock in the stomach. Rock doubled over, then yelled and threw a sloppy swing. The boy bobbed left and called him a chickadee.

This wasn't sparring.

This was the spring exploding with no ratchet to catch it. This was the beginning of war.

I realized the staff was shaking in my grip. A hot, rigid tingle pooled in my limbs. I shot forward, forgetting my stomach, forgetting the timer, forgetting everything—

"Stop it!" I shrieked. "Stop it!"

I grabbed the back of Rock's vest and yanked him back. He whirled around and struck my shoulder with his palm, sending me staggering back. Then he froze.

"Fling?—"

"You Husekai caw and strut about honor day and night, but you brought your baby brother to fight for you?!" the boy bellowed, and lunged to headbutt with his horns. Rock sprang in front of me and grabbed the back of the boy's collar, snapping him back by his momentum.

"He isn't part of this!" Rock shouted in the boy's face, jerking the fistful of shirt.

"Rock, stop!" I yelled.

"Go home!" Rock roared at me. The boy shoved him back and threw an elbow that landed across Rock's chin, and Rock yelped.

My lungs stuttered—locked—as I watched the constant exchange of blows. I couldn't swallow, move. I couldn't breathe. No one was stopping. Their faces were flushed and smeared with blood, both of them limping, both of them feral. They'd pause simultaneously to wheeze for air in a race to recover faster than the other.

I flew in and swung. I cracked the staff across the Bajul boy's thigh, then barreled my body into Rock so hard I managed to topple him.

They both hit the ground, groaning. I stood shaking, willing them to stay down.

The Bajul boy dragged himself away and very slowly lifted his weight onto one leg. He sent me a look of murder and cursed the eagle in Ts'nkai.

Rock hauled himself upright just as slowly. This close, I noticed he was trembling.

He, too, shot me a look of murder.

"Please stop," I squeaked. My chest suddenly seized with stuttering hiccups and my vision blurred over.

Rock swayed unsteadily. He ran his nose over his sleeve with a wet snort, leaving a trail of red over the fabric. He winced with every shift of his weight. The skin had been busted open by his eyebrow, his knuckles swollen and splotchy. I had never seen him like this.

"I had it under control," he growled breathlessly.

"You're an idiot," I gasped out, wiping furiously at my eyes. Rock clenched his square jaw and looked away, as if the sight of my tears made him guilty.

It reminded me that outside of the walls of our house, he didn't really hate me.

The Bajul boy leaned against the wall miserably, like a discarded tool. His tail clung around one leg.

He and Rock made eye contact. I stiffened with the realization they might somehow be considering another round.

But then a horn blew in the distance, its echo flooding the town in a wave.

It blew again. And again.

That was the emergency tone.

The chatter of the streets silenced and the bustle froze. There was only one thing left moving—
I heard it.

Soles clapping rapidly, wildly, down the street.

"Sami-Sha hokti!" a voice screamed. "Sami-Sha hokti!"

The man screamed it over and over. He ran past the alley where we stood in a flash. I saw the outline of his mask.

Death-bringer messenger. The raven. Hokti meant death.

"Sami-Sha hokti!"

I looked at Rock, slowly. He stared back with wide pearly eyes. I saw him swallow hard.

We stood frozen with the city.

The chief was dead.

chapters.title: Chapter IV
chapters.content:
My soles pounded the streets as I flew. Each breath stabbed the back of my throat, too fast, too heavy, as I ran for the heart of the city. I still heard the death-bringer's cries in the distance, ringing out with the rhythmic groans of horns behind his voice.

The chief was gone. Flown away.

For many weeks we had known his time had been coming. But it had been one of those things I knew would happen some day—a distant hypothetical that would not be today, or tomorrow, or overmorrow, or any morrow; just some day.

But it was today. Today, Basnil-Sha had no chief.

No heir.

And the clans with no reason to wait anymore.

The moment that the city had held its breath and froze passed as quickly as it came, and the road soon clogged with frantic bustling; women hurrying to gather up their children, men rushing their tasks, others stampeding towards my own destination. I pushed and slid my way between them, and was pushed and ploughed through just as often as if no one registered my existence.

At last, the long, towering hall of the Ts'mi-Ka rose above the chaos like an ark, welcoming floods of people through its open maw. The eaves of its extensive roof—multiple layered plates of shining copper, glass, gold, and Hive shell—were so wide that I was in shade long before I actually entered.

On top of the roof was a massive curling horn with three mouthpieces, the blowers synchronizing. It uttered rhythmic, deep moans that spread through the air for miles and rumbled through the walls, calling mournfully for its people to gather.

The Ts'mi-Ka in all its oversized splendor was known as the ceremonial hall, though it took many forms by the day—temple, school, court. Today, this moment, I knew it hosted the elder council, and I knew Father would be there. I had to find him.

I wasn't sure what I'd do when I found him. I just had to find him. I had to do... something.

The open archway stretched three stories high, reducing every soul it admitted to a mite. The air thickened with oil and hot metal and the concentrated miasma of unwashed humanity as the crowd pushed me past the fire bowls standing resolute at the entry's sides, through the entry, and swallowed me whole.

I kept getting slapped by the agitated lashing of tails. I was pushed and nudged by all sides, and every sort of thing brushed against my skin; hair, fur, leather, cold metal, bare skin, something prickly that made me jump.

A voice cut through the chatter, amplified yet tinny as if funneled through a pipe. The chatter died down as the words took form.

"Jakatena e jakasi sejakai ts'nmau ohn!"

Hello all, and hello leaders, this fateful day!

"Ki'ti-sha Jarg Sami-Asubo."

I am Jarg, the chief's advisor.

I raised a brow. Ts'nkai didn't have R's, but "Jarg" wasn't any Hive English word I recognized.

At last, I found a tiny opening between people's torsos to peer through. At the center of the hall was an elevated ring lined with seats that the elder council occupied, and within that ring rose a higher circular platform the chief's empty chair sat upon.

Beside that empty chair stood the chief's advisor, the man shouting in Ts'nkai, with a great ceremonial beak that extended two feet forward in a pointed curve that sliced the air with the smallest turn of his head.

His strong, aged voice filled the great hall, audible even over the rhythmic, vibrating rumbles of the horn above. In Ts'nkai he declared that all able would set off tomorrow at dawn to the Wind Spiral, a Hive technology zone to the south of Basnil-Sha's territory, for the late chief's Ts'nea deliverance ritual.

He said the chief's successor would be settled between the highest leaders below the council, as he himself could not rise to the position officially; but until the succession was settled, he would act and speak as chief.

The highest leaders in question were the clans' chieftains—one of those being my father—just simply left to their own devices on the matter. Like leaving dogs to settle among themselves to whom the last piece of meat should go. And Father was the kind of dog to die long before he tucked his tail between his legs.

It was as if the council was so bored that they almost wanted war. They had full authority over the clans. They could stop this.

Why wouldn't they?

Jarg's speech drifted to the details of the ritual proceedings planned tomorrow. I turned my focus back onto trying to find Father in the thick maze of people. I pushed through them more aggressively, fighting my way to the front of the crowd closest to the council, where I knew Father would be standing.

I looked for his tall, curling brown horns. Maybe his beak. The way his armor framed his shoulder blades, or a stray lock of grizzled brown hair. Anything I could pick out among the crowd.

At the very front, around the elder council's ring, stood the leader of clan Bajul in his ornate owl mask. His wife and older relatives stood clustered behind him. I shrank and skittered past like a mouse, their beaks and eyes shifting toward me in silence.

I knew Father was on the other side because on the right hand of the head Bajul family was a buffer zone of guards. I slipped in between them, shoulders brushing plated leather armor; they let me pass, as I was tiny and unarmed.

Beyond the guards, I saw my three aunts and two uncles, and their children. I saw my eldest brother Blue. Then, beside him, I saw the tall, hulking build of Father, his curled, sharp eagle beak tipped a shining gold, tilted up towards the council.

I pushed through with muttered greetings towards my cousins, then lunged the last step and snatched Father by his studded wristband.

He jerked slightly as if startled, beak snapping downward and whirling at me, the opaque red screens of his eyeholes flashing in the thin stripes of light with the turn of his head. I flinched.

I remembered just now that I had no plan for what happened next. I spoke before I could hesitate, scrambling for an anchor within whatever words escaped—

"Father, it's already begun," I said, my voice raised over the low chatter of the crowd. "We can't go to war—"

"This is not the place, son," his voice said, low and sharp, the rough edge smoothed by his mask's slight muffle.

"There's no other time to tell you!" I cried. My words came out faster and faster; "Rock is hurt—he was fighting with a Bajul boy—they could have killed each other if I hadn't found them! What then? What if he had died today? Why would you want—"

Father grabbed my upper arm in a steel grip and hauled me towards the wall. There was a small side door. He pulled me through it and we stepped outside in the warm shade, the crowd and speeches muffling behind us when the door shut.

"This is not the place," he growled more vehemently in the semblance of privacy. He took off his mask, but the face behind the sharp eagle beak was no kinder; his browned, scarred visage, pearly white eyes, wild grizzled hair. "If a son of mine has bled today fighting for our name, so he has honored it."

"It was an alleyway brawl!" I snapped in indignation. Then stepped back with a jolt. I couldn't yell at him. Not here. Then he wouldn't listen at all—and this was likely my only chance.

"Father—" I stumbled, more quietly, more shakily, "why would—why do you want us to get hurt? Why is this the best to you?"

"It is our duty to bleed for our name," Father said. "We bleed, or be bled."

"But we don't have to! There's so many alternatives to war I can think of—a trial! A competition! The advisor picking someone! The elders changing the law so that—"

"Bleeding is the trial," Father cut in, stepping towards me, passion curling in his voice. "Bleeding is the competition. The Sami-Asubo will choose the one who stands triumphant. It will be one bearing our name."

"Do you care if we die?!" I cried, throwing my hands out, words coming too fast again. "Your family? Your sons and daughters? Your wife, your brothers and sisters, your nieces and nephews—you would have them all killed for the Mask and say they did well for dying?!"

Father's eyes narrowed by a fraction, holding mine in an unblinking stare. His face had a touch more color, his tail swaying in restrained jerks behind him. He was angry, I knew, and only holding back because the space was still slightly too public.

"You are a naive creature," he said, whisper-quiet, without any of the softness of a whisper. His breath came out in a hiss that cut the air. "And you would watch your tongue. Husekai-Sha will not lie down and submit to the Bajul because some of us are disinclined to fight for our honor."

I stared up at him, dumbfounded.

He was like a boulder. Immovable. Impossible.

I knew now that honor—or my father's version of it—wasn't something exalted. It wasn't something virtuous. It wasn't something strong and powerful.

It was something terrible. Something apathetic. Something loathsome.

"You would sacrifice all of us to your pride," I ground out.

I froze at my mistake. Father became very still.

There was a flash of motion. A burst of pain popped through my nose. I recoiled, cupping one hand over it, watching Father's hand fall back to his side.

Then I ran.

It didn't matter where. I just ran.

I couldn't understand it.

I couldn't understand what it could take for someone to look into his son's eyes and tell him he is worth as much as he bleeds. While in that son's eyes is the unspoken thought, the unspoken plea, Father, I love you. Even if you scare me sometimes and I think the way you think is stupid.

Mother, I love you. You're the only one who can stand me.

My brothers and sisters, I love you too. Even if every day you make me want to rip my hair out and every day I want to kick you all in the shins and every day I daydream about pushing one of you off a rooftop, I love you.

And that's why you can't fight for no reason.

I would never tell them that, though. To lay bare the deep storm in my chest, which made my eyes water if I rehearsed it to myself, was too vulnerable a truth.

I used to wonder if that was part of the problem, not telling them. Now it seemed even if I did go that far, nothing would change.

Because Father was in control of the family.

But the elder council were in control of Father—weren't they?

Someone had to listen. Someone had to.

I still heard, in the distance, the muffled cadence of the council projecting their voices within the Ts'mi-Ka.

I turned back around before the thought's suggestion could finish taking form. My eyes stung, my breaths kept hiccupping and seizing. Warmth oozed from one nostril.

It came away red instead of clear when I wiped it.

I came back under the shade of the Ts'mi-Ka's eaves, now at its backside lined with columns and pipes. I searched for a backdoor. I would speak to the council. They would listen. They had to listen.

The lingering ache in the bridge of my nose seeped deeper into my skull.

I had no mask. My nose was bleeding. My eyes were watering. I did not care how improper it was to approach them looking like this. After the funeral tomorrow, the clan families would start lining up with weapons. I was willing to exhaust every option I could fathom before it happened. There was no time left.

Perhaps this was my own way of fighting. Yet I had been struck for trying to stop the conflict.

Twice.

Why was I the only one trying to stop it?

I found an open doorway in the rear of the Ts'mi-Ka, so tiny compared to the grand archway of the front. I felt like a mouse sneaking through a hole. One armored guard stood by the door, hooked beak turning towards me, scrutinizing, but unmoving.

I stopped.

No one did this. No one went through the back door of the ceremonial hall like this. No one approached the council from behind; or at all, unless they were either summoned or dragged in by guards.

My breaths still shuddered in my chest as I stepped back inside the great hall, caged lanterns throwing meager striped light over the walls, the stone brick floor, the long, empty tables along the walls. The crowd on this side was much more sparse, leaving the stone brick floor vast and open.

It was striped with lines of sunlight. I looked up and saw the slitted openings in the tall, arched ceiling above. Gaps in the roof's layers to let the wind in and smoke out, angled into unpolished copper pipes lining the ceiling and walls like blueish veins to catch the intrusion of acid rain.

My lungs lurched involuntarily. I held my breath for a moment, and continued.

At the base of the council's ring platform, situated at its rear, was a long metal pole. It suspended a huge metal sculpture of a heron, spreading its polished iron wings so high above the elders they nearly touched the ceiling. From the front, it was a terribly prestigious sight; the elevated throne backed by a great metal bird. From my angle at the rear, I felt as though the heron was trying to protect the elders from my approach.

I marched in a straight line and passed under the sculpture. The elders sat with their backs to me, facing the front and the crowds. I saw white and grey braids tumbling down their backsides from out of their antlered headdresses. They wore extravagant robes piled with beads, metal chips, and red-and-blue Hive wire, and their ornate owl masks were adorned with real feathers.

They sat in silence. The bellowing announcements of the advisor had just come to a close. The crowd on the other side was shifting like a sea storm, some filing out.

My voice staggered out of me like a wounded creature. "Jakasami."

That was the formal greeting to the highest leaders.

The elders sat unmoving. Either I had spoken too softly for them to notice me, or they wouldn't acknowledge. My mouth went dry, suddenly very intimidated by the idea of speaking up.

But I was already here.

"Jakasami," I said, louder. My voice sounded much younger with the timid waver in it.

Two heads turned, goggled eyeholes flashing with the pivot. I read the confusion, maybe disdain, in the way their heads tilted slightly when they saw me. I swallowed the tension creeping up my throat. I shouldn't be here.

Committing to mistakes, particularly when I knew they would be mistakes beforehand, had seemingly always been my greatest talent.

Jarg's two-foot beak turned and brandished its point at me. The elders were sitting, but the advisor stood tall on the highest platform, a sharp-edged figure looming high over me.

"Atata ts'naualabu ki'sha i'la?" he asked.

Why do you stand behind us, child?

That was a great question. I suddenly found I didn't have an answer. I hadn't thought about any of this. It had just been the fastest way to get to them.

"Ki ami sa'la?" I said with a sharp, congested sniff.

May I speak to you?

I didn't know if that was the right thing to say. I had already done everything else wrong so far. It was too late to turn back now, but I had the creeping suspicion I was merely making a fool of myself.

But someone had to.

Jarg answered in Ts'nkai through his mask, voice rough from shouting; "Of what matter, boy?"

I answered in Ts'nkai. My voice wobbled pathetically as I scrambled for what remaining scraps of formality were still within my reach. "I am Husekai-Sha, son of Akduk Sami-Husekai Sanika Master Warrior-Hunter-Guardian."

Father had a very long name. I was momentarily impressed at myself for getting every syllable out in one breath, and continued. "I want to ask if there can be an alternative to allowing the head clan families to go to war."

"It reflects poorly on us that you would speak to a child," I heard one elder grumble at Jarg.

"It is his war," Jarg responded simply, beak turning towards whoever among the ring had spoken, then back down at me.

"You do not want to fight the Bajul?" Jarg asked me.

"I don't want anyone to fight anyone," I said. "War isn't necessary, is it?"

"Necessary," Jarg echoed.

I blinked.

"No," Jarg continued. "But it is what the chieftains want."

"But why? Can't your council forbid it?" I burst out.

"Yes," Jarg said. "But is that necessary?"

I blinked again, swallowing as a hot rush of fury jolted through my veins.

"Yes," I said, too firmly. "What do you get from allowing us to destroy each other?"

The man cocked his head. He looked uncomfortably like a real bird for a moment. Something in his tick of silence—in that small change of posture—made me shrink, because I didn't know what he was thinking.

It was the same question I had just asked Father. But I knew how to read Father.

"I'm not going to fight," I suddenly dared add.

"Insolent child," another elder growled. Jarg hummed, an odd, muffled tone ricocheting within his mask that didn't sound condescending.

"Very well," Jarg said—in English. I replayed the word in my mind to test if I'd heard him right. It was incredibly informal of him.

I found myself unable to generate a response. I didn't know what to do anymore.

"Anka dun ite," Jarg said.

Begone, boy.

He turned around to face the front again. The two elders that had been eyeing our interaction also retired their attention. I no longer existed.

I stood there, staring in disbelief.

I had thought for a moment that the advisor had almost been listening. At the very least, he had engaged me on some level. That was more than I'd expected.

It almost made his dismissal even more crushing. Like I'd actually had a chance. Maybe if I had done it right. If I had done anything I just did right.

The hall suddenly felt enormous. I felt like I was a speck on the bottom of someone's shoe. Blood was drying under my nose and flavoring the back of my throat. My stomach turned.

I spun around and ran the way I'd come. My footsteps made a rapid, childish pitter-patter on the stone, and again was I a mouse sneaking through a hole as I pushed through the back door.

A mouse.

That was all I was in the face of such immovable ideology, of such authoritative apathy—in the face of a bizarre system that, by some enigmatic force, appeared to accommodate everyone but myself.

Or perhaps it was I that did not accommodate the system. Perhaps I, somehow, was the one wrong for not wanting my family to die in a pointless clan war that wouldn't even have to happen. I was the only one afraid. I was the only one trying to stop it. And it seemed as though I was the only one who saw it for it was.

Pointless.

Why?

Did I need to be older to understand how it made sense, or did everyone else need to be younger?

I had run home to find the mansion nearly empty; only the servants, and Mother administering herbs to Rock in the washroom. The house rarely saw such silence. It made every room far too large, the ceilings too high. My ears rang as if to fill the silence, and I moved ceaselessly as if to fill the stillness.

I paced endlessly in the first living room like a caged animal. Nausea sat like a rope around my throat, and my heart still raced in my chest as if it hadn't realized I'd stopped running half an hour ago. It would rebel and skip each time I attempted a painfully slow, deliberate breath. If I held still, I only became more aware of it.

Nothing was simple anymore. The overcomplication of the outside seemed to have followed me in. Never before had I found myself repeatedly distracted, annoyed each time, by the loud, extravagant excess of everything—mammoth horns on the walls, painted in bright, loud tessellates; the centered seating arrangement too big with too many patterns and tassels on materials too expensive for mere chairs; ornate mantles along the walls heaped with trophies, the walls themselves lined endlessly with prestigious masks; the patterned rugs over patterned tile; the sunlit gleam of unnecessary shell plating around the window frames, and the ceiling was a complicated tangle of layered ribs of bone and lacquered wood plated with decorative brass, none of it necessary for structural support.

I suddenly found my forehead leaned against one wall, sucking in long, deep breaths that dragged against the ghost of a gag in the back of my throat.

It had always been like this. I didn't know where my body had gotten the idea that cramping and throwing up cured nerves.

I didn't know what to do.

I heard the front door creak open, close. Light footsteps in the entry.

I turned and saw Howl walking into the living room, her course angled towards a hall, but she stopped when she noticed me.

"You look pale," she said. She looked frazzled herself; more flyaway locks of her brown hair than usual, a squared tension of her shoulders that bunched the sleeves of her summer dress.

"Yeah." I glanced away. I didn't expect Howl to keep looking at me.

"What happened to your nose?" she asked.

"Nothing."

Howl tilted her head just short of either a nod or a shrug. I could not determine whether the scrutiny in her lingering attention was suspicion or concern. Then she turned and eased back into a stiff, purposed trajectory.

"Wait—" I lurched after her. She stopped again.

"Do you think this really has to happen?" I asked. My voice sounded small to my own ears.

Howl looked at me again, one brow tugged, a graceful hand smoothing a tress behind her ear.

"What?" Howl said.

"War," I murmured, bracing my arm against the wall. "It doesn't have to happen, does it?"

"What do you mean?"

She looked genuinely confused. I paused for a moment, trying to part something logical from the tension in my chest.

"It's only happening because Father wants it to—that's it."

That twitch played in her brows again, the wrinkle between them deepening. "We can't argue with him."

"No. But we don't have to listen, either. He can't make us fight, can he?"

"But he will," Howl said. "He'll shame us if we don't."

"Shame won't kill you. Death will," I said, my hands coming alive with violent gesticulations in the air. "We don't have to fight. You don't hear the Bajul's chieftain prattling on about the honor of bleeding for his people. They probably don't even want to fight, either. It's just Father making it happen because he refuses any alternative!"

Howl looked away with a sudden jerk, as if afraid someone might hear me. She came a little closer, voice lowered into a hissing whisper, "You wouldn't speak dishonor of Father in his own house."

"Maybe I care about you all a lot more than Father does!" I yelled, simultaneously relieved and disappointed that Father was not home to hear those words ricochet off the walls.

I hadn't expected to say that. I didn't want to deal with Howl's response to that, so I continued, quieter.

"If we don't listen and don't fight, he can't make us—so we don't have to die, and we can all figure out a different way to decide the next chief." I sucked in a breath, listening to my voice degrade into a frustrated plea. "Don't you get it? All we have to do is not listen."

"I—" Her voice sounded strained. I wasn't sure if she was tongue-tied, or genuinely emotional.

A long moment ticked by, filled with paranoid pivots of her head, adjustments to the lay of her hair, tugs at her dress.

"I guess it makes sense in theory," she murmured.

I suddenly felt so light I hardly felt the rug under my boots. Someone—someone older than me, someone in this house—was listening.

"We just have to convince our brothers," I said quickly. "It'll be hard, but—"

"Convince our brothers not to fight!" Howl exclaimed, shaking her head with a laugh devoid of mirth. "Perhaps when the sun goes black!"

I got an idea.

"Howl, what does Clan Bajul stand for?"

She blinked, caught off guard.

"Wisdom?" she said.

"And what does wisdom mean?"

Her face tightened in suspicion. "Doing things in a smart way?"

I shrugged. My own definition would have been about the same. "And what does Clan Husekai-Sha stand for?"

"Honor."

"What is honor?" I asked. I wondered if I was pushing too hard with the rapid-fire of questions, but—

Howl paused, as if she'd heard the word so many times that she had to recall its original meaning. "Doing... things... with dignity and fairness?"

"Sure. Whatever. Do you see the difference?"

Howl squinted.

"What's your point?" she asked, voice clipped.

"My point is... bias aside, which clan would actually rule the tribe better?"

Her face darkened. I shifted on my feet with an immediate flare of uncertainty.

But there was no mistake that I would start without finishing.

"What are you saying?" Howl demanded.

"I'm saying," I uttered slowly, as if to delay whatever aftermath, "wouldn't Bajul's rule be more pragmatic anyway?"

"Where'd you hear that word?"

"I've known that word since I was eleven!"

"You're saying it'd be better if Clan Bajul took the Mask instead of Husekai-Sha?" Howl cried, a raised note between disbelief and offense.

Offense.

Pride.

Like Father.

"That's too far, Fling," she said, shaking her head slowly, drifting closer to the entry of the hall. "I don't know who put these ideas in your head, who you've spoken to, but that's too far."

She turned and left.

I stood still.

I turned suddenly, allowing my knuckles to strike the wall with half-force, and I cried out.

It was night.

The chief's funeral ritual march would be at dawn tomorrow.

I had hid in my room the rest of the day. Hid from Father. Hid from everyone. My stomach ached—empty, yet still too sour to consider swiping whatever remained of dinner.

My looking glass reflected me with my hand pressed against my gut. The mirror was built for someone twice my height, framed with ornate swirls and eddies of polished brass. I had never asked for it to be in my room; the most use it saw was when I flexed my skinny arms naked if I got distracted in the middle of dressing. In those moments, it told me I was anything I pleased.

Now it told me what I was. I wasn't used to the look on my face I saw now. It looked like pale stone. Like I was half someone else.

Someone both the mirror and I didn't have a name for.

The others wanted that name to be Warrior.

Fling Husekai Fighter-Warrior.

I had been training with staff and hand-to-hand combat all of my life, as was the custom; and on a ceremonial testing day, I had landed a single strike on the chief in the time before he had fallen ill. That had granted me the name Fighter. But that was all I was.

I had been born too small. I had barely survived the first three years of my life; Mother and Father told me my upbringing had been one medical catastrophe after the other, each related to whatever malfunction had stunted my growth. By now, I had stabilized into a thirteen-year-old boy with the stature of a nine-year-old one.

And I was thin. Not terribly so, but my elbows were sharp, and my arms and legs were like sticks—I had mostly grown out of my infant plumpness, but some still stuck to my cheeks like a stubborn last word.
My eyes were still large and round, solid white, slightly pearlescent like oil on water when the light hit them just so. My horns had emerged about a year ago, but had only recently begun to take shape. I had not the barest hint of a chin or chest hair. Or even underarm hair. The only hair I had was two thin, near-invisible blonde brows, my backstripe—some called it a spinecrest, the strip of hair that continued from my nape down my back—and a wild head of curls haloed with frizz that made me permanently look like I had just strutted through a windstorm.

And they wanted this to be a warrior.

The mirror disagreed. The mirror was not very imaginative today. I could not tell by the honesty of its reflection whether it was defending me or mocking me.

"Fling Husekai-Fighter," I declared authoritatively to the boy in the glass, "you are now a warrior, and you're going to fight for your family's honor so that you may see one of your brothers or sisters on the throne."

The boy in the glass giggled as if I'd told a joke so terrible he laughed only out of pity.

Then he looked utterly crushed.

data.author: rockingwithrocky
data.summary: This story is told from the point of view of a young boy growing up in a world that feels modern, with a subtle 90s influence. At its core, it’s about the bond between him and his grandpa, who introduces him to root beer something small that turns into a meaningful connection filled with memories and stories. The beginning focuses on everyday life, their shared moments, and the simple comfort of being a kid. But as the story goes on, it starts to explore heavier topics like the loss of his grandpa, school bullying, and racism, all seen through the boy’s perspective. What starts as a basic story about a kid’s life slowly becomes more emotional, showing how he deals with growing up, facing unfairness in the world, and holding onto the lessons and memories his grandpa gave him.

chapters.content:
everyone's probably seen Willy Wonka before.
I’ve watched Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory more times than I can count.
 And the remake of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.
When I was younger, they just felt like different versions of the same story.
But watching them again last year, something felt different.
Every kid who won… every story…
It always came down to the same thing.
What they did when they had something worth sharing.
It was always chocolate.
That’s what brought me back to when I was a teenager. I was around 16 and i couldnt drive but this brought me back to a particular part of my life so i was going to visit my grandpa particularly stay the night I couldn't drive so my mother had to drive me i was staying at my grandpas i can recall my mom taking me because i knew my dad couldn't bc he always worked and if he came home he usually ignored us and just watched tv or read a random newspaper. So i was going to my grandpas and my mother drove me and dropped me off and handed me my overnight bag and i could see my grandpa outside on the porch having a smoke and my mother didn't just leave me she insisted to walk up with me she never usually let me be when i wanted to hang out at my grandpas even if i just wanted to stay for the day she always had a bond with her dad my grandpa was from my mom side i never went to see my grandmas because she had passed before i could never say a thing but when i got up to my grandpa without hesitating he wanted to give me a hug and staring back at my mother she gave me the look of either do it or get a time out so i hugged my grandpa but i could smell that cigarette all over his body. Me and my grandpa were close basically like brothers from another mother but of course we had differences of interest. So we headed inside and I put my bag in the bedroom where i would be staying and i came out to see my grandpa and mother chatting it up so i just sat at my grandpas tv my grandpa didn't really have any new tech so he had one of those old cable boxes and like possibly what looks to be the cheapest tv that was on the market so i watched whatever i could fine on and watched it after about a few hours my mother finally decided to leave and let me and my grandpa be so i saw her leaving out the door i said my goodbyes and off she went once my mom left my grandpa went out to take another cigarette break so i just went back to watch more tv when my grandpa came back in he asked me if i wanted a drink i ask him what he shad and he said he got rootbeer that why i talk about willy wonka because my grandpa was basically wonka when it comes to owning rootbeer because he was stacked .
